title: AI for Wind Energy Systems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI Technologies for Renewable Energy Systems and Intelligent Grid Optimization
d6d8adf202aed253644ed73dead2e3bcff980f7b.abstract: <jats:p>The renewable energy is being transformed by Artificial Intelligence (AI) to create smarter, efficient, and adaptive wind systems. AI forecasts the wind using machine learning and neural networks and optimizes the performance of turbines and minimizes costs related to maintenance using predictive analytics. These inventions assist the operators in predicting the changes, setting the turbines, and reducing downtime. Urban deployment of AI facilitates the seamless synchronization of mass-scaled wind energy with smart grids as well as the systems of IoT. It balances loads dynamically, for instance, it trades energy in real time and improves stability in the grid. Heavy reliance on fossil fuels and extensive reliance on carbon emissions and fossil fuels can be reduced through the implementation of AI-driven systems that enhance energy efficiency, reliability, and sustainability through the integration of renewable sources, storage, and intelligent control.</jats:p>

title: AI for Wind Energy Systems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI Technologies for Renewable Energy Systems and Intelligent Grid Optimization
4f4dc990deb9ecb4d79f7eb21160b4d6a0c8d4aa.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the wind energy sector, marking a major step toward sustainable and intelligent societies. As global energy demands rise and carbon reduction becomes urgent, AI offers powerful tools to enhance the efficiency, reliability, and scalability of wind power systems. Through technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, digital twins, and predictive analytics, AI optimizes turbine design, predictive maintenance, load forecasting, and smart grid integration. By leveraging big data from sensors, meteorological sources, and operational parameters, AI enables accurate wind prediction, timely fault detection, and real-time performance optimization. Additionally, AI-driven systems play an emerging role in urban wind integration by improving micro-wind utilization, energy storage, and distributed generation within smart cities. The chapter also addresses economic feasibility, environmental sustainability, and ethical implications of AI-enabled wind energy applications.</jats:p>

title: Aspect–Sentiment Triplet Extraction in Low-Resource Odia Language Using a Tri-Channel GCN
container-title: ACM Transactions on Asian and Low-Resource Language Information Processing
59165272f90e12f65ea2a5d353109678a1feea6a.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    With the proliferation of digital platforms and smartphones, users increasingly express opinions in their native languages through online reviews. However, fine-grained sentiment analysis for such low-resource languages remains underexplored, as most Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA) methods target resource-rich languages such as English. To address this gap, we present Odia-TriGCN, a hybrid framework for Aspect Sentiment Triplet Extraction in the low-resource Odia language. It integrates tree-distance relations (dependency and constituent trees), syntactic dependencies, and biaffine semantic attention to capture rich structural and semantic cues. The model further leverages auxiliary features from an Odia news corpus and cross-lingual supervision using an Odia–English parallel corpus. We also incorporate a
                    <jats:bold>customized dependency parser</jats:bold>
                    trained on manually annotated data following the Universal Dependencies (UD) scheme, to obtain consistent head-dependent relations. Additionally, we extend the existing Odia ABSA dataset and introduce
                    <jats:bold>Odia-Triplet</jats:bold>
                    , a manually annotated dataset comprising aspect-opinion-sentiment triplets. Experiments across five domains show that Odia-TriGCN outperforms the strongest compared non-LLM baseline in each domain by 5.6 to 7.1 absolute F1 points. The framework is further evaluated in cross-lingual (Odia→Hindi, Odia→Bengali) and code-mixed (Odia–English, Odia–Hindi–English, Odia–Bengali–English) settings, providing further evidence of its applicability in multilingual contexts.
                  </jats:p>

title: Impact of inoculum effect on in vitro activity of intermittent and continuous piperacillin-tazobactam infusion against ESBL-producing Escherichia coli in a hollow-fiber infection model
container-title: Microbiology Spectrum
f6976a53f13352681d179f4ad8625f6e55828a7a.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title/>
                    <jats:p>
                      Use of piperacillin-tazobactam (TZP) in the treatment of severe extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Escherichia coli</jats:italic>
                      (ESBL-EC) infections is controversial. Two features may explain treatment failures: the inoculum effect and suboptimal pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) target attainment, particularly in critically ill patients. To study the combined impact of the inoculum effect and a PK/PD optimization on the
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">in vitro</jats:italic>
                      efficacy of TZP against ESBL-EC infections. Five-day hollow-fiber infection model simulating TZP pharmacokinetics in critically ill patients was performed: two TZP infusion regimens (4/0.5 g q6h over 30 min, and 16/2 g q24h continuous infusion), three ESBL-EC clinical strains:
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">1146</jats:italic>
                      (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">bla</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>CTX-M-15</jats:sub>
                      , MIC = 2 mg/L),
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">3383</jats:italic>
                      (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">bla</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>CTX-M-15</jats:sub>
                      +
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">bla</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>TEM-1</jats:sub>
                      , MIC = 4 mg/L), and
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">2262</jats:italic>
                      (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">bla</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>CTX-M-15</jats:sub>
                      +
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">bla</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>OXA-1</jats:sub>
                      , MIC = 8 mg/L), and two initial inocula (5 and 7 log
                      <jats:sub>10</jats:sub>
                      CFU/mL). Intermittent infusion was associated with systematic bacterial regrowth within 24 h, consistent with failure to reach the 100%fT >4× MIC threshold. Continuous infusion resulted in undetectable bacterial count for the strains
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">3383</jats:italic>
                      (MIC = 4 mg/L, low inoculum) and
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">1146</jats:italic>
                      (MIC = 2 mg/L, low and high inocula). For strain
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">3383</jats:italic>
                      , the inoculum effect was demonstrated by total bacterial killing in continuous infusion with low inoculum, whereas early regrowth (>10 log
                      <jats:sub>10</jats:sub>
                      CFU/mL) with resistance emergence (MIC > 256 mg/L) was observed with high inoculum. Strain
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">2262</jats:italic>
                      (MIC = 8 mg/L) exhibited systematic treatment failure regardless of infusion mode or inoculum size. Continuous infusion of TZP may be considered as a carbapenem-sparing agent in ESBL-EC infection with a TZP MIC ≤ 2 mg/L regardless of inoculum, or a TZP MIC of 4 mg/L at low inoculum. TZP should not be used for strains with an MIC of 8 mg/L or suspected OXA-1 co-production, irrespective of the infusion mode.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>IMPORTANCE</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Infections caused by extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Escherichia coli</jats:italic>
                      represent a growing therapeutic challenge, particularly in critically ill patients. Carbapenems remain the reference treatment, but their overuse drives resistance emergence. Piperacillin-tazobactam is a potential carbapenem-sparing agent, but its clinical efficacy remains debated, partly due to the inoculum effect (a reduction in antibiotic activity at high bacterial densities) and suboptimal dosing regimens. Using a hollow-fiber infection model simulating the pharmacokinetics of critically ill patients, this study demonstrates that continuous infusion of piperacillin-tazobactam can overcome the inoculum effect under specific conditions, defined by the MIC of the infecting strain and the estimated bacterial density. These findings support a stratified approach to piperacillin-tazobactam use in severe ESBL-producing
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">E. coli</jats:italic>
                      infections, based on MIC, inoculum size, and β-lactamase profile, and may help clinicians identify patients who could safely receive piperacillin-tazobactam instead of a carbapenem.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Psychotherapy is a primary treatment for many mental health conditions, yet the dynamic interplay among therapist behaviors, client responses, and the therapeutic relationship remains difficult to disentangle at scale. Traditional process research relies on labor-intensive human coding, limiting the ability to model moment-to-moment therapeutic dynamics across large datasets.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to develop and validate a computational framework for modeling therapist-client interaction processes and to examine how therapist behaviors and relational qualities relate to client self-disclosure and emotional expression in psychotherapy sessions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We developed automated assessment pipelines using large language models (LLMs) to measure therapist behaviors (empathy or exploration), relational quality (rapport), and client outcomes (self-disclosure, self-directed negative emotion, or outward-directed negative emotion). Model-generated scores were validated against human annotations. We then applied these measures to approximately 2000 hours of psychotherapy transcripts from the Alexander Street corpus. This yielded an estimation sample of 119,233 client utterances from 1573 sessions and 37 clients. Because utterances are nested within sessions and sessions within clients, we estimated a saturated multivariate structural equation model with SEs clustered at the session level. Results were confirmed in a multilevel regression model with random intercepts for session and client.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Following comparative validation of 6 candidate language models, automated measures showed good to excellent agreement with human annotations (intraclass correlation coefficient [ICC]=0.60-0.81) for rapport (ICC=0.81), self-disclosure (ICC=0.78), empathy components (ICC=0.60-0.75), and emotion measurements (ICC=0.66-0.80). Structural equation modeling analyses revealed that therapist empathy and exploration were each associated with increased client disclosure (empathy: β=.086, 95% CI 0.078-0.095; exploration: β=.086, 95% CI 0.078-0.094; both P<.001) and increased expression of self-directed negative emotions, comprising sadness, anxiety, fear, and depression (empathy: β=.118, 95% CI 0.110-0.127; exploration: β=.078, 95% CI 0.070-0.087; both P<.001). Both behaviors were also associated with reduced expressions of enjoyment (empathy: β=–.037; exploration: β=–.041; both P<.001). Surprisingly, rapport in the prior session showed no association with client self-disclosure or negative emotion expression.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study demonstrates that LLM-based measurement combined with structural modeling can capture core therapeutic processes at scale. Empathy and exploration showed small but consistent turn-level associations with client disclosure and emotional expression, whereas prior-session rapport did not show a robust association. These findings provide a computational foundation for precision modeling of psychotherapy processes and may offer actionable insights for scalable therapist training and AI-supported clinical education systems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Reduced-order statistical model for optical vortex singularity displacement in atmospheric turbulence
container-title: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
9b5d20a35977c346d5bef26afeee92d7b8db6ae9.abstract: <jats:p>The propagation of optical vortex beams through atmospheric turbulence leads to stochastic displacement and structural evolution of phase singularities, with important implications for singular optics and free-space optical communication. We present a reduced-order, semi-empirical statistical model for the ensemble-averaged radial displacement of vortex singularities, which decomposes the normalized displacement into two physically distinct contributions: a first-order (tilt-like) term that follows the classical Kolmogorov exponent, and a topology-dependent splitting term that grows with topological charge. The model is validated quantitatively against high-resolution numerical simulation of phase-screen turbulence and angular-spectrum propagation, with residuals, goodness-of-fit measures, and hold-out errors reported over its stated range of validity. Phase contour maps and intensity profiles further illustrate the turbulence-induced distortion of the helical phase structure and the emergence of multiple unit-charge singularities for higher-order modes. The framework offers a practical basis for assessing vortex beam stability in free-space optical systems.</jats:p>

title: Mobile Technology Engagement Among Caregivers and Its Implications for Childhood Antibiotic Stewardship in Northern Vietnam: Mixed Methods Community-Based Study
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
c305776fc7a17d9be4a5588ca0d1f0bbb7e0a81d.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In Vietnam, antibiotic use without involvement of health care professionals is common in the community, despite the legal requirement for a prescription. In low- and middle-income countries, mobile health (mHealth) is perceived as having the potential to improve community health care at low cost.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this study, we aimed to explore the relationship between mobile phone ownership and health-seeking behaviors among caregivers of children aged 5 years or younger to inform the design of an mHealth intervention to improve antibiotic use practices in the community.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A convergent mixed methods approach combined a cross-sectional household survey and in-depth interviews (IDIs). We surveyed 450 households with children aged 5 years or younger and interviewed caregivers about their health-seeking behaviors and how they engage with mobile technology to inform their health care decisions and antibiotic use. Qualitative data were collected through IDIs and focus group discussions (FGDs) with a purposive sample of household survey respondents. Data collection was conducted between June and September 2023 at 2 sites: 1 urban and 1 rural area in a northern province of Vietnam. Factors associated with using mobile phones to seek health care information were identified through multivariable logistic regression and thematic analysis. Quantitative and qualitative findings were then integrated to provide contextual insights.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>For the quantitative household survey, 450 of 460 approached households completed the survey. For the qualitative component, 38 of 60 approached caregivers participated in 4 FGDs and 6 IDIs. Almost all households had an internet connection (444/450, 98.7%, 95% CI 97.1%-99.4%). While 80.2% (308/384, 95% CI 75.9%-83.9%) of caregivers used mobile devices to access child health care information, only 27.1% (29/107, 95% CI 19.6%-36.2%) reported using the internet to obtain antibiotic-related information. Older caregivers (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.65, 95% CI 0.43-0.99) and caregivers living in the urban area (aOR 0.45, 95% CI 0.24-0.85) were less likely to seek health-related information online using mobile devices than younger or rural caregivers, respectively. In contrast, a higher level of caregiver education was significantly associated with more favorable engagement in online health information–seeking behavior (aOR 2.73, 95% CI 1.61-4.61). Caregivers demonstrated highly active and intentional online information-seeking behaviors, driven by a strong desire to enhance their knowledge and confidence in making childcare and treatment decisions. Qualitative findings highlighted a need for trustworthy, professionally supported digital health platforms tailored to child health and antibiotic use.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study highlights caregivers’ health care information–seeking behaviors and engagement with digital technologies for antibiotic-related information, demonstrating the potential of mobile phones to support antibiotic-related decision-making and improve antibiotic use practices. These findings provide insights to inform the design of context-appropriate mHealth interventions to support caregivers in making decisions about antibiotic use.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Stuttering Treatment Priorities and Clinical Challenges Across the Lifespan in Iran: A Mixed-Methods Study of Speech-Language Pathologists
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
4689889123860e45750d2786a63d56293b4303c2.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study provided an initial exploration of Iranian speech-language pathologists' (SLPs') treatment priorities, reported intervention approaches, and perceived clinical challenges for stuttering across the lifespan.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Seventy-four Iranian SLPs completed a Farsi online survey ranking three treatment aspects aligned with the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health—overt stuttering behaviors, reactions to stuttering, and communication participation—across preschool, school-age/adolescent, and adult clients. They also rated intervention use frequency and described clinical challenges. Quantitative data were analyzed using nonparametric tests, qualitative responses were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis, and exploratory mixed-methods integration linked clinician priority profiles to qualitative themes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Across all three age groups, clinicians ranked overt behaviors highest, reactions intermediate, and communication participation lowest. This hierarchy did not shift meaningfully across age groups and was not associated with education or clinical experience. Qualitative themes highlighted pressure for fluency, relapse, acceptance, generalization difficulties, emotional burden, and clinician uncertainty. Exploratory participant-level integration showed that clinicians with stronger fluency-anchored profiles appeared less likely to describe challenges related to relapse, generalization, and pressure for fluency.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this initial sample, clinicians' self-reported priorities remained strongly oriented toward overt speech behaviors despite contemporary multidimensional models of stuttering. Findings should be regarded as exploratory and as a basis for larger replication studies. Findings highlight the need for training and service models that more explicitly integrate participation, counseling-informed support, and stigma-responsive care across the lifespan.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Clinical Interpretation and Structured Reporting of Velopharyngeal Magnetic Resonance Imaging: A Framework for Multidisciplinary Decision Making
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
1108a9c74c2bb18f13f24e47f4b208b3a289c4cc.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables direct visualization of the velopharyngeal (VP) mechanism, including the soft palate, pharyngeal walls, adenoid tissue, and levator veli palatini (LVP) musculature. As VP MRI becomes more integrated into multidisciplinary craniofacial care, speech-language pathologists (SLPs) are increasingly involved in image interpretation. However, structured guidance for translating MRI findings into clinically relevant multidisciplinary decision making remains limited. This study presents a clinically oriented framework for interpretation of VP MRI and introduces a structured reporting approach to support consistent documentation and interdisciplinary communication.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A literature-informed, consensus-based framework for interpreting VP MRI was developed. Scoping review first identified MRI-derived anatomic variables relevant to VP function. These variables were organized into interpretive domains through multidisciplinary discussion among SLPs, surgeons, and radiologists. The framework was operationalized into structured reporting templates for speech-language pathology and radiology documentation and prospectively piloted in clinical VP MRI cases.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The resulting framework organizes interpretation across five domains: VP proportional relationships, LVP morphology and function, VP closure dynamics, additional structural contributors, and articulatory context. Structured templates integrate quantitative measurements, qualitative observations, and clinical synthesis. The framework was successfully applied across pilot cases, supporting consistent interpretation and documentation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This framework provides clinicians with a practical method for integrating VP MRI observations with speech assessment to enhance clinical reasoning and inform multidisciplinary treatment planning for individuals with VP dysfunction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Supplemental Material:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>

title: A TWO-HIDDEN-LAYER SHALLOW NEURAL NETWORK FOR SOLVING THE NONLINEAR RUMOR SPREADING MODEL
container-title: Journal of Mechanics in Medicine and Biology
e1d2afadfd1c534d81d0bb8992383cca2a8d3d6e.abstract: <jats:p>Motive: The design of a shallow neural network with two hidden layers is presented for solving a mathematical rumor-spreading model, which is divided into exposed, stiflers, and ignorant. Method: A structure of shallow neural networks is designed using two hidden layers, taking log- sigmoid and radial basis functions with 14 and 26 neurons. The optimization is performed by the Levenberg–Marquardt backpropagation, which is a robust technique for nonlinear models. An Euler’s scheme is executed to obtain the dataset, which reduces mean squared error by separating the data into testing (12%), training (75%), and validation (13%). Results: The exactness of the solver is obtained through the comparison of results, best validation values, and small absolute error values. In addition, the accuracy of the designed shallow neural structure is assessed by the histogram error, regression values, and transition of state routines.</jats:p>

title: Pentosan polysulfate sodium limits pulmonary inflammation in a SARS-CoV-2 mouse model
container-title: Microbiology Spectrum
93ffcacb668992c3684105823afacb0518071004.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title/>
                    <jats:p>
                      Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection remains prevalent globally, causing severe pulmonary inflammation and mortality in up to 10% of patients. While the introduction of effective vaccines has substantially reduced the number of severe coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) cases, there are currently few available therapeutics that have been developed. Pentosan polysulfate sodium (PPS) has been shown to possess potent anti-inflammatory activity in influenza infection and allergen-induced rhinitis models and was recently demonstrated to inhibit SARS-CoV-2 infection
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">in vitro</jats:italic>
                      . As such, we hypothesized that PPS may represent an attractive therapeutic that could be utilized for SARS-CoV-2 infection and COVID-19. Using the K18-hACE2 mouse model of SARS-CoV-2 infection, we administered PPS (6 mg/kg) from either 1 (early) or 3 (late) days post-infection via intranasal instillation and then examined the efficacy in mitigating viral-induced inflammation and severe disease outcomes. We found that the early administration of PPS was accompanied by significant improvements in weight loss, clinical disease presentation, and neutrophilic airway inflammation. Early PPS administration also significantly reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production at both the mRNA and protein levels while having no impact on viral titers or interferon and antiviral gene expression. Histologically, early treatment significantly prevented severe pulmonary inflammation and tissue remodeling. Comparatively, late administration of PPS worsened weight loss and clinical disease presentation following SARS-CoV-2 infection. Moreover, late administration was unable to prevent significant increases in pro-inflammatory cytokines and was further associated with significantly downregulated antiviral-associated genes. Histological examination also showed no protection in the late PPS administered groups. Taken together, these findings underscore the significance of time-dependent administration and demonstrate the therapeutic potential of PPS for treatment of SARS-CoV-2-induced inflammation.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>IMPORTANCE</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) continues to cause infections globally, with most cases resulting in mild to moderate disease outcomes. However, approximately 10% of patients experience virally induced hyperinflammation leading to poor outcomes. As such, new or repurposed therapeutics need to be rapidly implemented to address this urgent medical need. Here, we show that pentosan polysulfate sodium (PPS) is a leading Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved therapeutic that significantly mitigates SARS-CoV-2-induced pulmonary inflammation. Critically, timing of PPS during the infection establishment and progression is critical for PPS efficacy, highlighting time-dependent responses that must be considered for further human clinical implementation. The findings from this study demonstrate that PPS holds significant promise as a repurposed anti-inflammatory agent for SARS-CoV-2 infection.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Population pharmacokinetics of piperacillin based on multicenter data to support model-informed precision dosing in critically ill women
container-title: Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy
a03c20349df948ad9f7b4247caaf02cb9613015f.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title/>
                    <jats:p>
                      Sex-specific differences in pharmacokinetics are increasingly recognized as clinically relevant, yet most population pharmacokinetic models for antibiotics have been developed in predominantly male populations with limited transferability to female patients. This study aimed to develop and externally evaluate a population pharmacokinetic model of piperacillin specifically for critically ill women to support model-informed precision dosing (MIPD). A total of 923 samples from 165 critically ill women (from four previously published studies) receiving piperacillin/tazobactam were analyzed. The data set was randomly split into a training set (80%) and an independent external evaluation set (20%). Non-linear mixed-effects modeling was employed based on the training data using NONMEM, and covariates were identified using stepwise covariate modeling with cross-validation. Prediction accuracy and bias were quantified using the median prediction error (MDPE) and the median absolute prediction error (MDAPE) in an MIPD scenario. Model predictions for future concentrations were generated both
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">a priori</jats:italic>
                      and through Bayesian forecasting based on one prior sample. A two-compartment model provided the best fit for the data. Clearance was significantly affected by renal function estimated by the Cockcroft–Gault equation, along with procalcitonin and serum albumin. The external evaluation demonstrated strong predictive performance with very low systematic bias. In the MIPD scenario,
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">a priori</jats:italic>
                      predictions exhibited good predictive performance (MDPE < |5.2|%, MDAPE < 33.4%), which substantially improved with Bayesian forecasting (MDPE < |3.2|%, MDAPE < 19.1%). A female-specific population pharmacokinetic model of piperacillin was developed and externally validated, demonstrating robust predictive performance and clear benefits for Bayesian forecasting.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: GBDT-based rapid evaluation model for laser propagation in atmospheric turbulence
container-title: Applied Optics
d367b4f387ec2d3d841f12fe31b3f2c5b574752b.abstract: <jats:p>To address beam quality degradation and enable rapid evaluation in turbulent laser atmospheric transmission, a GBDT regression model is proposed using real experimental data. Trained on 1000 samples, it employs launch diameter and refractive-index structure constant values at four path points to jointly predict the 63.2% and 83.9% encircled-energy radii of the long-exposure spot and the corresponding beam expansion factors. SHAP is further employed for interpretation. The model achieves coefficients of determination above 0.95 and lower relative errors than Lasso, random forest, XGBoost, and MLP, while retaining lightweight, real-time performance with 146,000 parameters and a 4.5 µs single-sample inference.</jats:p>

title: Tangential-sagittal decomposition-combination design method for a large-field anamorphic extreme ultraviolet lithography projection objective
container-title: Applied Optics
faababb9fbcb42568533f58a2d34fcac6b9285bd.abstract:
<jats:p>Extreme ultraviolet lithography (EUVL) for 2 nm and below node is impacted by
					the projection objective performance. Anamorphic projection objectives
					have been employed for high-numerical aperture (NA=0.55) EUVL systems. Existing design
					methods for anamorphic projection objectives construct initial
					structures from coaxial subsystems and have been demonstrated for
					relatively small fields of view. The freeform surfaces during
					optimization have not matched the optical characteristics of
					anamorphic systems. A novel tangential-sagittal
					decomposition-combination (TSDC) design method, to our knowledge, is
					proposed for an anamorphic initial structure. By adopting an
					anamorphic XY polynomial freeform surface during optimization, the
					final system has a root mean square wavefront error of less than
					0.92 nm and a maximum distortion of less than 0.48 nm.
					Its image-side field of view reaches 26mm×1mm, doubling the field width reported in
					previous studies.</jats:p>

title: Assistive Monitoring and Support Quality in Cognitive Disability Care
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Advancing Disability Inclusion Through AI
db5a35fb0006e94c20dd6e10396daf586441ad4d.abstract: <jats:p>Disability support organisations must maintain safety while supporting independence for people with cognitive disabilities. Traditional supervision relies on routine observation, manual documentation, and reactive intervention, which often creates workload pressure and inconsistent outcomes. Intelligent monitoring systems provide continuous behavioural observation and automated alerts. Many organisations fail to achieve measurable improvement because monitoring data is not integrated into staff workflows, response responsibility, and performance evaluation. This chapter examines monitoring as an organisational decision integration challenge using implementation science, socio-technical theory, and technology adoption theory, explains how monitoring signals influence staff decisions, workflow coordination, and service performance. Introduces the Institutional Integration Framework, which translates monitoring signals into structured workforce response and measurable performance outcomes</jats:p>

title: Phase model for analysis and compensation of metalens fabrication errors in a refractive–metalens hybrid imaging system
container-title: Optics Express
d765f14593140388c92c9a2dbf67960c1883979d.abstract: <jats:p>Fabrication-induced deviations in metalens unit cells can produce full-aperture phase errors and degrade hybrid imaging performance. A first-order model is developed for a 3.3–5 μm refractive–metalens MWIR system to relate pillar-height, radius, and sidewall-angle errors to phase deviations through the effective propagation constant. The predictions are assessed using three-dimensional local-cell finite-difference time-domain calculations and a non-axisymmetric composite-error realization. The errors reduce the on-axis and edge-field MTFs at 33 lp/mm from 0.63 and 0.44 to 0.41 and 0.38, respectively. Re-optimization of the refractive group restores them to 0.63 and 0.43. The FDTD-assembled phase produces comparable system performance. The ideal and composite-error metalenses have forward transmittances of 80.40% and 77.65%, respectively. The model therefore provides an efficient basis for tolerance analysis and compensation of refractive–metalens hybrid systems.</jats:p>

title: What Was Observatio(n)?
container-title: Philological Observation
45c92472372ca1dedba6c2b602ca2e736cf8524a.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter explores how early modern scholars of language conceptualized and used the terms observatio and observare. It begins with a survey of the terminology in ancient sources before showing how circumstances specific to the later humanist revival of Latinity adapted and inflected its sense. “Observation” proved a way for quattrocento scholars to stake out an epistemic position—true to the humanist linguistic predicament—between unregulated vulgarism and the artificial absolutism of rules. Used in the plural—Observationes—it became a marker also for the developing genre of “miscellaneous” philological commentary. In both senses, it was not only an apt keyword for lexicographical and grammatical work, but also commanded an epistemic significance whose recovery has been attributed elsewhere to medical practitioners. The common thread between physicians and lexical scholars was their embrace of an “empiric accent” available in rhetorical-grammatical as well as in medical-philosophical texts. Language-scholars, too, were empiricists.</jats:p>

title: Preliminary Reliability and Validity of Asynchronous Speech Screening to Support Clinical Triage for Children With Cleft Palate and Velopharyngeal Dysfunction
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
9b8be710f43e8a6a0acf2a7e5763f3ae256b5368.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Children with cleft and craniofacial conditions require ongoing monitoring and evaluation to manage persistent speech and resonance disorders. Regular assessment allows clinicians to detect emerging problems, evaluate intervention efficacy, and adjust treatment plans accordingly. However, socioeconomic and logistical barriers place many children at risk for sporadic or absent follow-up, leading to undiagnosed or underaddressed velopharyngeal dysfunction. This pilot study examined the reliability and use of asynchronous speech and resonance screenings to identify children who need comprehensive imaging assessment versus those suitable for continued monitoring and local speech therapy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twenty children with repaired cleft palate and/or noncleft velopharyngeal dysfunction completed in-clinic speech evaluations, during which standardized audio-only and audio–video samples were simultaneously recorded using telephone and web-conferencing platforms. During the evaluation, speech samples were rated in real time using the Cleft Audit Protocol for Speech-Americleft Modification. Each of the 40 recording files, including 20 audio-only and 20 audio–video recordings, were blinded, randomized, and independently reviewed by two asynchronous raters, yielding 80 asynchronous rating events. Interrater agreement and reliability were evaluated using percentage agreement and unweighted kappa coefficients across modalities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Across parameters and modalities, asynchronous ratings closely approximated in-person ratings. Reliability was very good for intelligibility and acceptability (κ = .81–.83), good for resonance and cleft speech characteristics (κ = .63–.75), and moderate for audible nasal emission and weak pressure consonants (κ = .45–.57). Asynchronous raters demonstrated high agreement with in-person ratings for therapy recommendations (80%–85%; κ = .57–.69) and clinical triage decisions (70%–90%; κ = .41–.79).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Preliminary findings support the feasibility and reliability of asynchronous speech and resonance screening to inform clinical triage decisions. Audio-only and audio–video recordings yielded generally comparable ratings and triage recommendations, with video offering potential added value for select speech features. Future development of asynchronous monitoring platforms has promise for reducing unnecessary clinic visits, streamlining interventions, and ensuring timely follow-up for those in need of higher level care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Supplemental Material:</jats:title>

title: Diagnosing Rare Genetic Diseases From Facial Images Using Visual Prompting With Multimodal Large Language Models: Diagnostic Accuracy Study
container-title: JMIR Medical Informatics
b2890e6f677a010f907d94d0d4a0bd1ec54c67e2.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Rare genetic diseases often present with recognizable facial phenotypes. Whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can prioritize the diagnosis of rare genetic diseases from facial images and whether image enhancement or visual prompting can improve this process remain unclear.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of MLLMs for rare genetic diseases using facial images and to assess whether super-resolution enhancement or red-circle visual prompting improved performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This diagnostic accuracy study used 4746 facial images from the GestaltMatcher Database (GMDB), including 882 images in GMDB-Frequent from diseases with at least 6 images and 3864 images in GMDB-Rare from diseases with fewer than 6 images. Three locally deployed open-weight MLLMs—Gemma-4-31B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and Qwen3.8-27B—generated 50 ranked candidate diagnoses under raw image, CodeFormer-enhanced, Qwen-Image-Edit-2511–generated red-circle–prompted, mismatched red-circle, and 2-stage image-to-phenotype conditions. Candidate diagnoses were mapped to Mondo Disease Ontology (MONDO) identifiers. In addition, we evaluated a random baseline, visual-prompt quality, expert-annotated regions, repeated-inference stability, model-reported confidence, diagnostic-list perplexity, prediction overlap, and disease composition.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Top-50 accuracy ranged from 13.95% to 18.25% in GMDB-Frequent and from 0.57% to 1.35% in GMDB-Rare. Red-circle prompting produced numerical accuracy increases in 5 of 6 model-subset comparisons. Qwen3.8-27B showed a significant improvement in GMDB-Rare, with accuracy increasing from 0.57% to 1.27% (adjusted P=.009). In the good visual-prompt subgroup of GMDB-Frequent, Gemma-4-31B showed significant improvements over the super-resolution condition in both physician-rated analyses, with accuracy increases of 5.76 percentage points (Holm-adjusted P=.005) and 4.46 percentage points (Holm-adjusted P=.048), respectively. Matched red-circle inputs yielded higher accuracy than mismatched inputs across all model-subset comparisons, with adjusted P>.05. The image-to-phenotype workflow improved accuracy for Gemma-4-31B in GMDB-Frequent and Qwen3.8-27B in GMDB-Rare. In GMDB-Rare, the random baseline achieved 8.15% accuracy and exceeded all 3 models under the raw image and red-circle conditions. Prediction sets remained substantially overlapping after patient-image replacement, and top-1 predictions concentrated on a small number of diseases.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Under the evaluated experimental settings, the 3 MLLMs showed limited ability to diagnose rare genetic diseases from facial images, particularly diseases in GMDB-Rare. Visual prompting and image-to-phenotype diagnosis produced benefits in specific models and subgroups. The prediction-overlap, mismatched-image, and disease-composition analyses indicate that model outputs were only weakly constrained by patient-specific facial information. Further studies should evaluate physician comparisons, prospective multicenter data, and phenotype-grounded multimodal diagnostic workflows.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: AI-Driven Educational Innovation
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
0304897651337a7bb39664e76309ee3a7ff3c822.abstract: <jats:p>The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) has revolutionized modern education, changing the way teaching and learning are designed, delivered, and experienced. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping the landscape of modern education by reimagining the instructional design and development, personalization of learning, and engagement in learning through adaptive and data-driven systems of education. This chapter explores how AI can be applied to curriculum innovation, interactive learning environments, intelligent tutoring systems, and pedagogies that focus on the learner. It also examines the ways in which AI-powered tools enhance accessibility, motivation, and immediate feedback and aid teachers in planning and assessing instruction. The chapter also assesses critically ethical, social, and pedagogical issues such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, and digital inequality. Last but not least, it identifies future directions and strategic implications for the sustainable integration of AI in the education sector.</jats:p>

title: Ethical Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Education Through Human Agency, Equity, and Sustainable Innovation
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
a9d3e453c30184c487d1b8cef1ee54e51d76277d.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the ethical integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education, emphasizing the need to align technological advancement with human agency, equity and sustainable innovation. It explores how AI is reshaping instructional practices, assessment systems, and educational governance across global and African contexts. Drawing on framework s such as UNESCO's recommendations on AI ethics and the OECD principles, this chapter per the authors analyses critical issues including algorithmic bias, overdependence, and the erosion of creativity. It further highlights the central role of teachers as ethical stewards, mediators, and facilitators of responsible AI use. The discussion underscores the importance of inclusive and assistive AI technologies in expanding access for marginalised learners while cautioning against reinforcing existing inequalities. Additionally, the chapter addresses policy, governance and accountability mechanisms necessary for ethical AI development advocating a human-centered approach that ensures AI supports educational goals.</jats:p>

title: Integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence in Flipped Classrooms
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
1e4670d3841466f96a03163cc6c1855c53c8ffb3.abstract: <jats:p>This study explores the impact of integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into a flipped classroom in higher education. Using a quantitative approach with complementary qualitative data, the research involved 136 management students, yielding 77 valid responses. Data were analysed via IBM SPSS 29.0, employing descriptive, inferential, and Exploratory Factorial Analysis. Findings indicate that GenAI integration enhances student engagement and promotes a deeper understanding of AI tools. Students reported increased awareness of GenAI's capabilities and limitations, and improved critical evaluation skills. Class size emerged as a significant factor influencing participation and organizational effectiveness. Overall, results provide empirical evidence of the educational benefits of GenAI in flipped settings, supporting teaching and learning. The study contributes to discussions on fostering critical GenAI use and offers practical implications for AI-driven pedagogical strategies.</jats:p>

title: A DEEP LEARNING TRANSFORMER MODEL FOR MEDICAL VOCAL EMOTION RECOGNITION
container-title: Journal of Mechanics in Medicine and Biology
d6f1989cc62d42ba62741095ed54de01ed027696.abstract: <jats:p>Vocal music has demonstrated considerable potential for emotion regulation in clinical interventions. Conventional Music Emotion Recognition models, however, have limited capability to capture the subtle and gradually evolving emotional dynamics encountered in medical scenarios. To address this limitation, this study proposes PLANTR, a hybrid framework that integrates a parallel local attention network (PLAN) with a Transformer architecture. The proposed model employs VGGish16 as the backbone acoustic feature extractor. A dual-branch PLAN captures local features at multiple temporal scales, while a Convolutional Block Attention Module enhances emotionally salient representations. A Transformer encoder models global temporal dependencies to overcome the limitations of recurrent networks in long-sequence modeling. Local and global representations are subsequently fused through an adaptive weighting strategy to predict continuous emotions in the two-dimensional valence–arousal (V-A) space. Experiments conducted on the public DEAM and PMEmo datasets demonstrate that the proposed model achieves an RMSE of 0.177 and an [Formula: see text] value of 0.659 for arousal prediction, together with an RMSE of 0.180 and an [Formula: see text] value of 0.573 for valence prediction. The model consistently outperforms the source separation model EmoMucs, a pure Transformer architecture, and comparable hybrid models. The proposed framework establishes a music emotion modeling pipeline for clinical vocal intervention scenarios and provides a proof-of-concept based on publicly available datasets annotated by general listeners. The experimental results demonstrate the technical feasibility of employing a transformer-based architecture for continuous V-A modeling of vocal music. At its current stage, however, the model predicts only the intrinsic V-A characteristics of vocal music segments and has not been validated using data collected from clinical populations. Applications such as real-time emotion monitoring for patients with aphasia or cognitive impairment, personalized music intervention selection, and objective evaluation of therapeutic outcomes remain prospective research directions that require validation using dedicated clinical datasets.</jats:p>

title: Shape and orientation in tissue polarimetry: a comparative forward-model study of collagen fibrils and cell nuclei across index contrast
container-title: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
8cb48b7400afccd704a81559724f61429cd19233.abstract: <jats:p>Tissue polarimetry reads scattered-light polarization as a fingerprint of microstructure, but a single observable cannot separate scatterer shape from the orientation order of the population. I compute the single-scattering Mueller matrix for the two dominant soft-tissue scatterers, prolate collagen fibrils and oblate cell nuclei, with a Lorenz–Mie-validated T-matrix method, and reduce each by Lu–Chipman decomposition into degree of linear polarization, retardance, and depolarization across aspect ratio, orientation concentration, wavelength, and relative index. The degree of polarization is a weak discriminator, varying by only a few percentage points across the full parameter grid; retardance and depolarization recover the lost contrast, with opposite signatures for the two scatterers—collagen’s retardance responds to orientation order roughly 2.3× more strongly than the nucleus’s, and the two scatterers depolarize with opposite dependence on shape. The orientation sensitivity of the signal thus flags a fibrous rather than nuclear origin, a discriminant that agrees in direction with independent Mueller-matrix measurements of cervical collagen remodeling and axonal white-matter tracts. The forward model is validated against exact Lorenz–Mie theory and full-wave FDTD simulation, and its outputs, including a newly resolved depolarization-anisotropy channel, supply the single-scattering kernel needed to interpret bulk-tissue polarimetry.</jats:p>

title: Autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in a patient with relapsed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and type 3 von Willebrand disease: a case report
container-title: Blood Coagulation & Fibrinolysis
3896ef2b4088f15725b49ec1c86eabd250ed7fbb.abstract: <jats:p>Autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (auto-HSCT) is standard therapy for eligible patients with relapsed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). Type 3 von Willebrand disease (VWD) poses additional haemostatic challenges during postconditioning aplasia. We report a 65-year-old man with DLBCL in second complete remission and type 3 VWD who underwent auto-HSCT. During bone marrow aplasia, complicated by mucositis and melena, intensified VWF/FVIII replacement and transfusion support were required. Following a switch to a concentrate with a higher VWF-to-FVIII ratio, improved haemostatic control was achieved. Poor platelet increments were associated with anti-HLA class I antibodies, indicating immune-mediated platelet refractoriness. Bleeding was controlled with twice-daily platelet transfusions, full-dose antifibrinolytic therapy, and VWF/FVIII replacement maintaining trough levels above 0.50 IU/ml. To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of auto-HSCT in a patient with a severe congenital bleeding disorder, highlighting the importance of individualized VWF/FVIII replacement and optimized transfusion support.</jats:p>

title: A Proposed Model for Teachers' AI Competencies Based on UNESCO and DigCompEdu Frameworks: A Qualitative Study
container-title: Arid International Journal of Educational and physcological sciences
7a8fb5e87b709a8a3bc5fe456897cd79f3dc7754.abstract:
<jats:p>Teachers’ competencies in artificial intelligence (AI) constitute a fundamental element for achieving innovative and effective education aligned with the demands of the twenty-first century. This study aims to propose a comprehensive model of teachers’ AI competencies based on the UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers and the European Digital Competence Framework for Educators (DigCompEdu), while adapting them to suit the needs of teacher preparation programs in faculties of education.

The study adopts a qualitative approach using focus groups with experts in curriculum and instruction as well as educational technology. The domains, standards, and indicators of both frameworks were analyzed and discussed in order to derive a practical and contextually relevant model.

The study resulted in a proposed model comprising five main domains, 15 standards, and 48 performance indicators, covering cognitive, pedagogical, ethical, professional, and assessment dimensions. It also provides practical recommendations for developing teacher preparation and continuous professional development programs, with a focus on integrating artificial intelligence in a responsible and effective manner to support interactive and inclusive learning for students.</jats:p>

title: Renormalization, cutoff, and gluing for a quartic model with boundary
container-title: Physical Review D
7bb964ca6bdd39b8bd44eb970bbd1766328f4be1.abstract: <jats:p>In this paper, we study the renormalization of a three-dimensional quartic model on a compact connected Riemannian manifold with a boundary. We show that, in addition to the standard shift of the mass parameter, it is necessary to take into account boundary contributions involving singular coefficients. This indicates the need to extend the classical action within the framework of standard renormalization theory. The requirements of consistency regarding the gluing of manifolds lead to renormalization of an operator on the boundary.</jats:p>

title: A Comparison of Simulation Modalities to Train Graduate-Level Clinical Reasoning for Clinical Swallow Evaluation
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
836baa35a547eadbde56a0df6fa68e26bbab09d9.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Changes in graduate-level clinical reasoning for clinical swallow evaluation were examined and compared between video simulation and standardized patient simulation training. The purpose of this study was to provide information for speech-language pathology programs to consider when integrating simulation for clinical reasoning for clinical swallow evaluation within the graduate-level curriculum to support intentional, evidence-based use of academic resources for teaching and learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A randomized pretest/posttest mixed-methods design was implemented to compare a video simulation training group and a standardized patient simulation training group. Stratified randomization was used to assign first-year graduate speech-language pathology students to either a video simulation (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                      = 15) or standardized patient simulation (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                      = 15) group. Before and after participating in either video simulation or standardized patient simulation, participants completed concept maps to evaluate changes in cognitive schema development for clinical reasoning and clinical vignettes to evaluate changes in clinical reasoning within a novel written case. Participants rated the design of their assigned simulation modality following the simulation using the National League for Nursing Simulation Design Scale (SDS; Student Version). Participants also provided qualitative responses to question prompts based on the Lasater Clinical Judgment Rubric following the simulation to detail clinical reasoning that was employed during the simulation.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There were no significant differences in total scores between groups for concept maps, clinical vignettes, and SDS. Within-group differences demonstrated a significant gain from pretest to posttest for concept map performance for both groups. Qualitative analysis of participant responses yielded insight into group differences in clinical reasoning development, with qualitative analysis suggesting that video simulation–based learning aligned more closely with participants' level of experience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Both video simulation and standardized patient simulation were effective for training clinical reasoning. Video simulation may be particularly appropriate for novice learners. Given the cost of high-fidelity simulation, video simulation may be beneficial to consider for contextualized learning at the novice level followed by standardized patient simulation as students gain experience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Identifying the Content and Pedagogical Practices Used by Educators Teaching Stuttering and Cluttering Modules
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
83c89335c97a624aa03f514362b63a0dec9271e3.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Research has demonstrated that many speech-language pathologists (SLPs) have reported having reduced knowledge and competence in the assessment and intervention of children and adults who stutter and clutter. One potential reason for this is embedded in a suboptimal educational foundation at a university level.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to identify the content taught and the pedagogical practices used by speech-language pathology educators teaching a module on stuttering and cluttering as part of an undergraduate or postgraduate program in speech-language pathology.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An online survey was developed by the authors, and questions reflected the All Ireland Society for Higher Education (AISHE) model for module design. Participants were recruited in Australia, Canada, Ireland, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics. Participants' qualitative responses were analyzed using inductive content analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Eighty-six educators completed the survey. Descriptive data, including qualitative findings, were reported on the seven components of the AISHE model. Self-reported expertise in stuttering or cluttering was associated with greater amount of teaching content (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                      = .018). Participants reported teaching significantly more about stuttering than cluttering (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                      < .001).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study identified the range of content and pedagogical practices used by educators delivering stuttering and cluttering modules. Results highlighted that educators with expertise in stuttering and/or cluttering taught a higher number of content areas.</jats:p>

title: Beyond constant error: Heteroscedastic Bayesian model combination for modeling unmeasured nuclei
container-title: Physical Review Research
b802b92eaa6b799601c9f8f9b3dd72c96cc8cc5e.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Experimentally inaccessible regions of the nuclear chart remain a challenge for global models of atomic nuclei to predict. This includes exotic nuclei near particle drip lines, superheavy elements at the extremes of mass and charge, and the neutron-rich pathways of astrophysical processes in explosive stellar environments where heavy elements are created. Given that individual nuclear models are imperfect, deep extrapolations are best approached using model ensembles, which allow for the systematic combination of diverse theoretical predictions. In this study, we employ the recently introduced Bayesian model combination (BMC) method, based on statistical machine learning, that provides robust uncertainty quantification for forecasts using model ensembles. To account for the inherent degradation of predictive power as models extrapolate into the yet-unexplored domain, we introduce a heteroscedastic BMC framework in which the combined theoretical uncertainty is treated as a dynamic quantity. We apply this methodology to an ensemble of realistic energy density functionals with a specific focus on the
                    <a:math xmlns:a="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                      <a:mrow>
                        <a:mi>Z</a:mi>
                        <a:mo>=</a:mo>
                        <a:mn>46</a:mn>
                        <a:mo>–</a:mo>
                        <a:mn>52</a:mn>
                      </a:mrow>
                    </a:math>
                    isotopic chains. We rigorously validate the approach using both experimental data and synthetic data designed to assess performance in the deep extrapolation regime. Our results demonstrate that the proposed heteroscedastic approach yields superior calibration metrics and provides statistically principled assessments of the particle drip lines.
                  </jats:p>

title: On a cosmological Oppenheimer–Snyder model: matching McVittie and FLRW spacetimes
container-title: Classical and Quantum Gravity
71c07c32d6ec40ea1db2c58aa610a755426d9ba3.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We consider the necessary and sufficient conditions for the smooth matching of an expanding McVittie spacetime and a spatially flat Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker (FLRW) spacetime across a general hypersurface—that is, a hypersurface of arbitrary causal character, where the character possibly changes from point to point. We identify a number of special cases, giving a complete description of (for example) constant radius matching hypersurfaces. In the general case, we show that the full set of matching conditions is equivalent to a 3-dimensional non-linear system of first order ODEs, subject to a single initial value constraint. Taking the perspective that the McVittie region is specified, we prove a semi-global existence result for this system and interpret these solutions in terms of the physical set-up. Solutions exist and are unique globally to the future. In this direction, the required FLRW spacetime exists and is unique and the matching hypersurface exists almost everywhere and is unique. However, the necessary embedding conditions for the hypersurface necessarily fail at least once—but only at isolated points—along the putative hypersurface. To the past, the matching hypersurface extends to meet the past singularity of the McVittie region. We determine the causal character of the matching hypersurface in these limits, and consider the implications for the existence (or otherwise) of an isotropic source of the McVittie cosmological black hole spacetime. We find that generically, the matching hypersurface has spacelike as well as timelike portions, and so the isotropic region cannot be considered to be an interior for the McVittie exterior. This is in distinction to the Oppenheimer–Snyder model, in which an isotropic dust sphere matches across an everywhere-timelike boundary to the Schwarzschild exterior. On the basis of the sometimes-spacelike nature of the hypersurface, we conclude that an isotropic source of the McVittie spacetime does not exist in a global sense.</jats:p>

title: From Black-Scholes to Jump-Diffusion: A Narrative Review of Option Pricing Model Evolution
container-title: Exploring Science Academic Conference Series
ea8c6dd1a8c81faa3604a1cf748f02b7cbd84960.abstract: <jats:p>Option pricing theory is a cornerstone of modern financial engineering, but the classical Black-Scholes framework relies on continuous price trajectories, constant volatility, and lognormally distributed returns. These assumptions are difficult to reconcile with empirical features such as volatility smiles, fat-tailed returns, volatility clustering, and abrupt price movements. This review examines the evolution of Option pricing models from the Black-Scholes benchmark to stochastic-volatility, jump-diffusion, stochastic-volatility-jump, and affine jump-diffusion specifications. It shows that richer models generally improve cross-sectional pricing accuracy, especially for short-maturity and out-of-the-money options, but that this improvement is accompanied by higher parameter uncertainty, calibration complexity, and hedging instability. The review further emphasizes that evidence from emerging markets, particularly China’s domestic derivatives market, remains comparatively limited and may require models that account for liquidity constraints, retail participation, and clustered jump behavior.  </jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study investigates the second language (L2) development of wh-questions in English and French under a usage-based linguistic framework. It draws on two longitudinal corpora documenting spoken production data from different groups of classroom-taught learners; the French Progression Corpus, tracking twenty-four learners over three years, and the Barcelona English Language Corpus, tracking nine learners over seven years. Learners’ earliest wh-questions appear as similar prototypical multiword units and lexically specific constructions used in predictable role-play interactions. Progression-level differences across the datasets are found to be dependent on a learner’s ability to interact with lexically specific material and schematize related constructions from this. The paper discusses the implications of these findings for construction-grammar-informed pedagogies and highlights the value of teaching constructions as form-function pairings to accelerate early productive abilities in foreign language classrooms.</jats:p>

c64b35887affbcba9fcccf262b8e7d6f72b73e59.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Affective polarization and political sorting drive public antagonism around climate change and other issues at the science-policy nexus. We study cross-domain spillover of incivility in public engagements with climate change and public health on English-language Twitter and Reddit using the COVID-19 period as a case study. To assess whether spillover exists between these two policy domains, we examined how the incivility of climate discussions on social media varied by their co-occurrence with COVID-19 content and temporal coincidence with pandemic events. We find strong evidence of the signatures of affective polarization surrounding COVID-19 spilling into the climate change domain. Across different social media systems, COVID-19 content is associated with incivility in climate discussions. These patterns of increased antagonism were responsive to pandemic events that made the link between science and public policy more salient. We also looked at how climate discussions about international organizations and elites changed with the pandemic’s onset to show that the observed incivility spillover activated along overlapping pre-pandemic political cleavages, specifically anti-internationalist populist beliefs that linked climate policy opposition to vaccine hesitancy. Our findings show how affective polarization in public engagement with science becomes entrenched across policy domains, which has implications for how the public engages with and communicates about issues such as climate change and public health.</jats:p>

title: Level 2.5 Large Deviations and Uncertainty Relations for Non-Markov Self-Interacting Dynamics
container-title: Physical Review Letters
c300b217ca33b24fa56c6fdc4a9348aff455ffc9.abstract: <jats:p>We address the general problem of formulating the dynamical large deviations of non-Markovian systems in a closed form. Specifically, we consider a broad class of “self-interacting” jump processes whose dynamics depends on the past through a functional of a state-dependent empirical observable. Exploiting a natural separation of timescales, and under the corresponding mixing conditions, we obtain the exact (so-called “level 2.5”) large deviation joint statistics of the empirical measure over configurations and of the empirical flux of transitions. As an application of this general framework, we derive explicit general bounds on the fluctuations of trajectory observables, generalizing to the non-Markovian case both thermodynamic and kinetic uncertainty relations. We illustrate our theory with simple examples, and discuss potential applications of these results.</jats:p>

title: Prompting Strategies for Readability Alignment Between User-Generated Ophthalmology Questions and Large Language Model Answers: Comparative Evaluation Study
container-title: JMIR Formative Research
df84797e48d54a341d65b2f7252499a9baa4ee0a.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Accessible health communication is essential for effective patient education, yet most medical information remains written at a level above the general population’s recommended reading level. Large language models (LLMs) can simplify complex medical information, but it remains unclear whether responses can be automatically adapted to match the linguistic complexity of user-generated questions seeking medical information.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To evaluate whether the LLM-generated responses to user-generated ophthalmology questions align with their readability and to compare different prompting strategies for readability control across multiple LLM architectures, including their impact on response quality as well as computational cost and efficiency.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 400 user-generated ophthalmology questions collected from public YouTube comments were categorized into 3 readability tiers based on the Flesch Reading Ease Score. A controlled comparative evaluation of responses generated by 4 LLMs (GPT 5.2, Gemini 3, Claude Opus 4.5, and OSS-20b) was performed under 4 prompting conditions: Baseline (no readability control), Formula-Informed Readability Prompt, Semantic Readability Inference, and External Calculator–Guided Prompt. Agreement between question and response readability was assessed using quadratic-weighted Cohen kappa. Response quality was evaluated using BERTScore and LLM-as-a-judge assessments. Computational efficiency was evaluated through token usage, estimated cost per response, and latency.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The external calculator–guided strategy produced the strongest alignment in readability across models, achieving the highest agreement (Gemini 3: κ=0.94; GPT 5.2: κ=0.90), while maintaining favorable computational efficiency. Formula-informed prompting showed intermediate performance, whereas semantic inference demonstrated poor agreement due to unreliable readability estimation. High-performing models (GPT 5.2 and Gemini 3) maintained very high factual accuracy (>98%) across strategies, indicating that readability control did not substantially degrade correctness. In contrast, the open-source OSS-20b model showed lower accuracy (83.75%‐90%) and greater sensitivity to readability constraints. Semantic similarity remained high across models (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers Score [BERTScore]
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      >0.87). Longer questions were associated with slightly lower accuracy, particularly in lower-performing configurations.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Aligning LLM responses to the readability of user-generated questions is feasible and can be reliably achieved using externally guided readability signals. Hybrid pipelines that combine traditional readability metrics with LLM-generated content may therefore represent a practical approach for scalable, readability-adaptive health communication systems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Using Artificial Intelligence in Qualitative Lupus Pregnancy Research: The Potential of Large Language Models and Prompting Strategies

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our objective was to evaluate the ability of different large language models (LLMs) to translate and analyze qualitative interviews describing pregnancy experiences among women with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). An additional objective was to compare themes identified by LLMs with those identified by human researchers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analyzed 26 semistructured interviews originally conducted in Portuguese by Rodrigues et al among women with SLE exploring their perinatal care experiences. Three prompting strategies (zero‐shot, few‐shot, and chain‐of‐thought) were used on the transcripts across four state‐of‐the‐art LLMs (GPT‐4o, OpenAI; Claude Sonnet 4.5, Anthropic; Gemini 2.5 Flash, Google; and DeepSeek R, DeepSeek) to generate key themes. Model outputs were evaluated using an LLM‐as‐a‐judge framework assessing thematic coverage, thematic unity, and semantic similarity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Across models and prompting strategies, LLMs generated similar themes that closely aligned with those identified by human researchers. LLM‐as‐a‐judge evaluations demonstrated high thematic unity and semantic similarity. Claude Sonnet 4.5 showed the most consistent performance. Few‐shot prompting consistently outperformed zero‐shot and chain‐of‐thought approaches.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>LLMs show promise as supportive tools for analyzing qualitative research by preserving thematic coherence and capturing the complexity of pregnancy experiences in women with SLE. Although zero‐shot prompting is widely used, it produced lower thematic results in our study, whereas few‐shot prompting achieved the most comprehensive and coherent theme extraction. LLM‐assisted qualitative analysis may complement human interpretation and has the potential to support the inclusion of non–English language data and diverse patient perspectives in lupus research.</jats:p>
