                  <jats:p>The framework was applied within a brownfield onshore asset comprising more than fifty-three producing wells and multiple flow stations, integrating daily production surveillance, maintenance planning, and operational data into structured short-interval control cycles with defined ownership. Implementation reduced decision cycle time, from issue identification to approved intervention, by approximately 30 to 45 percent, reduced unresolved productionimpacting constraints by approximately 35 percent over a twelve-week period, and delivered sustained production recovery of 3 to 7 percent relative to the preceding three-year baseline, achieved without major capital investment.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The proposed framework formalizes production constraint management into a repeatable execution methodology that links operational data directly to execution decisions. It is asset-agnostic and offers a practical pathway to improved production delivery without requiring major organizational restructuring or new technology investment.</jats:p>

title: A Three-Dimensional Integrated Numerical Model for Fracture Propagation and Production Performance in Oil Reservoir
container-title: ADIPEC
4a2279371d6874ea7ee358d1ca6af87e1525c3d6.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Hydraulic fracturing represents a cornerstone technique in reservoir stimulation operations. To maximize single-well productivity and enhance ultimate oil recovery, a fully coupled numerical framework integrating fracture propagation, proppant transport, and production performance prediction has been established. Through systematic simulation and parametric analysis of production performance under varying fracturing parameters, an optimized stimulation scheme with optimized treatment parameters is derived. Within the integrated framework, fracture propagation is characterized by a combination of the displacement discontinuity method (DDM), the finite volume method (FVM), and the embedded discrete fracture model (EDFM), with proppant transport characterized by an Eulerian–Eulerian two-fluid model to capture particle dynamics within the hydraulic fracture (HF). Moreover, bidirectional coupling between proppant transport and fracture propagation is considered. Fracture porosity and permeability are quantified at the end of hydraulic fracturing and integrated with an oil-water two-phase flow model to predict production performance of the fracturing stage. Stress interference among multiple fractures exerts a pronounced influence on hydraulic fracture geometry, and fracture width substantially governs the transport dynamics and spatial redistribution of proppant. Upon cessation of injection, HFs remain only partially propped, with proppant preferentially accumulating in the tip and lower regions of the fracture. The governing mechanisms through which injection rate modulates fracture propagation and proppant transport are distinct. Achieving effective proppant placement along extended fracture lengths is important to post-fracture production performance. Different pump schedules yield variations in proppant distribution, underscoring the critical importance of fracturing design optimization in maximizing single-well production. The combination of staircase proppant schedule and reasonable injection rate demonstrably enhances proppant transport and distribution, thereby augmenting single-well production. Relative to typical optimization strategies focused on fracture parameters or static proppant placement results, the proposed numerical framework is explicitly oriented toward maximizing production performance. By integrating reservoir numerical simulations with hydraulic fracturing modeling, this approach effectively overcomes the limitations of conventional models with static fractures geometries and spatially uniform proppant distribution, substantially broadening its applicability to field-scale engineering contexts.</jats:p>

title: Technical Accuracy Challenges and Solutions for Non-Radioactive Multiphase Flow Meters at Large Scale
container-title: ADIPEC
0e15a88b8337ed9885e3fc9a10c685d8236c82d6.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper documents the measurement-accuracy challenges encountered during the deployment and first operational year of 90 nonradioactive impedance-based multiphase flow meters (MPFMs) installed at the wellhead by Kuwait Oil Company (KOC) across one onshore oilfield. The fleet comprised 73 electric-submersible-pump (ESP)-lifted and 17 naturally flowing wells. The objective was to identify the main causes of measurement deviation, document the corrective engineering actions, and establish an operator-led framework for sustaining MPFMs accuracy.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Approximately 60% of the meters were outside project acceptance criteria at first commissioning verification. Root causes were associated principally with fluid-property inputs and sampling, model/configuration mismatch, transition-zone behavior, high-GVF/low- DP operation, and changes in well conditions. Diagnosis combined raw differential-pressure (DP), impedance, and velocity signals with PGOR reference measurements and manual water-cut samples. Corrective actions included fluid-property updates, model/software changes, flow-conditioning trials, and a constrained calculation for an out-of-envelope wet-gas well.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Four field cases demonstrate distinct intervention paths: correction of an unstable gas-liquid split, constrained oil-rate estimation above 98% gas volume fraction (GVF), fluid-property reconfiguration for persistent water-cut bias, and transition-zone mitigation using mixing trials followed by an improved transition interpretation model.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Quarterly fleet accuracy ranged from 94.4% to 98.1%, with a first-year average of 95.97%. An independent blind PGOR campaign on 67 wells achieved a 95.5% pass rate (64 of 67). The results show that sustained performance of a non-radioactive MPFM fleet depends on representative fluid properties, controlled configuration, operating-envelope awareness, independent verification, and continuous operator-led surveillance.</jats:p>

title: Dynamic Evaluation Method for Development Units Based on a Discrete Fracture-Vug Network Model
container-title: ADIPEC
b5a78dd186e4ec929c7395ac4fa9fc9dc869c0f0.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The heterogeneity and coupling effects in fracture-cavity carbonate reservoirs pose severe challenges for their efficient exploitation. Existing evaluation frameworks mainly emphasize well-by-well and stage-based analyses, which fail to capture the intrinsic relationships among fracture-vug configuration patterns, fluid flow behaviors, and development dynamics. Therefore, this study proposes a development performance evaluation framework for different types of fault-controlled fractured-vuggy units by integrating nodal network modeling, indicator weighting, and fuzzy comprehensive evaluation. Seismic geobodies and production data were used to construct a nodal network model of fractured-vuggy units incorporating non-Darcy flow and vertical fluid equilibrium. On this basis, a development performance evaluation indicator system was established using liquid production rate, injection-production ratio, injector-producer placement, and injection-production mode. Multifactor numerical simulations were then conducted to determine the indicator weights, and fuzzy comprehensive evaluation was subsequently applied to assess the development performance of representative fractured-vuggy units. Finally, targeted recommendations were formulated for spatial well-pattern design and volumetric development strategies in representative fractured-vuggy units. The results indicate pronounced differences in the dominant controls on development performance among fracture-vug configuration patterns. For throughgoing fractured-vuggy units, development performance is controlled primarily by liquid production rate; for staggered-parallel fault-bounded units, by injector-producer placement; and for parallel fault-bounded units, jointly by liquid production rate and injector-producer placement. Application of the method to representative fractured-vuggy units in the Fuyuan 210 fault zone of the Fuman Oilfield showed that the FY1-4 fractured-vuggy unit was rated as "good," whereas the FY1-3 and FY1-5 fractured-vuggy units were rated as "moderate". Differentiated adjustment strategies were proposed for FY1-3 and FY1-5, resulting in five-year recovery factor improvements of 9.49 and 15.36 percentage points, respectively, compared with the pre-adjustment development schemes. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed method and provide a basis for evaluating development performance and formulating adjustment plans for similar reservoirs.</jats:p>

title: AI-Enabled Competency Development for Rig Technicians – A New Model for Workforce Transformation
container-title: ADIPEC
58724ba4b8af3e87b1dbf81e264eda56d779c1fe.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives/Scope</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Digitalization on both land rigs and offshore jack-ups has introduced new layers of complexity into electrical, control, and mechanical systems. Many technicians still struggle with basic digital tasks—such as accessing PLCs, interpreting controller alarms, or troubleshooting VFD faults—despite prior training. This paper presents an AI-enabled competency development model designed to accelerate technician learning, improve diagnostic consistency, and strengthen structured troubleshooting behavior across mixed-fleet drilling operations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods, Procedures, Process</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The model combines hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) and software-in-the-loop (SIL) simulators, scenario-based simulations, and a rule-based troubleshooting assistant. Competency gaps were identified through technician interactions with simulated rig systems, including real failure modes such as SCR misfiring, VFD overheating, and PLC interlock faults. Adaptive learning concepts were incorporated to outline how future modules may tailor training based on technician behavior. Field observations from actual rig support—such as hesitation to access PLC logic or reliance on intuition instead of diagnostic tools—were integrated to ensure realism and relevance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results, Observations, Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Technicians trained within the simulator-based environment demonstrated measurable improvements, including a 35% increase in troubleshooting accuracy and a 40% reduction in diagnostic time. Simulation results indicate potential for more consistent diagnostic behavior, improved alarm interpretation, and reduced reliance on senior personnel. These improvements were achieved without live-rig deployment and therefore represent expected performance gains under controlled validation conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Novel/Additive Information</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This work introduces a competency development ecosystem built specifically for rig technicians, integrating HIL/SIL simulators, structured diagnostic workflows, and real failure data into a scalable training model. The approach addresses longstanding gaps in conventional training—particularly the lack of realistic digital scenarios—and provides a practical pathway for modernizing technician development in increasingly digitalized rig environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Innovative Design and Application Research of Gas-Tight Threads for Large-Diameter, Thick-Wall Casing in 10,000-Meter-Deep Wells
container-title: ADIPEC
5a4e46439778a52e44ac2949f22f5e3a539a32f5.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>With the continuous deepening of oil and gas exploration, 10,000-meter-deep wells are becoming increasingly common. To facilitate downhole operations in such ultra-deep wells, both intermediate and production casings now employ large-diameter, high-grade, thick-wall casings. However, these casings introduce new challenges for thread connections, including misalignment during make-up, severe galling leading to downhole casing string disconnection, and high-temperature (260°C) thread sealing failures that result in annular pressure buildup. These issues critically threaten the safe operation of 10,000-meter-deep wells. This study focuses on the development of a high-performance, regular coupling-type gas-tight thread for 125TS-grade technical casings (OD 365.12 mm, wall thickness 13.88mm) deployed in two 10,000-meter-deep wells drilled by China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC). Field investigations of gas-tight thread failures in large-diameter casings revealed that the significant weight and length of the casings cause tilting and oscillation during wellhead make-up, hindering vertical alignment between the external and coupling internal threads. This misalignment induces severe compressive deformation of thread guiding surfaces. Logging data indicated a 5–8 mm gap between the casing external thread end and the coupling shoulder, confirming inadequate make-up as the root cause of disconnection and sealing failure. Structural analysis of failed threads, characterized by a 1:16 taper and crest/root parallelism to the pitch diameter, demonstrated that the API Spec 5B buttress thread form is unsuitable for thick-wall casings with a 365.12 mm OD. Building on failure mechanism analysis, this research proposes an innovative gas-tight thread design methodology: (1) A thread profile integrating alignment guidance, anti-impact protection, and self-correcting make-up capabilities to prevent misalignment; (2) Load-bearing surfaces, guiding surfaces, and sealing surfaces optimized for anti-galling under over-torque conditions. Finite element analysis (FEA) was employed to optimize thread height, full thread count, and sealing interference based on structural and sealing integrity requirements under a 260°C combined load envelope (VME90%). Full-scale physical testing under extreme tolerances verified that the new design doubles galling torque resistance compared to field-used threads while maintaining VME90% structural and sealing integrity at 260°C. Field applications achieved a 100% first-attempt make-up success rate, with shoulder torque stabilized within 23–64% of the total make-up torque, resulting in zero disconnections or sealing leaks in the one 10,000-meter wells. The novel thread profile significantly enhances alignment accuracy and galling resistance. During deployment in ultra-deep wells, wellhead make-up torque curves for large-diameter casing threads exhibited clarity and consistency, with stable shoulder torque. Optimized sealing structures improved galling resistance, damage tolerance, and high-temperature sealing integrity. Successful field applications validated the superior performance of the new gas-tight threads for large-diameter, thick-wall casings in 10,000-meter environments. This study establishes an innovative design methodology for large-diameter, thick-wall casings, yielding a high-performance gas-tight thread tailored for ultra-deep wells. The design demonstrates exceptional wellhead operability and adaptability to downhole ultra-high-temperature conditions.</jats:p>

title: Real-Time Digital Twin Model for Optimizing Drilling Performance and Support Intelligent Decision Making
container-title: ADIPEC
4f4599e4f35cfff5576017d8d10a556782e1441b.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Maintaining efficient and sustainable drilling performance is a key challenge in well delivery, particularly in deciding whether drilling dysfunctions can be corrected through parameter optimization or require pull-out-of-hole (POOH) and run-in-hole (RIH) operations. This paper presents a real-time digital twin model using Mechanical Specific Energy (MSE) analytics to optimize drilling performance, reduce non-productive time (NPT), and improve well delivery efficiency across multiple fields in Oman.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>A real-time digital twin workflow — a continuously updated virtual model of the drilling process that stays synchronized with live rig data and closes the loop with an operational recommendation, as distinct from a static or periodically refreshed decision-support review — was developed to continuously monitor drilling performance using live rig sensor data integrated with MSE analysis. The model processes key parameters — weight on bit, rotary speed, torque, rate of penetration, flow rate, standpipe pressure, and drilling fluid properties — to build a continuous picture of downhole conditions. MSE is dynamically benchmarked against offset-well performance to evaluate efficiency. Combined physics-based and rule-based logic classifies drilling states as stable drilling, optimization required, or critical failure requiring POOH and RIH, while generating real-time operational recommendations and supporting integration with rig surveillance systems.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The model was validated using data from more than 500 wells across 15 fields in Oman, achieving 99.1% accuracy — measured as agreement between the model's recommended action and the independently recorded operational outcome of each bit run — in identifying inefficient drilling conditions and recommending the appropriate corrective action. Field implementation demonstrated improved decision consistency and operational efficiency in real drilling environments. In Well A case study, the reservoir section was drilled in three bit runs compared with eight in an offset well, significantly reducing drilling time and tripping frequency. The system effectively differentiated between conditions requiring parameter optimization and those requiring BHA replacement, enabling timely interventions and avoiding unnecessary POOH operations. Overall, the approach reduced drilling time by up to 17% and well cost by approximately 6%. In addition, fewer tripping operations and more efficient drilling contributed to lower rig energy consumption, improved operational performance, and better well delivery outcomes across multiple field applications.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This work introduces a digital twin-based drilling decision framework that extends conventional MSE analysis into real-time operational intelligence. Its novelty lies in integrating MSE with structured decision logic to classify drilling states and enable proactive interventions, supporting more autonomous, efficient, and lower-carbon drilling operations in complex field environments.</jats:p>

title: Intelligent Closed-Loop Well Model Calibration: A Fully Automated, Physics-Based, and Database-Driven Solution for ESP and NF Wells in KOC
container-title: ADIPEC
4d3b98c48498368ef8b81487301f61b596de333c.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper presents a fully automated, end-to-end well model calibration framework integrated with the Kuwait Oil Company (KOC) enterprise database. The solution employs a closed-loop, physics-based methodology to dynamically calibrate ESP and NF wells using well test data. It standardizes calibration, minimizes manual intervention, and enables scalable, continuous model maintenance across a large asset base with thousands of wells in North and West Kuwait.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The workflow is connected to KOC corporate database which contains approved well test data. The well test data is extracted and saved in the workflow database using a complex Extract Transform and load (ETL) code. The automated calibration runs every two hours ensuring that the well models are calibrated to the most recent well test and in turn represent the current reality in the field. For ESP wells, Pump Discharge Pressure (PDP) is matched through sequential tuning of GOR and WCUT, followed by Pump Intake Pressure (PIP) calibration via pump wear factor adjustment. In absence of gas handler pumps, surrogate configurations are introduced with optimized stage count. Liquid rate is matched by calibrating PI, with reservoir pressure as a boundary condition. Calibration quality is quantified across key variables, with iterative convergence and user-driven override capabilities for critical parameters.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The workflow has been fully deployed across North and West Kuwait assets, covering thousands of wells, and has demonstrated substantial improvements in calibration efficiency, consistency, and model reliability. The architecture integrates tightly with the corporate data infrastructure, enabling automated ingestion, validation, and processing of well test data. A built-in data quality assurance layer performs completeness checks, identifies missing or inconsistent parameters, and enforces correction workflows to prevent propagation of erroneous calibration states.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Operational events such as workovers, recompletions, or rigless interventions are captured through event-driven triggers that automatically invalidate existing model states, ensuring recalibration is deferred until acquisition of representative post-intervention well test data. This guarantees model integrity and alignment with updated well configurations.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The system supports continuous, closed-loop recalibration, maintaining dynamic synchronization between simulation outputs and evolving field conditions. Advanced exception handling mechanisms, including surrogate equipment modeling (e.g., assumed gas handler pumps with optimized stage configurations), ensure robustness under incomplete data scenarios. Collectively, the workflow enhances surveillance accuracy, supports real-time production optimization, and enables scalable, data-driven decision-making across the asset.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This work presents a fully integrated, closed-loop calibration framework combining enterprise database connectivity, automated parameter optimization, and embedded data validation. Key innovations include hierarchical, physics-constrained calibration logic, adaptive exception handling under data uncertainty, and continuous near–real-time execution at field scale. Integration of event-driven model invalidation and dynamic state management further enhances robustness, establishing a comprehensive digital solution for scalable production surveillance and intelligent well model lifecycle management.</jats:p>

title: Integrating Downhole Corrosion Evaluation with Metallurgical Analysis for AI-Driven Well Failure Prediction Model
container-title: ADIPEC
17fa540456a44a64bd997c96b18459954f729a0e.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives/Scope</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Recurring tubing failures driven by aggressive downhole corrosion represent a critical operational and economic challenge in ESP-lifted production wells of the EKI field, East Kuwait 1. With an average corrosion rate of 4 mm/year and 325 documented tubing failures across the South East Kuwait (SEK) portfolio, the lack of a mechanistic corrosion management framework has sustained a reactive workover cycle with production deferment and integrity risk. This paper presents the first deployment of a 64-element fixed-array advanced ultrasonic cement and corrosion tool within 3½-inch production tubing, enabling simultaneous 360° azimuthal corrosion evaluation in a single rigless pass. The objective is to integrate high-resolution corrosion mapping with laboratory metallurgical analysis, establish the corrosion mechanism for the study well, and translate the findings into the foundation of an AI-driven Corrosion Management System (CMS) and well failure prediction model.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods, Procedures, Process</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A two-run rigless wireline evaluation was executed. The first run deployed a 24-arm multi-finger caliper and electromagnetic multi-string tool to assess inner surface morphology and average wall thickness across four nested casing strings. The second run deployed the 64-element fixed-array ultrasonic tool, commercially known as Reveal Barrier (SLB), in its first deployment within 3½-inch production tubing, acquiring simultaneous 360° azimuthal inner wall and thickness maps in a single monocable pass. Six tubing samples, selected using the corrosion map, underwent laboratory investigation comprising X-ray diffraction, X-ray fluorescence, ion chromatography, optical emission spectroscopy, tensile testing, electrochemical corrosion modeling, and quantitative PCR microbiological analysis. An operational SOP was established to enable safe and repeatable deployment across the portfolio.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results, Observations, Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The deployment enabled a proactive, data-driven workover decision that achieved zero non-productive time (NPT) during tubing retrieval. Laboratory analysis confirmed two distinct corrosion mechanisms: internal chloride-induced CO2/H2S pitting above the ESP, where mechanical scale disruption initiates deep anodic pits; and external crevice corrosion below the ESP, driven by clamp contact geometry in a stagnant H2S-enriched annulus. CO2 and H2S were identified as likely byproducts of excess water production, enabling targeted mitigation. Microbiologically influenced corrosion was ruled out. The integrated dataset supports an AI predictive model trained on 133 wells in the EKI/SEK portfolio, demonstrating promising first-pass corrosion-rate predictions and ongoing refinement using time-lapse data. Chemical injection has been identified as the preferred mitigation strategy targeting a reduction from 4 mm/year to below 1 mm/year.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Novel/Additive Information</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This work establishes three original contributions to well integrity and corrosion management: (1) the first deployment of a 64-element fixed-array ultrasonic tool in 3½-inch production tubing, enabling combined corrosion and cement evaluation in a previously inaccessible completion size; (2) the first use of full 360° azimuthal pre-workover corrosion mapping to support a zero-NPT, data-driven workover decision for tubing retrieval in this completion size; and (3) the integration of downhole ultrasonic thickness mapping with laboratory metallurgical analysis to derive a spatially resolved corrosion mechanism, forming the foundation of an AI-driven field-wide CMS and well failure prediction model scalable across the KOC's portfolio.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: ADNOC Pre-Retirement Program: A Strategic Workforce Transition Model Advancing Employee Wellbeing, Readiness, Through Sustainable Culture Approach
container-title: ADIPEC
d1fcb4956be5124a8a81aec6b991034da23cae8c.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Organizations worldwide are experiencing a major demographic shift driven by longer life expectancy, changing retirement expectations, evolving economic conditions, and rapid technological advancement. As a result, retirement is increasingly viewed as a structured workforce transition rather than the end of employment. Effective preparation supports employees in maintaining financial security, psychological resilience, social connection, and physical wellbeing after active service.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Historically, retirement planning in many organizations focused on pension administration, end-of-service benefits, and procedural compliance. These processes remain essential; however, they do not fully address the practical and personal challenges employees may face when transitioning from employment to retirement.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Modern organizations increasingly recognize that support across the full employment lifecycle strengthens organizational culture, employee trust, employer reputation, and long-term workforce sustainability. Retirement preparation is therefore better positioned as a strategic human capital investment than as a purely administrative activity.</jats:p>

title: From Fragmented Interpretations to an Automated Unified Full-Column Subsurface Framework: Enabling High-Fidelity Subsurface Model and Reliable Horizontal Well Placement, and Agentic AI–Driven Structural Quality Control
container-title: ADIPEC
b665b4b3dc4753f079f9cd6e33d75b999016b01b.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Mature carbonate assets with dense well control and stacked reservoir architecture commonly evolve through multiple generations of reservoir-specific structural interpretations. Although each local model may be technically valid within its own reservoir interval, the combination of fragmented interpretations across the full stratigraphic column can introduce structural aliasing, inconsistent fault geometries, horizon overlaps, vertical contradictions, and uncertainty propagation into field-development decisions. These inconsistencies have direct operational consequences: reduced confidence in horizontal well landing, greater uncertainty in target depth, repeated model rework, weaker linkage between static and dynamic models, and avoidable risk during drilling execution. (Salib et al. 2024).</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Traditional structural modeling methods struggle with time-consuming updates and imprecise well placements within reservoir models. In fact, they are nothing but workarounds to overcome the shortfalls of structure framework algorithms by introducing fake or dummy wells with fake well tops to constrain the structure, resulting in neglected models and potential financial losses and/or missed opportunities. It's crucial to overcome these obstacles for a more reliable reservoir modeling and well placement strategy in the subsurface industry.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This paper presents an automated, unified full-column subsurface framework that integrates overburden, faults, horizons, formation tops, well trajectories, reservoir-specific interpretations, uncertainty propagation, and model-governance logic into a single authoritative structural model without using any dummy wells or well tops. The framework combines Bayesian-based Horizon Uncertainty Modeling, referred to in this work as COHIBA, Automated Structural Modeling (ASM), automated surface stacking, embedded validation rules, evergreen model-regeneration practices, and an Agentic AI Structural Quality Control (QC) Assistant. The AI assistant continuously reviews structural surfaces, verifies stratigraphic ordering, detects truncated surfaces, screens well-top mismatches, and provides explainable recommendations to geomodelers within a human-in-the-loop governance process. (Salib et al. 2024; Abrahamsen 2005; Abrahamsen and Benth 2001).</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Application of the workflow in a congested carbonate field-development setting demonstrated measurable improvements in structural integrity and model-governance efficiency. Automated surface stacking, validation, and reconciliation eliminated 15 identified cross-reservoir structural conflicts and horizon-stacking violations, resulting in a structurally consistent full-column framework. The Agentic AI QC Assistant evaluated 293 wells across 57 modeled reservoir zones within minutes, reducing structural quality-control effort by more than 95% compared with approximately one week of manual review per iteration. In addition, the AI-driven workflow identified and prioritized 25 well-top mismatches requiring expert review, enabling faster model updates, improved structural consistency, and increased confidence in horizontal well planning and multidisciplinary development decisions.</jats:p>

title: Unified Transient Gas-Liquid Flow Model for Simultaneous Influx-Loss and Safe MPD Drilling Time Evaluation in Fractured Carbonate Wells
container-title: ADIPEC
567123d85e058085cbebb816b741d0f9d6de28c8.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Fractured-vuggy carbonate reservoirs feature strong heterogeneity, and multiple pressure systems are commonly developed vertically. Gas influx and drilling fluid loss may occur simultaneously during drilling operations, significantly complicating wellbore pressure response, surface influx-loss characterization and pressure control operation. To quantitatively describe this type of working condition, this paper establishes a one-dimensional transient gas-liquid two-phase drift flux model applicable to multiple influx points and multiple loss points. Dynamic gas influx and loss source terms are introduced into the mass conservation equations of gas phase and liquid phase respectively, and the model is coupled with wellbore momentum equation, fluid temperature-pressure physical property model and surface choke boundary to calculate wellbore pressure, gas holdup, casing pressure, pit volume and gas migration process. Validation with field logging data shows that the average relative errors of the model for pit volume, casing pressure and gas arrival time at the wellhead are 1.62%, 3.31% and 3.21%, respectively. Under the condition of consistent pressure difference between influx and loss, the overall pressure response of three working conditions, namely influx in the upper interval with loss in the lower interval, loss in the upper interval with influx in the lower interval, and coexistence of influx and loss in the same interval, is similar. The pressure difference of source terms is the main factor controlling the flow state, while the position variation of influx and loss points within 400 m has limited influence. Reducing flow rate can slow down gas upward migration and casing pressure growth, but it also reduces bottomhole pressure; decreasing choke opening can compensate bottomhole pressure, but it restricts outlet flow rate. Therefore, adjusting a single parameter can hardly balance bottomhole pressure and safe MPD drilling time. Calculation of a case well shows that on the premise of meeting the critical flow rate for cuttings carrying, jointly adjusting choke opening and drilling fluid flow rate can extend the safe MPD drilling time from 61 min to 71 min, an increase of 16.4%. This model can provide a calculation basis for the identification of simultaneous influx and loss, casing pressure early warning and pressure control parameter optimization in fractured carbonate gas wells. This study provides a transient-modeling contribution by establishing a unified framework for simultaneous influx and loss during MPD, which enables quantitative evaluation of safe MPD drilling time under complex downhole conditions.</jats:p>

title: Seismic Foundation Model Assisted Rapid Seismic Interpretation
container-title: ADIPEC
dff05d07fb2ff47fcd6691e2d7b550119aed0469.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Training deep learning models for seismic interpretation tasks—such as geobody segmentation, stratigraphic interpretation, and salt body modeling—traditionally demands substantial labeled data, computational power, and time. To address these inefficiencies, this paper introduces a self-supervised learning approach to develop a seismic foundation model (FM) trained on a vast volume of unlabeled data. Utilizing Vision Transformer architecture guided by the DINOv2 paradigm, the foundation model learns robust visual representations from over 30 public datasets. The training framework employs student-teacher self-distillation with a weighted sum of cross-entropy losses to ensure consistency across augmented views. For efficient downstream adaptation, we freeze the core foundation model and employ a lightweight, convolutional neural network (CNN)-based segmentation head. This architecture minimizes computational costs and enables rapid model convergence using only a handful of labeled samples. We evaluate the framework on three critical seismic interpretation tasks: channel segmentation, clinoform extraction, and shallow gas field segmentation. When tested on the Parihaka seismic dataset, the model accurately segments complex channel systems and extracts sigmoidal-shaped clinoform structures with superior accuracy. Furthermore, evaluation on the Parihaka dataset demonstrates precise delineation of shallow gas field. Overall, these lightweight downstream models achieve a mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) of over 0.81 across all tasks, proving that the seismic foundation model offers a highly accurate, data-efficient, and computationally viable solution for modern subsurface interpretation</jats:p>

title: A Neural-Network Surrogate Model for Rapid Performance Prediction of Gas-Gas Supersonic Ejectors in Low-Pressure Gas Recovery Applications
container-title: ADIPEC
9182c2304603eefcf22d932c457ea6542a7e4ce3.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper presents a multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural-network surrogate model for predicting the performance of a gas-gas supersonic ejector across a wide range of operating conditions. The model enables rapid evaluation of multiple production scenarios, eliminating the need for time-consuming computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations to optimize ejector sizing and operating strategy for gas production applications where low-pressure wells require assisted recovery through high-pressure power fluid gas. A supersonic ejector geometry was developed through iterative CFD optimization comprising over 11,000 simulations of compressible isentropic methane flow. Three convergent-divergent nozzle configurations with throat diameters of 24, 27, and 30 mm cover power fluid flow rates from approximately 21 to 93 MMscfd. A structured design of experiments produced 13,724 CFD cases spanning power fluid pressures of 1,000–2,500 psi, secondary pressures of 50–600 psi, backpressures up to 1,000 psi, and temperatures of 273–344 K. MLP neural networks were trained on this dataset to predict power fluid and secondary flow rates, critical backpressure, minimum secondary pressure, off-design curves, and methane phase-change boundaries. The neural-network models achieved high predictive accuracy: R2 values of 1.000 for power fluid flow rate, 0.9989 for secondary flow rate, and 0.9996 for critical-point backpressure, with RMS errors of 0.015 MMscfd, 0.65 MMscfd, and 2.5 psi, respectively. Phase-change classification models reached accuracies of at least 98.7% across all three nozzle configurations. Independent validation against 514 CFD cases, run at operating conditions deliberately excluded from the training set, confirmed the model's generalization capability across intermediate pressures and temperatures. The surrogate model reproduces the full ejector performance map, including on-design and off-Design operating zones, phase-change boundaries, and efficiency contours in seconds rather than the hours required by each CFD run. This enables engineers to rapidly screen hundreds of production scenarios, optimizing nozzle throat-diameter selection, power fluid and secondary pressure combinations, and backpressure settings. The tool reliably identifies operating envelopes where secondary-gas recovery is maximized while avoiding methane condensation and off-design instabilities. These results demonstrate that neural-network-based surrogate modeling is a practical and accurate approach for accelerating the engineering workflow of supersonic ejector systems in gas production optimization. Unlike conventional approaches that require dedicated CFD specialists and hours of computation per scenario, this surrogate model compresses the entire ejector performance envelope into a tool that any production engineer can query in seconds. This shifts supersonic ejector evaluation from a specialized simulation exercise to a routine field-development screening task, enabling faster investment decisions and reducing engineering costs in low-pressure gas recovery projects.</jats:p>

title: Optimizing Large Scale Well Portfolios in Three Giant Middle Eastern Fields: A Data Driven Approach to Enhancing Production and Efficiency Through Proactive Opportunity Screening and Intervention Planning
container-title: ADIPEC
cbba580ad2520eb495561a3f3f0006c57a7f961c.abstract:
<jats:p>The upstream industry has spent the last decade instrumenting its wells and facilities, and the result is a steady stream of production, pressure, and surveillance data that grows faster than any team can read it. In large mature carbonate assets this creates a strange imbalance. The data needed to spot the next good intervention almost always exists somewhere, yet the process of finding, screening, and maturing that opportunity still depends on a handful of experienced engineers working through wells one at a time. Reviews that should take days often stretch into weeks, and by the time a candidate is agreed the production it was meant to protect has already been deferred. The scale only sharpens the point. A giant onshore field can hold a large and constantly shifting inventory of candidates, and the subset that is genuinely worth acting on this month is small, moves around, and rarely announces itself.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Well Portfolio Optimization, referred to here as WPO, was built to close that gap. It is an automated advisory system that continuously scans the full well stock, both active and inactive, and surfaces the interventions most likely to add value. Rather than replacing the reservoir or production engineer, it does the heavy lifting of screening and ranking so that scarce petrotechnical effort is spent on judgement rather than on data gathering. The system draws on subsurface data, production history, and engineering rules, and combines them inside a single framework that prioritizes candidates by production potential, economics, and probability of success.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This paper describes the thinking behind WPO, the elements that make up the solution, the workflows that run on top of it, and how a data driven screening philosophy differs from the physics driven studies engineers are used to. It also shares early field experience from deployment across three giant onshore fields, and it is candid about where the approach still needs a human in the loop.</jats:p>

title: A Model-Based Digital Thread Approach for Managing the Complexity of Next-Generation Offshore Support Vessels Design, Build, Delivery and Beyond
container-title: ADIPEC
aeabdfc9fa4ab5128a3847814ba06bbeaa3786ce.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives and Scope</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Growth in offshore wind, subsea construction, and carbon capture and storage is reshaping the missions OSVs are built to support. Traditionally designed to provide logistics, transportation, and operational support to offshore oil and gas installations, modern OSVs are now expected to support a much wider range of missions. These include offshore wind farm installation and maintenance, subsea construction and inspection activities, carbon capture and storage (CCS), low-carbon energy infrastructure remote and autonomous operations, environmental monitoring and operations involving increasingly sophisticated power and propulsion systems. At the same time, vessel owners and operators face growing pressure to improve sustainability, reduce emissions, enhance operational efficiency, and maintain compliance with increasingly demanding regulatory and classification requirements.</jats:p>
                    <jats:p>As a result, the design, construction, operation, and maintenance of OSVs have become substantially more complex than in previous generations of vessels. Modern vessels contain a greater number of integrated systems, including hybrid and electric propulsion architectures, advanced automation and control systems, dynamic positioning technologies, sensor networks, communication platforms, and mission-specific equipment. These interconnected systems generate large volumes of engineering, operational, maintenance, and regulatory information throughout the vessel lifecycle all the way from preliminary and initial designs to construction and further to operations and eventual refit.</jats:p>
                    <jats:p>Managing this information effectively has emerged as one of the primary challenges facing both shipbuilders and vessel operators. In many organizations, critical lifecycle information remains fragmented across multiple disconnected systems, databases, spreadsheets, documents, and departmental processes. This fragmentation often results in inconsistent information, duplicated effort, reduced traceability, delayed decision-making, and increased lifecycle costs. It also creates challenges when managing vessel modifications, upgrades, certification activities, and maintenance programs throughout decades of operation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Closing the Past, Securing the Future - Large-Scale Soil and Groundwater Remediation at ADNOC Refining Abu Dhabi Refinery, the UAE's First and Oldest Oil Refinery
container-title: ADIPEC
7c0bb8426ed324d1bb9a484e2e85edce31934fe0.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The Abu Dhabi Refinery (ADR), ADNOC's first and oldest oil refinery in the United Arab Emirates, has entered a new phase of its lifecycle: safe closure, environmental restoration, and preparation of the land for future community use. This paper presents the large-scale soil and groundwater remediation and land reclamation programme implemented as part of the Abu Dhabi Refinery Closure Project at Sas Al Nakhl. The objective of the programme was to remove or control historical hydrocarbon impacts, verify compliance with residential and open-space land-use criteria, and provide a technically defensible basis for land handover to support plan Abu Dhabi 2030. The overall closure programme was structured in three sequential phases: hydrocarbon-free decontamination and waste disposal; dismantling, demolition, and disposal of process units, buildings, foundations, and underground services; and soil remediation with land reclamation. Site characterization and remedial design were aligned with the Abu Dhabi Specification for Soil Contamination, ADS 19/2017, the Environment Agency - Abu Dhabi Soil Contamination User Guide, project-specific Scope of Work requirements, and internationally recognized risk-based remediation principles. The investigation and remediation works addressed petroleum hydrocarbon impacts associated with historical refinery infrastructure, including tanks, pipelines, utility corridors, process areas, and hydrocarbon handling zones. The final remediation strategy combined excavation, ex- situ soil washing, ex-situ bioremediation, in-situ bioremediation of soil and groundwater, and in-situ chemical oxidation. The programme was validated using a systematic sampling network supported by laboratory analysis of surface soil, composite subsurface soil, and groundwater. Verification results confirmed that remediation objectives were achieved, with post-remediation conditions suitable for the intended residential and open-space use. The project demonstrates how a legacy hydrocarbon asset can be closed responsibly through integrated engineering, regulatory engagement, environmental stewardship, and community care.</jats:p>

title: Red Palm Oil Administration in Undernourished Wistar Rats: Effects on Cognitive, Gastrointestinal, Skeletal, and Organ Parameters
container-title: An Idea Health Journal
e0f104d2a2eaedbeac3776f2088ad73e7d068247.abstract:
<jats:p>Background: Malnutrition affects multiple physiological systems, including cognitive, gastrointestinal, skeletal, and organ functions. Red palm oil (RPO) contains bioactive compounds that may influence physiological responses to malnutrition. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of RPO on biomedical parameters in undernourished Wistar rats.
Methods: This experimental laboratory study integrated several sub-studies using post-test-only and pretest-posttest control group designs. Male Wistar rats aged 3–4 weeks underwent 50% feed restriction for 14 days, followed by RPO administration at doses of 2, 4, or 6 mL/kgBW for 28 days. Groups included normal, negative, and selected positive vitamin A controls. Sample sizes varied across sub-studies. Data were analyzed using ANOVA, Kruskal– Wallis, post hoc tests, and correlation analyses, with p < 0.05 considered significant.
Result: Significant differences were observed in Y-maze cognitive performance (p = 0.031), intestinal weight (p = 0.003), femur weight (ANOVA p = 0.037; Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.048), and heart (p = 0.010), liver (p = 0.002), and kidney (p = 0.004) indices. Femur length differed significantly using Kruskal–Wallis (p = 0.042), but not ANOVA (p = 0.052). No significant differences were observed in hemoglobin levels (p = 0.494),motor performance (p = 0.120), lung (p = 0.070), or spleen (p = 0.120) indices.
Contribution for Practice: RPO administration produced variable responses across biomedical parameters, providing preliminary preclinical evidence for further nutritional research. However, inconsistent dose-response patterns and the absence of significant effects on several outcomes limit its clinical applicability. Further mechanistic and clinical studies are required before RPO can be recommended for nutritional rehabilitation.</jats:p>

title: Proppant Pack Conductivity Under Closure Stress: Physically Bounded Permeability Model
container-title: ADIPEC
a783e593f4fc68cc356f0ac22349d1c2e0a58939.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Reservoir stimulation enables production from low permeability reservoirs by creating hydraulic fractures that serve as flow pathways between the formation and the wellbore. Proppants keep these fractures open against the closure stress of the formation, and the conductivity of the proppant pack is critical for well deliverability throughout the life of the field. In the industry, engineers estimate the decay of proppant permeability using exponential decay functions, but these functions carry a fundamental defect: they predict both zero porosity and zero permeability as the effective closure stress increases, with no physically bounded lower limit. This study proposes new asymptotically correct relations between proppant permeability and applied stress that serve as potential substitutes for the conventional exponential decay models. The work reformulates three established compressibility models (hyperbolic, exponential, and power) in terms of the yield stress, computed at the point of maximum curvature of the compression curve consistent with the Casagrande method, and derives permeability models with bounded asymptotes through the power relation between permeability and void ratio. We compare the predictions of the proposed models with proppant and sand data compiled from published studies, and evaluate performance against the conventional exponential model. The hyperbolic model fits the compression data best, including the sharp decrease in void ratio after yield in brittle sands. The proposed permeability models predict the hydraulic conductivity from the fitted compressibility parameters with a single free λ-exponent, while the conventional model underpredicts or overpredicts the conductivity around the yield stress and the difference grows at high stress where the pack retains a finite residual conductivity. The framework implements in three stages: characterize the proppant once through standard laboratory tests, predict the permeability at any effective closure stress, and integrate the revised equations into fracture models for production forecasting in unconventional and geothermal operations.</jats:p>

title: Accelerating CO2 Plume Interpretation Using a Pre-Trained Seismic Foundation Model: An Example of Sleipner CO2 Storage Site
container-title: ADIPEC
1ca5a2b0843ded931b6c09a06dd7b1654b3bcb0b.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Accurate and robust CO2 monitoring is essential to ensure both the safety and sustainability of carbon capture and storage (CCS). While 4D seismic monitoring is among the most effective approaches, time-lapse data processing and interpretation remains costly, time-consuming, and labor-intensive. To reduce both the computational cost of data analysis and the dependence on human intervention, this study proposes two novel automated schemes for interpreting CO2 anomalies from migrated seismic images: one for rapid CO2 plume screening and the other for 4D anomaly extraction. Both leverage a pretrained seismic foundation model (SFM) to efficiently identify seismic patterns associated with CO2 accumulation and migration. Neither scheme requires manual labeling or additional model training, and therefore they significantly reduce the dependence on time-lapse data reprocessing and calibration. Specifically, the screening scheme rapidly scans an entire survey to locate sub-areas whose seismic patterns resemble a reference CO2 plume, based on similarity within the SFM embedding space. The anomaly-extraction scheme compares a pair of baseline and monitor seismic images in the same embedding space and extracts the geobodies associated with strong amplitude variations. The publicly available Sleipner CO2 storage site in the North Sea is used to evaluate both schemes. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed methods successfully identify and delineate the spatiotemporal evolution of the CO2 plume between 1999 and 2010. In addition to capturing the overall north-northeast to south-southwest (NNE-SSW) migration trend of the injected CO2, the methods accurately resolve its characteristic layered distribution within the reservoir. These observations are consistent with published seismic interpretations and numerous scientific studies of the Sleipner site, highlighting the capability of foundation-model-based workflows to deliver rapid, reliable, and scalable solutions for CCS monitoring applications.</jats:p>

title: In-House Refurbishment of Marine Breakaway Couplings: Transition from OEM Factory Refurbishment to an OEM-Authorized In-House Model
container-title: ADIPEC
c55c1bc929933c348296aa96d0bd5a2f1b4e246a.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Marine Breakaway Couplings (MBCs) are safety-critical devices in offshore tanker loading systems. They protect hoses, pipelines and terminal infrastructure by separating at a calibrated load and sealing both flow paths during excessive tension, tanker breakout or surge events. For Single Point Mooring (SPM) operations, reliable MBC performance underpins containment assurance, environmental protection and export continuity.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Terminals traditionally remove MBCs from service and export them to the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) for disassembly, inspection, critical-part replacement, testing and certification. This paper presents an OEM-authorized in-house refurbishment model that retains OEM technical authority while relocating routine execution to the asset owner through approved training, original procedures, traceable spare parts, calibrated tooling, independent witnessing and full lifecycle records.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The model is demonstrated at Fujairah Terminal, where 16 in. NB, ASME 300 lb controlled double-closure MBCs serve crude-oil SPM systems. A refurbishment programme valued at USD 600,000 across SPM-1, SPM-2 and SPM-3 in 2026 and 2028.</jats:p>

title: AI-Driven Facility Inspection Using Vision-Language Models and Image Classification: Model Selection and Prompt Design
container-title: ADIPEC
d8265c76ae65e95545cb9a875584fb23fb6e1b74.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Visual inspection remains essential at dispersed oil and gas facilities because many operating conditions cannot be inferred from instruments alone. Routine site visits provide this visual evidence, but they become difficult to scale when facilities are numerous and most inspections find nothing actionable. FieldView addresses this challenge through scheduled photography, automated image assessment, and human review. In the studied deployment, 200 cameras across 100 facilities produce about 2,000 images per day.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This paper considers two practical decisions in designing image-based inspections. The first is whether a task is better suited to an object detector, which locates and classifies a defined target, or a vision-language model (VLM), which can interpret evidence across a wider scene. The second is how much instruction a VLM prompt should contain. Rain-cap, flare, smoke, and spill inspections are used to examine how the visual evidence required by an engineering decision can guide model and prompt selection.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The study evaluates fixed detector and VLM configurations on expert-labeled field images for rain-cap, flare, smoke, and spill inspections. Matched-image comparisons are used where possible, with class-level metrics, statistical analysis, and error review used to interpret overall performance. The rain-cap detector achieved 97.72% mAP@0.5 on its validation set, demonstrating strong performance for a localized and consistently labeled target. For flare-state classification, the full-image VLM achieved 91.2% accuracy on the 227-image benchmark, compared with 69.2% for the fine-tuned detector workflow. The smoke configuration achieved 96.2% accuracy, while the selected spill configuration achieved 77.0% accuracy and a macro F1 of 0.756. Controlled prompt comparisons also showed that additional instructions, response fields, and decision procedures did not consistently improve accuracy. Together, the evaluations provide quantitative evidence across both localized targets and scene-level inspection decisions. These results are used to support engineering selection and validation of complete inspection configurations rather than to claim that one model family is universally superior.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The results indicate that model choice should follow the structure of the inspection rather than a preference for one model family. A detector performed well for the localized rain-cap task, while a full-image VLM was more effective for flare-state classification on the studied benchmark. Across flare and spill evaluations, additional prompt detail did not consistently improve accuracy. These findings support a measured workflow: define the visual evidence needed for the decision, test complete configurations on representative images, retain prompt additions only when they demonstrate value, and preserve human review for operational disposition.</jats:p>

title: From Flaring to Value: A Scalable and Digital Enabled Multi Well Pad Green Completion Model Delivering 94% Emissions Reduction in Oman
container-title: ADIPEC
2896e50a42d196c6b42bb4333256e788f4518459.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Hydraulically fractured gas wells commonly require extended cleanup and testing periods during which significant volumes of hydrocarbons may be flared. Strategies to reduce emissions by capturing and exporting hydrocarbons during well flowback, commonly called "Green Completions", have been deployed in several producing basins in the middle east, however widespread implementation remains challenged by facility interfaces, solids and water management requirements, process safety considerations, and operational complexity. The need for scalable solutions is increasing as operators seek to simultaneously reduce emissions and improve project value.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Shell Development Oman is advancing Green Completions as a component of its low carbon strategy by deploying reduced emission completion frameworks with a focus on enhancing asset performance during post-frac flowback operations. This addresses the dual challenge of maintaining production excellence while meeting stringent decarbonization targets.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This paper presents a novel case study of the design, planning, and execution of Green Completions in a tight gas condensate asset in Oman, constituting a next-generation model integrating multi-well pad operations, direct tie-in to production facilities, advanced four-phase separation and solids management, digital real-time surveillance, and simultaneous operations framework into a low-carbon value stream. The case study presents a roadmap for operators to reduce flaring while improving operational efficiency and value.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The case study highlights the successful integration of decarbonization objectives, process safety, and digital operational excellence, positioning Green Completions as a scalable and commercially viable solution for sustainable upstream development.</jats:p>

title: Hydrogen Fuel Switching in Refining Assets: Technical Integration and Economic Barriers to Large-Scale Deployment
container-title: ADIPEC
f87d0ed9aedc848dc3015c9f819ad9963e2acbfb.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The increased risks of climate change are becoming increasingly prevalent worldwide. Many refiners and operators have therefore made ambitious pledges to meet net zero emissions. This has led to growing interest in decarbonization opportunities to reduce Scope 1 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. While hydrogen firing has been demonstrated on individual refinery assets, refinery-wide deployment remains largely unexplored. This paper presents one of the first published refinery-scale assessments of hydrogen fuel switching, evaluating the technical integration requirements, economic performance, and decarbonization potential of large-scale deployment across a representative Middle Eastern refinery.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>A structured methodology was developed using experience from multiple refinery concept studies to assess hydrogen production, distribution, combustion equipment modifications, refinery fuel gas (RFG) management, and site integration requirements. Four fuelswitching pathways were evaluated: Existing Hydrogen Capacity - Partial Fuel Switching,Existing Hydrogen Capacity - Full Fuel Switching of Selected Consumers,Additional Blue Hydrogen Capacity - Full Fuel Switching,Additional Green Hydrogen Capacity - Full Fuel Switching.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Economic performance was assessed using the levelized cost of abatement (LCOA) over a 25-year project life.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The assessment identified fuel gas network limitations, hydrogen distribution infrastructure, management of displaced RFG, and plot space availability as the principal factors governing refinery-scale implementation. Results show that large-scale blue hydrogen production with integrated carbon capture emerged as the most economically attractive hydrogen fuel-switching option. The process proved to be more energy efficient for hydrogen production and carbon capture compared to the case using existing hydrogen capacity. This meant that over the 25 years operation it was much more economically attractive, as the fuel gas requirements make up a large proportion of overall project costs. Compared to the green hydrogen case the CAPEX costs are substantially lower. Green hydrogen production requires significant infrastructure for electricity production, electrolysis and energy storage.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Comparison with a representative refinery Carbon Capture, and Storage concept demonstrated that under the baseline pricing conditions the CCS concept returns slightly better economics for carbon abatement. However, sensitivity analysis showed that hydrogen fuel switching becomes increasingly competitive under conditions of high fuel gas prices, low electricity prices, and refinery layouts that constrain CCS deployment.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The study demonstrates that no single decarbonization pathway is universally optimal and highlights the importance of refinery-wide techno-economic assessments to identify the most effective site-specific decarbonization strategy and support long-term investment decisions.</jats:p>

title: The Power of Culture Innovative Strategies for Boosting Employee Engagement and Local Development
container-title: ADIPEC
a4aa52dfdf733917d4bff849ce5ab33d545f37cb.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The dual role of organizational culture as a catalyst for employee engagement and an enabler of local development outcomes was investigated using five expressive pillars: people, performance, innovation, sustainability, and partnership, that drive shifting values and behaviors within an organization.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The study employed a critical literature review to identify ten foundational cultural pillars; a semi-quantitative questionnaire with open-ended questions as a data instrument; mapping to design the ADNOC cultural model; and a culture matrix and predictive model for investigating the impact of the investment mix on the four cultural pillars on employee engagement and local community development.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The survey results indicated that 89% of respondents agreed that investing in organizational culture has a significant impact on employee engagement and local area development. Additionally, 81% agreed that it helps local development, while only a small number of respondents, 18% disagreed. These results are in agreement with Cameron and Quinn's contrasting values framework and align with Deal and Kennedy's corporate culture model. Our findings also confirm what other studies have found: investing in culture improves employee performance and enhances local development. The survey data also revealed that investing in people makes a significant difference in how employees behave and how engaged they are. On the other hand, investing in innovation empowers employees and leads to more new businesses and creative industries in the area. This is important because it shows that companies can make a real difference in their local communities by investing in culture. By focusing on the right cultural pillars, like people and innovation, they can create a positive impact that goes beyond just their own business.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>One of the outputs of the study, the cultural model, serves as a guide for what a good culture should look like, and the cultural matrix is a diagnostic tool to check how well a company is doing and what it needs to do to improve. The insights gained from the culture model and matrix fill the significant gap in the industry and advocate for the adoption of an intentional, data-driven cultural model by companies to sustain employee engagement and local development.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The study developed a predictive model that demonstrates how a good balance of investments across four culture pillars (people, innovation, sustainability, performance) can bring a positive impact on employee engagement and socioeconomic development of the local community. The sensitivity analysis demonstrated how investment mixes across the four cultural pillars influence employee satisfaction, community growth, company stability, creativity, entrepreneurship, and competitiveness.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Overall, our findings suggest that investing in organizational culture is key if companies want to make a positive impact on their local communities. By focusing on the cultural pillars and investing in the right ways, companies can create a win-win situation that benefits both their business and the community.</jats:p>

title: Virtual Flow Metering of ESP Wells Under Intermittent and Alternating Frequency Operation Using an Integrated Hydraulic and Electric Model
container-title: ADIPEC
663fd1a3999be4bd5134e6e4ee66d7a8ead1fc4c.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper considers an extension of an integrated approach to virtual flow metering model for wells equipped with electric submersible pumps and operated under periodic and alternating-frequency regimes.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>In recent years, many production companies in Western Siberia have concluded that one of the effective methods for operating low-rate wells equipped with ESPs is intermittent operation. The primary focus of this research is placed on the methodology for telemetry data preparation under intermittent operation, including operating-mode identification, separation of operating intervals from fluid accumulation periods, filtering of local outliers and communication losses, and conversion of integral flow-rate measurements into an instantaneous profile using reference telemetry parameters.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The proposed data-processing sequence is intended to exclude non-operating and transient states from the computational core and to generate physically consistent adaptation points suitable for subsequent hydraulic and electrical adaptation of the model by using ESP motor load, frequency, control station power and other parameters.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The main value and novelty of the study is that the article presents a new approach to virtual flow metering, including the calculation of the hydraulic and electrical components of a well with an ESP for a periodic mode and a mode with alternating frequencies.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The methodology was validated on 70 wells under intermittent operation, 50 continuously operating wells, and 45 wells under alternating-frequency operation. The median adaptation MAPE was 7.61%, 6.98%, and 7.25%, respectively, while the median virtual flow metering MAPE was 11.43%, 6.29%, and 9.59%, respectively.</jats:p>

title: A Novel LSTM Based Auto-Encoder Model for Reliable Mud Loss Detection
container-title: ADIPEC
26e767079aa04e0d2ea3f7ad09aae9d19a4709ea.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The mud loss incidents arise in drilling operations owing to various mechanical and operational factors. The complications related to a mud loss event are both cost inducive and a safety concern. Major challenges in mud loss detection studies are the wide variety and possible combination of reasons leading to mud loss incidents. As the database of mud loss incidents identified and categorized is not significant, datasets tend to be exceedingly imbalanced, rendering even the most advanced machine learning techniques ineffective. The problem of high class-imbalance is addressed in this research by using a state-of-the-art multivariate time-series LSTM (Long Term Short Memory) autoencoder based anomaly detector that is trained using a large quantum of normal drilling data. Another challenge to mud loss detection is the abrupt fluctuations during normal drilling operations, that can deceive the anomaly detector. To overcome this challenge, the study introduces a novel segmented time-series correlation function, which is the continuous correlation coefficient of particular drilling variables along the time axis that captures their correlated behavioral changes as opposed to their individual patterns. An LSTM autoencoder based anomaly detector is developed for reliable mud loss detection model by utilizing the coupled pattern provided by the correlation index of selected drilling variables that contribute to mud loss events. The proposed model has shown promising results for various classification metrics with a precision of 0.9597, recall of 0.9455 and F1-score of 0.9525. The test results obtained demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model in distinguishing mud loss events from normal drilling operations with good accuracy.</jats:p>

title: Digital Revolution in Coiled Tubing Operations: Pioneering a Remote Operations Center Framework that Redefines Intervention Efficiency, Asset Reliability, and Sustainability Across a Large-Scale CT Fleet
container-title: ADIPEC
41f76fd9cd9c133d5eddd6c981bdc5b9dc53e0c1.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Coiled tubing (CT) interventions have traditionally required significant field presence, intensive personnel deployment, and reactive decision-making. A Remote Operations Center (ROC) framework, integrating real-time asset health monitoring, live operational parameter surveillance, and remote expert engagement, fundamentally challenges this model. Deployed across a long fleet of CT units and validated in more than 100 jobs, this framework redefines how interventions are monitored, managed, and optimized by reducing well-site personnel dependency.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The framework operates through two integrated digital layers and three synchronized pillars. An asset health and monitoring platform delivers real-time visibility across injector head performance, pressure control equipment supply pressures, hydraulic readings, engine diagnostics, maintenance status, and operational parameters for each CT unit. A remote screen access and communication interface enables live data viewing, direct supervisor engagement, and real-time technical intervention without physical presence. Three pillars govern execution: a Field Team responsible for on-location job execution, a ROC Team providing live monitoring, engineering oversight, and technical decision support, and a Reliability Team managing equipment anomaly detection, alarm generation, and notification workflows.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Deployed across a fully digitalized fleet of CT units, the ROC framework consistently demonstrated its ability to detect and resolve critical deviations before escalation—including job design, treatment execution, equipment performance, tubing force verification, injector head chain behavior, and BOP supply conditions—interventions that conventional field-only execution models would have missed or delayed.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Operational efficiency increased by 80% year-on-year. Pipe failures were eliminated entirely in the first full deployment year. CT pipe life extension reached 39% in underbalanced operations and 78% in conventional operations, delivering combined maintenance savings exceeding 20% of the annual cost in supplies. Injector head chain twist incidents dropped 64% year-on-year. Sustainability outcomes proved equally transformative: diesel consumption fell 45% year-on-year, saving over 2.6 million liters, with reductions of 27 metric tons CO2e in Scope 1 and 545 metric tons CO2e in Scope 3 emissions. These combined results establish remote operations not as a support function, but as a core enabler of safer, smarter, and more sustainable coiled tubing intervention delivery.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Remote monitoring concepts exist broadly across oil and gas, yet a purpose-built ROC governing an entire CT fleet through integrated asset health surveillance, live parameter monitoring, and synchronized three-pillar expert engagement represents a step change in how coiled tubing interventions are managed. This framework establishes a new operational benchmark for the industry, offering a scalable and replicable blueprint to elevate CT intervention performance, asset reliability, and sustainability through structured digital transformation</jats:p>

title: A Data Driven Approach for Unlocking the Remaining Oil in a Large Heterogeneous Carbonate Field in Kuwait: Implications for CO2 EOR Full Field Development
container-title: ADIPEC
bc539d49260fbe2d2da32e8886dca72847fc9c48.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper describes a unique approach to unlock the remaining oil in a multi-layered heterogeneous carbonate reservoir in Kuwait undergoing peripheral waterflood since 1990's. The approach was instrumental in (i) Locating The Remaining Oil (LTRO), providing new insights into reservoir characterization, pore scale and sweep efficiency (ii) interpreting reservoir performance, considering interplay of geology and balance between viscous/gravity forces, and (iii) high-grading new opportunities, including strategies to unlock full-field CO2 EOR potential.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Analysis of the field production data, time-lapse logs and Miscible Gas Injection Pilot results concluded that existing reservoir models cannot fully capture detailed flow geology and saturation variations behind flood front in this large heterogeneous field. A data-driven/data-first workflow, that complements and challenges conventional modeling approaches, was created by integrating all available data into an interactive digital dashboard developed using python scripts. The field was subdivided into sectors to assess water movement in time steps. The visualization dashboards combined with regional geological insights enabled to explore the dataset to provide new insights and learnings of the field performance.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The LTRO exercise demonstrated that oil drainage primarily occurs from better-permeability reservoirs ahead of the advancing water flood front in reservoir sections close to initial oil saturation, leaving behind (i) un-swept less accessible better-permeability reservoirs, (ii) partially swept intermediate-higher- permeability reservoirs, and (iii) poorly swept, bypassed oil, occurring in lower-permeability reservoirs. This flow geology investigation enhanced understanding of the field's heterogeneity, highlighting the role of hydraulic flow units and baffles in causing water override and preferential flow regimes. An integrated review of all available data from the miscible gas-injection pilot provided added insight into reservoir de-saturation, inflow, and sweep during both the water and gas-injection phases. LTRO opportunities were identified to target those parts of the field where injection water throughput volume is low or negligible. Various development strategies were identified to unlock these opportunities across different parts of the reservoir and maximizing the full potential of the field using range of Improved Oil Recovery (IOR) techniques, including horizontal wells with Inflow Control Devices (ICD) to drain inaccessible and poorly swept areas, targeted infill drilling, rigorous well and reservoir management in partially-swept areas, followed by implementation of full-field miscible CO2 Water Alternating Gas (WAG) EOR.</jats:p>
