title: Functions of pairs of commuting self-adjoint operators under relatively bounded perturbations
container-title: Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society
b30bb1c47411841e45e3820ca30d3d4d03752d32.abstract: We study the behaviour of functions of pairs of commuting self-adjoint operators under perturbations by relatively bounded operators. We obtain analogs of our earlier results for functions of a single self-adjoint operator under relatively bounded perturbations. The main tool is double operator integrals.

title: Fostering Connections
container-title: Enhancing Classroom Well-Being Through Relational Teaching
a42383536037923b070c4b814d7202924804e25f.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the transformative potential of integrating Social-Emotional Learning (SEL) into relational teaching to create nurturing and dynamic educational environments. Relational teaching focuses on building meaningful, trust-based connections between teachers and students, recognizing that positive relationships are foundational for effective learning. By embedding SEL principles within this framework, educators can enhance students' emotional intelligence, resilience, self-awareness, and interpersonal skills, fostering both academic excellence and personal growth. Drawing from established theoretical models, the chapter provides a comprehensive exploration of SEL as a critical component of relational teaching. It presents evidence-based strategies, including classroom practices and teacher-student interaction techniques, to seamlessly incorporate SEL into daily pedagogical routines. Real-world case studies further illustrate the impact of this integration on classroom dynamics, student engagement, and overall well-being. Through these insights, the chapter offers a practical roadmap for educators to harmonize SEL and relational teaching, ultimately contributing to the development of emotionally intelligent, socially competent, and academically successful learners.</jats:p>

title: Higher Well-Being With Social-Emotional Learning and Relational Teaching in Early Childhood Classrooms
container-title: Enhancing Classroom Well-Being Through Relational Teaching
67d9cf36b839281d826ac5cbb247118262964f93.abstract: <jats:p>Research has shown that many adverse experiences negatively affect children's physical, social, and emotional development and well-being both in childhood and adulthood. Social Emotional Learning (SEL) is one of the many concepts and methods recommended to promote well-being. SEL skills help children understand, express, and regulate their emotions and adapt to adverse childhood experiences. Relational teaching (RT), on the other hand, is an approach that emphasizes that learning occurs as a result of the interaction between teachers and students, and therefore the role and attitude of the teacher in this interaction is important in the child's learning process. It supports the provision of a positive classroom climate and teacher-child interaction by shaping the teacher's classroom behavior. In this context, it can be said that RT can be a method and tool that will support and facilitate the SEL process with the teacher's stance. Developing SEL skills at an early age with the support of RT contributes to children's well-being by enabling them to cope with adverse life events.</jats:p>

title: Conceptualizing, Designing and Implementing Literacy Ecosystems for Sustainable Learning
container-title: Designing and Implementing Literacy Ecosystems
6471ade5e76190e4fceeeaa158568adcd727d116.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter discusses the concept, design and implementation of literacy ecosystems as an innovative approach to promoting sustainable learning in the twenty-first century. It defines literacy beyond the traditional ability to read and write; to include ecological, digital, cultural and systems literacies that prepare persons and communities to engage an increasingly complex world. Literacy ecosystems are contextualized as interconnected networks of learners, families, schools, communities, institutions, technologies and resources that collectively support lifelong learning and development. The chapter determines core principles instrumental in the development of effective literacy ecosystems, including inclusivity, adaptability, sustainability and collaboration among stakeholders. It links formal, non-formal and informal learning environments, generating continuous learning opportunities. Basing on case studies, the chapter establishes how literacy ecosystems encourage educational access, social inclusion, cultural preservation, economic empowerment and community resilience.</jats:p>

title: STEM Learning Through Functional Literacy in Primary Schools
container-title: Designing and Implementing Literacy Ecosystems
dcd4fb1f79905357d0f7a90b953a6814ebcf4355.abstract: <jats:p>Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts and Mathematics (STEM) aspirations have not translated into literacy-rich instruction. This study examined the role of functional literacy in STEM learning in Tanzanian primary schools through teachers' perceptions and practices and students' learning experiences. A convergent parallel mixed-methods design involved 89 teachers and 253 students from 12 schools across six low-performing districts. Data were collected through questionnaires, interviews, focus group discussions, classroom observations, and document analysis. Findings showed that teachers valued functional literacy but demonstrated limited understanding and implementation. Students reported weak classroom support and reliance on self-directed learning. Resource availability emerged as the strongest predictor of STEM learning. The study recommends improving STEM resources, training, and assessment.</jats:p>

title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
Project-Based Learning in Music Education
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
897f56ad810b9538a8cdca2c7451ed319c1a08fd.abstract: <jats:p>Music education is undergoing a global shift toward creativity, collaboration, and real-world relevance. Project-Based Learning (PBL) has emerged as an effective approach that engages students in meaningful, context-based musical experiences. This chapter presents a case study of a community-centered music project implemented in an undergraduate setting. Students assumed diverse roles as composers, performers, cultural curators, and event organizers, collaboratively creating and presenting a live community performance. The project followed a structured PBL framework integrating cultural exploration, original composition, and community engagement. Results show notable improvements in student motivation, creative confidence, ensemble performance, and intercultural awareness. This study contributes to innovative music pedagogy and provides practical insights for integrating PBL into music education.</jats:p>

title: Reviving Traditions Through Project-Based Learning and Innovative Technology in Punjabi Folk Music
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
a4d83da8d5d0e8762371da1d3d301b958fb96366.abstract: <jats:p>The Folk music of Punjab including famous folk forms has been the core of its cultural identity. However, due to modernization and impact of mainstream media, these traditional punjabi folk forms are being forgotten. This chapter provides a summary of previous and existing studies that use project-based learning (PBL) and innovative technologies to preserve Punjabi Folk music. Analyzing current literature and practical strategies, it examines how PBL involves students and communities in recording and performing traditional folk arts. It also investigates how technology such as virtual reality (VR) performances, artificial intelligence (AI)-powered music analysis and digital archives, improve accessibility and preservation of Punjabi Folk traditions. It emphasizes the opportunities of future research, effective practices and ethical awareness resulting into interdisciplinary collaborations between educators, technologists and folk artists in developing the authentic and community rooted experiences.</jats:p>

title: Lessons From China's Music-Led Aesthetic Education
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
1f21b1a7b696591986213a55df0f84a6394a7a9e.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter presents lessons from China on how project-based learning (PBL) can support aesthetic education in primary school music education through a design-oriented approach. The chapter argues that aesthetic learning does not emerge automatically through artistic activities but requires a coherent pedagogical design that connects participation, reflection, embodiment, and meaning-making across lessons. The chapter presents “Dream Theatre,” a music-led PBL in which students transform the traditional Chinese story “The Shepherd Who Mended His Fence After Losing Sheep” into a musical performance. The LivePBL DEEP Method (Direction–Education–Event–Project) is adapted to structure learning across project phases, interactions, and progression. Lessons learned from China indicate that aesthetic learning must be intentionally designed rather than assumed, embodied and collaborative participation is central to artistic PBL; the fragmentation in PBL is fundamentally due to a lack of project design methodology.</jats:p>

title: Effect of Nazrul Sangeet on Academic Achievement of Elementary School Students
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
d6db59cc87cbbbe13f4407fb6ca3e43d18501d92.abstract: <jats:p>This study examined the effect of Nazrul Sangeet on the academic achievement of elementary school students in Purba Bardhaman district, West Bengal, India. Using a quasi-experimental pre-test–post-test design, 50 Class VIII students were purposively selected and divided equally into an experimental group (n = 25), receiving traditional instruction augmented by weekly Nazrul Sangeet sessions, and a control group (n = 25), receiving conventional instruction only. Academic achievement in Bengali, English, and Mathematics was measured using a researcher-developed, expert-validated 30-item multiple-choice test. Results indicated a large negative effect size within the experimental group (Cohen's d = −0.715) and a moderate effect size between groups at post-test (Cohen's d = −0.665). A significant between-group difference emerged in Mathematics but not in Bengali or English. Among demographic variables, study duration and frequency of song listening significantly influenced post-test scores in the experimental group, whereas gender, location, and caste did not.</jats:p>

title: Beyond Musicology and Language, Not Beyond Culture
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
8345a25b5f58e41e2d4d64c1c9e449084f8bda42.abstract: <jats:p>Music allows rituals of emotional connection that transcend language, while dialogue offers an opportunity to interpret and articulate cultural perspectives across different eras. Cultural meaning-making processes through both affective engagement and reflective practice are possible through project-based approaches to musicology. Collaborations across civilizations highlight how effective communication between nations enables critical discussion of historical and social contexts regarding the patterns of cultural expression through emotions in music. This process also encourages students to develop critical thinking as they navigate the complexities of musical symbolism, cultural narratives, and the ways emotions are encoded and expressed. Ultimately, this approach highlights how cross-cultural musical engagement can cultivate empathy, insight, and collaborative understanding in global music education.</jats:p>

title: On Community-Based and Intergenerational Music Projects
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
fcda546019d160917ecddbbc8b8128d7709f97bf.abstract: <jats:p>PPPs and innovation ecosystems can be discussed as important tools in scaling development, accessing governmental assistance and commercial expertise and technology. Such partnership form vibrant worlds in which the stakeholders, firms, institutions, and policymakers push innovation, resources and knowledge exchange. PPP models allow financial freedom, policy facilitation, and risk dispersion whereas innovation systems facilitate innovation and dissemination of ideas. The two are together to help in scalable solutions in the different fields such as energy, health, and education. Proper governance, digitalism, and strategy alignment are needed to provide sustainability and an inclusive growth in these collaborative systems.</jats:p>

title: From Singing to Social Support
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
7b4983ef4de6a769e93cb8bdcb25560ba74645a5.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter discusses elderly singing as a socially embedded learning process. While existing research highlights the wellbeing and social benefits of group singing, it often treats these outcomes as natural results of participation without explaining how they are produced. Drawing on cases from Inner Mongolia, China, this study proposes a LivePBL DEEP (Direction, Education, Event, Project) design framework to structure elderly choirs as project-based learning networks. The framework views participants as active contributors whose roles develop from personal expression to collaboration and community engagement. Through three design cases, the chapter demonstrates that role development is a key mechanism for generating and sustaining social support. The study provides a practical approach for organising community music activities and supporting social networks through participation.</jats:p>

title: Raga to Reality
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
d3da0d818fee2c8236865688c262c44bc07e6ae3.abstract: <jats:p>Project-Based Learning (PBL) is increasingly considered a pedagogical approach that integrates creativity, collaboration, and experiential learning across learning contexts. PBL within Carnatic music classes, which shifts the learning context from a traditional, teacher-centered classroom to a rich, student-centered learning context. Employing constructivist and experiential learning theories, Through lesson observations, student reflections, and the analyses of descriptions of the project work, this study describes how PBL prompted deeper musical meaning, critical thinking, and independence as artists' in learning about raga, kriti, tala, and performance delivery. The chapter makes visible the institutional enablers and barriers, and the findings reveal how PBL scaffolds deeper conceptual engagement and aesthetic engagements in Carnatic music while improving engagement, motivation, cross-disciplinary connections and confidence in performance. PBL approach aiming to reinforce and encourage project based learning experiences in Indian classical music education</jats:p>

title: From Guru to Group
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
34b44ebf48ee6aec9ed0560ded23de783d64606d.abstract: <jats:p>Hindustani Classical Music is an Art form that is transmitted traditionally through the Guru-Shishya Parampara. There is no need to change teaching strategies because students' interests have broadened and collaborative skills are now essential. The Guru-Shishya Parampara preserves the style and depth of music, but it is necessary to combine contemporary teaching with it. Based on youth festival preparations, this study aims to understand how group rehearsal performances benefit students' learning. PBL in this chapter is a medium to bridge the gap between the modern education system and conventional training. According to practice sessions and observation interviews, this method improves students' tala grasp, raga understanding and stage confidence. It develops soft skills like teamwork and a collaborative learning environment, which boosts students' confidence. The study concludes that festival-based PBL is an excellent model for music institutions since it keeps Guru-Shishya Parampara while preparing students for modern-world challenges.</jats:p>

title: A Life-Cycle Social Foundation in Music Learning
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
27ff3cf21e019629c18ec0fcdec0b40d4206de47.abstract: <jats:p>This China-based chapter reconceptualises early years music curriculum as a design methodology for building a social foundation that supports life-cycle learning. Rather than viewing curriculum as content delivery, it argues that learning develops through structured interaction among children, teachers, families, and communities. Project-based learning (PBL) is explored as an approach for organising participation within existing curriculum systems, addressing fragmentation, limited continuity, and weak stakeholder integration. The chapter introduces the LivePBL DEEP (i.e., Direction, Education, Event, and Project) framework as a methodology for structuring developmental missions, relational engagement, shared action, and cumulative learning. Three design cases—rhythm games, chanting, and instrument exploration—demonstrate how everyday activities can function as socially embedded curriculum practices, offering implications for educational practice and research across diverse contexts.</jats:p>

title: Integrating Music, Movement, and PBL
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
f26b46b4f6abf5d9a07c431beeccc1630053e5a3.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the ways in which using music, movement and Project based learning (PBL) can enhance the learning and general development of the students. It offers a real-life example, in which the students collaborated to produce and perform their own music and movement-based projects on the theme of the community. The research indicates that this method enhances creativity, motivation, teamwork, and emotional abilities of students. It also makes students more attached to their culture and community. The chapter addresses issues like scarcity of resources, time management, and assessment problems in addition to the positive aspects. There are practical recommendations that can be given to teachers that desire to employ this method in their classrooms. On the whole, the chapter helps to appreciate the importance of learning based on creative and hands-on experiences to make the educational process more meaningful, inclusive, and enjoyable to students.</jats:p>

title: Orchestrating Children as Young Creators in the Curriculum
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
d3fedd17769b47ed2dac3101b7a9dd998ae68ae3.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter explores how young children become creators in music education. Here, orchestration means the coordination of social relationships and interactive participation through which creative learning develops. Although Project-Based Learning (PBL) research often discusses creativity and collaboration, less attention has been given to micro-level design structures for organising learning processes. The chapter presents a design-oriented PBL approach by adapting the LivePBL DEEP framework (Direction, Education, Event, Project) for creativity-oriented learning. In the Chinese context, the project case of “Our Sound Concert” is presented as three interconnected micro-projects involving sound exploration, experimentation, and collaborative performance. Based on a small-scale qualitative experiment, the study analyses how creativity develops through sound, peer interaction, and collective performance. The findings suggest that orchestrating learning processes is critical in fostering creativity in early childhood education.</jats:p>

title: Body, Voice, and Story
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
373321c91a2334110f0841ec2370f0d21a10546f.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter explores the incorporation of Theatre and Music through the PBL approach in child-oriented education through the concept of Body, Voice, and Story. In light of the increasing need for multidisciplinary education and experiences, this chapter highlights how movement, voice, music, and storytelling may contribute to the overall growth and development of children socially, emotionally, cognitively, and creatively. In terms of the Body dimension, it promotes movement, rhythm, gesture, and space; the Voice aspect stresses breathing, songs, sound, and speaking. PBL is further described here as having a natural fit for the use in performing arts education since activities related to theatre and music naturally include collaboration, inquiry, rehearsing, reflecting, and performing. Emphasis is also placed on the importance of cultural tradition, folk tales, oral histories, and community theatre to encourage multilingualism and intergenerational learning processes.</jats:p>

title: Coexistence of AI Nurse and AI-Simulated Patient in Nursing Education Using a Bidirectional Fine-Tuning Pipeline: Development and Content Analysis Study
container-title: JMIR Biomedical Engineering
83be49219b02021add3414e1cbea9cacaa7c21ab.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Simulated patient systems are essential in nursing education but face actor scarcity, instructor burden, cost, and disrupted continuity where in-person simulation cannot be sustained. Existing large language model (LLM)–based systems address these issues but treat the dialogic partner—the AI nurse—as a static prompt or unspecialized model, compromising data collection quality and pedagogical applicability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We report (1) the construction of 2 specialized fine-tuned models, NURSE-ONE (AI nurse) and PATIENT-ONE (AI-simulated patient), via a 5-step bidirectional fine-tuning pipeline; (2) their evaluation using Berelson content analysis validated by independent human coders; (3) an exploratory third-party evaluation by nursing faculty; and (4) the design of a coexistence simulation ecosystem supporting 3 operating modes, including offline disaster preparedness applicability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>On a single consumer-grade graphics processing unit (NVIDIA RTX 4090; 24 GB video random access memory), the multimodal base model gemma4-E4B-it was fine-tuned via low-rank adaptation in five steps: (1) a 251-scenario base from 29 institutionally authored nursing care plans and 20 items from the 115th Japanese National Nursing Examination; (2) a provisional dialogue system (AutoGen v18, maxmsg=25) to collect training dialogues; (3) NURSE-ONE fine-tuning across 3 training volume conditions (245, 735, and 1225 cases); (4) 4-condition Berelson comparison; and (5) PATIENT-ONE fine-tuning on NURSE-ONE–generated dialogues with a 3-condition comparison. Interrater reliability was confirmed by 2 independent nursing experts (196 blinded utterances, κ=0.770) and corroborated by 2 LLM raters (κ=0.742). Ten nursing faculty evaluated 3 coexistence modes in a working web user interface (21-item rubric; item-level content validity index=1.00).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Four-condition Berelson analysis (
                      <jats:italic>χ</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      <jats:sub>15</jats:sub>
                      =42.0,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001) identified the 735-case nurse-side condition (open question rate=21.5%) as NURSE-ONE; information collection rate reached 15.5% (~4× baseline) at 1225 cases. PATIENT-ONE A/B/C analysis (
                      <jats:italic>χ</jats:italic>

Third-party evaluation rated the AI-simulated patient, AI nurse, and dyadic interaction at 90.3%, 69.0%, and 84.8%, respectively, with role maintenance at ceiling (mean 5, SD 0).                     <jats:p>A 5-step bidirectional fine-tuning pipeline produced 2 specialized models whose joint deployment constitutes a design pattern for nursing education simulation. The preliminarily observed functional asymmetry between qualitative nurse-side variation and quantitative patient-side stabilization appears to underwrite the system’s coherence, supporting 3 operating modes on consumer-grade hardware and deployable offline in disaster preparedness contexts. Third-party evaluation confirmed exploratory educational applicability, with all evaluators rating the system as usable, providing a foundation for future learner outcome studies.</jats:p>

                      -score 0.493, exact match accuracy 0.621,±1-class accuracy 0.981). On the validation set used for architecture selection, the ensemble outperformed structured-only ML (XGBoost macro-
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>

                      -score=0.333,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001), and the LLM-only model reached a macro-
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>

                      -score of 0.642 (95% CI 0.525‐0.691), nominally exceeding the expert panel ceiling. Per-class analysis attributed this to a perfect score on the 2 validation ASA-PS 5 cases. Excluding that class, the adjusted macro-
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>

                    <jats:p>The parallel ML-LLM ensemble achieved performance approaching the theoretical ceiling established by the expert panel benchmark while providing interpretable clinical explanations. The ±1-class accuracy of 0.980 (95% CI 0.968‐0.992) may enhance operational safety by minimizing extreme misclassifications. This approach demonstrates how complementary AI architectures can enhance perioperative risk assessment, which is particularly valuable given current health care workforce shortages.</jats:p>
