title: A TOE–RBV–TBL Integrated Model of AI-Enabled Sustainable Food Logistics
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Food Logistics and Supply Chains
40d1fa5cdd6cd6c42b1d66704eea0c7b9caed768.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping food logistics by enhancing operational efficiency, reducing waste, and promoting sustainable supply chain practices. This study develops and validates an integrated Technology–Organisation–Environment (TOE), Resource-Based View (RBV), and Triple Bottom Line (TBL) framework to examine the determinants and outcomes of AI-enabled sustainable food logistics. Primary data were collected from 312 professionals in India's food supply chain and analysed using CB-SEM. The findings reveal that technological readiness, organisational capability, and environmental pressure significantly drive AI adoption, while AI capability positively influences environmental, economic, and social sustainability. The study offers a comprehensive theoretical framework and practical insights for policymakers and industry stakeholders seeking to build resilient, intelligent, and sustainable food supply chains.</jats:p>

title: AI-Driven Cold Chain Optimization for Reducing Food Loss in Perishable Supply Chains
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Food Logistics and Supply Chains
f7b19d3fb02e51972e9a5e5f799a5064e20516bb.abstract: <jats:p>With the combination of IoT-based monitoring, predictive analytics, and intelligent decision-making, AI-powered optimization of cold-chains increases the efficiency, reliability, and sustainability of perishable chains. Sensors can provide real-time data, therefore, monitoring the temperature, humidity, and logistics status continuously and predict risks of spoilage and optimizing routing, storage, and inventory control with AI models. In case studies in dairy, seafood and fresh produce, there has been a substantial decrease in the spoilage and increased efficiency in work. Traceability and compliance are additionally improved with the help of the blockchain integration. In general, cold-chain systems with AI will help minimize food waste, advance food quality, and sustain logistics in complicated supply chains.</jats:p>

title: AI-Based Quality Monitoring and Food Safety Management
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Food Logistics and Supply Chains
2f988859afeb8045e1f8933ad6d0b777eed57974.abstract: <jats:p>AI has transformation in the area of food quality inspection and safety management due to the capabilities that have been introduced in rapid, precise, non-destructive and predictive assessment of food quality through the production process, processing, storage, transport, retailing and consumption. These techniques are applicable in fast monitoring and quick intervention in areas of dairy products, meat products, seafood, fruits and vegetables, cereals, beverages and ready to eat meals. This chapter discusses the principles, technologies, applications, benefits, challenges, and future prospects of AI-based food quality monitoring and safety management, with particular emphasis on intelligent sensors, real-time contamination detection, automated inspection, shelf-life prediction, process optimization, traceability, and predictive risk management across diverse food sectors.</jats:p>

title: AI-Based Predictive Analytics for Sustainable Demand Forecasting in Agri-Food Logistics
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Food Logistics and Supply Chains
ae908a7d83acc41af9c9be1d1de1a65faa9f8570.abstract: <jats:p>Predictive analytics, which is an AI technology, is changing the logistics of agri-foods by enhancing sustainability and demand forecasting. The conventional predictive approaches do not normally reflect their dynamic aspects, including weather fluctuations, market behavior and consumer behaviors, resulting into inefficiencies and food wastage. This chapter describes an AI-based framework that combines multi-source data, machine learning models, and decision support systems to come up with correct and real-time demand forecasts. The strategy facilitates optimal inventory control, effective distribution strategy, and minimized environmental concerns. There are enormous evidences of case studies showing enhancement of accuracy in forecasts, reduction of wastes, and efficiency in the operations. The results address the possible opportunities of AI assisting the resilient, adaptive, and sustainable food supply chains in the fast-changing global food system.</jats:p>

title: AI-Driven Innovations in Agri-Food Supply Chains
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Food Logistics and Supply Chains
700ec2c44d31bcf14cea8b84c21efb4ae0bd8c73.abstract: <jats:p>Algorithms and other AI tools are increasingly being used to improve the efficiency, sustainability, and resilience of the Integrated Agri-food Supply Chain (IASC) across several areas of the agri-food sector. Innovations enabled by using AI technologies in agri-food systems referred to in this chapter are the ones that will achieve the best production, processing, distribution and consumption. The predictive analytics, machine learning, and intelligence-supporting tools are all about ensuring that requirements are always checked and predictable, resources are deployed,, and risk minimisation is done in real time. AI and Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, blockchain platforms, and automated logistics are explored, and the potential for creating transparent, traceable supply chains that adapt to fluctuating demand and supply is investigated. Case studies have been presented that show successful applications and improvements in productivity, waste minimisation,, and operational costs.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Driven Real-Time Route Optimization for Dynamic Food Logistics and Supply Chains
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Food Logistics and Supply Chains
a3d254406bb275561bb5d6e8d0065c094ec34437.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter describes how to use real-time data analytics and machine learning to automatically simulate and execute alternative food logistics routes to predict supply chain bottlenecks (such as supplier failures or natural disasters) before they occur. Based on academic publications from 2024 to 2026, the chapter uses a systematic review and thematic content analysis. The findings show that AI and data analytics are transforming food logistics and supply chains into sustainable, efficient, and creative transportation. Traditional logistics systems suffer from poor order consolidation, low truck capacity utilization, static route planning, and significant environmental impacts. Efficiency losses increase operational expenses, delay supply, and increase carbon emissions, threatening sustainability. Cloud-based data platforms and reinforcement learning optimize logistics and route planning. Logistics sustainability demands data-driven decision-making and clever automation.</jats:p>

title: AI-Driven Sustainable Food Logistics
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Food Logistics and Supply Chains
1ca0d752e991777e60571046cca42e7e93889d3a.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the transformation of agri-food supply chains through artificial intelligence (AI), emphasizing sustainable food logistics, resilience, and human resource management (HRM). It highlights how AI-driven technologies such as machine learning, IoT, and predictive analytics enable real-time decision-making, demand forecasting, and supply chain optimization, thereby reducing food waste and improving efficiency. The study integrates sustainability dimensions—environmental, economic, and social—with resilience strategies to address disruptions and uncertainties. Furthermore, it explores the critical role of HRM in facilitating workforce transformation, human–AI collaboration, and organizational change. An integrated AI–Sustainability–HRM framework is proposed to enhance adaptability and long-term performance. The chapter contributes to theory and practice by presenting a holistic, data-driven approach to building intelligent, resilient, and sustainable food logistics systems.</jats:p>

title: AI-Powered Predictive Analytics for Food Waste Reduction in India's Perishable Supply Chains
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Food Logistics and Supply Chains
fc88c02780841f38b3f41c69dae42b101d38d76a.abstract: <jats:p>In this chapter, we focus on the role that AI-driven predictive analytics can play to assist with forecast accuracy, cold-chain orchestration, quality monitoring and speed of response upstream and downstream through the farm-to-market flows to abete food loss and waste in India´s perishable supply chains. It relies on a systematic secondary empirical synthesis of India-centric studies, policy papers, and analytics research on global experience pertaining to high perishability classes of vegetables, dairy, fish, and other fresh fruits. The chapter proves that besides infrastructural hurdles, food waste challenges of India is also a challenge of timing, visibility and coordination. Evidence from India reveals how much of the loss occurs is seasonally driven, how losses are correlated with harvest volume, storage, transport reliability, and the quality sorting and practices. This chapter presents a predictive analytics framework for agri-logistics, suggests how Indian firms and policymakers can implement the approach, and claims that digital traceability.</jats:p>

title: Predictive Business Intelligence Architectures for Cold-Chain Logistics Mitigating Food Waste Through AI-Driven IoT Sensor Integration
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Food Logistics and Supply Chains
791f2efff6e75d93d6ead2cbd5779a343d5628c2.abstract: <jats:p>Food loss and waste in cold-chain logistics result not only from refrigeration failures, but also from fragmented data, delayed responses, and weak coordination across supply-chain actors. This chapter presents an IGI-style conceptual and implementation framework for predictive business intelligence (BI) in cold-chain logistics. It argues that waste reduction is more effective when Internet of Things (IoT) sensing, event-driven data integration, and artificial intelligence (AI) analytics are designed as a layered architectural capability rather than as stand-alone monitoring tools. Drawing on literature in cold-chain management, food quality, wireless sensing, BI, predictive analytics, AI-enabled supply chains, and digital twins, the chapter shows how variables such as temperature, humidity, location, door events, shock, dwell time, and product condition can be transformed into risk scores, dynamic shelf-life estimates, prioritized exceptions, and closed-loop decisions. It also proposes architecture and seven implementation workstreams for deployment.</jats:p>

title: Sustainable Cold Chain Management Using AI and IoT
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Food Logistics and Supply Chains
60daab0ba3149ca77331fc247ab25917cceed633.abstract: <jats:p>The convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) is fundamentally reshaping cold chain logistics, enabling unprecedented levels of precision, transparency, and sustainability. This chapter examines how intelligent sensing, predictive analytics, blockchain-based traceability, and digital twin simulation collectively address the chronic inefficiencies of temperature-sensitive supply chains. Drawing on recent empirical and review studies, the chapter presents an integrated framework that links real-time data acquisition to AI-driven decision-making and blockchain-anchored accountability. Key themes include spoilage prevention, carbon footprint reduction, regulatory compliance, and consumer trust. The chapter concludes with a forward-looking perspective on challenges and emerging directions for scalable, equitable, and ethically grounded cold chain transformation.</jats:p>

title: Adolescents’ Perspectives on Uptake, Engagement, and Implementation to Inform the Development of a Preventive Transdiagnostic Digital Mental Health Intervention: Qualitative Interview Study
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
035d301ed77fce4e74ca0175c7cadf9839d24f1a.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Adolescence is a critical period for mental health prevention; yet, many young people face barriers to help-seeking, including stigma, limited mental health literacy, and restricted access to services. Preventive digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) offer a scalable, low-threshold approach to early support, but uptake and sustained engagement remain limited. Existing research has predominantly relied on quantitative methods and has only partly captured adolescents’ perspectives. Qualitative research is therefore needed to inform the design and implementation of preventive DMHIs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to explore adolescents’ perspectives on factors influencing the anticipated uptake, expected engagement, and implementation of preventive transdiagnostic DMHIs across person, intervention, and system levels.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This qualitative study was conducted in Switzerland using a single-interview design in the predesign phase of the development of a transdiagnostic preventive DMHI. Adolescents aged 12‐21 years were recruited through voluntary response sampling via social media and the project website. Semistructured interviews explored experiences with online help-seeking, factors influencing DMHI anticipated uptake and expected engagement, and recommendations for implementation. Interviews were conducted in person or via video call between January and June 2022, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using a hybrid deductive-inductive qualitative content analysis. Intercoder agreement was assessed using Cohen κ (κ=0.72).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 48 adolescents (mean age 16.52, SD 2.67 years; 32/48, 72.9% female) participated. In total, 8 main topics and multiple subtopics were identified across person, intervention, system, and cross levels. Person-level factors highlighted the importance of mental health literacy, preuptake communication, and relevance of social networks. Intervention-level factors emphasized usability, personalization, and privacy, while system-level findings reflected expectations for adaptive, integrated, and low-threshold mental health services. Trust and support emerged as cross-level factors for engagement. In addition, participants described several discrepancies between desired intervention characteristics and practical implementation, particularly regarding personalization, anonymity, peer exchange, and human support.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Adolescents’ perspectives highlight that successful implementation of preventive DMHIs requires attention beyond intervention design to preuptake communication strategies, mental health literacy promotion, and integration within adaptive care systems. The tension between adolescents’ desire for immediate human-delivered support and the self-guided nature of preventive DMHIs underscores the need for clear clinical boundaries and explicit escalation pathways.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Multi-task Learning with Active Learning for Arabic Offensive Speech Detection
container-title: ACM Transactions on Asian and Low-Resource Language Information Processing
e788316b806502944a78e6f59c6c7305715445d0.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid growth of social media has amplified the spread of offensive, violent, and vulgar speech, which poses serious societal and cybersecurity concerns. Detecting such content in Arabic text is particularly complex due to limited labeled data, dialectal variations, and the language’s inherent complexity. This article proposes a novel framework that integrates multi-task learning (MTL) with active learning to enhance offensive speech detection in Arabic social media text. By jointly training on two auxiliary tasks, violent and vulgar speech, the model leverages shared representations to improve the detection accuracy of offensive speech. Our approach dynamically adjusts task weights during training to balance the contribution of each task and optimize performance. To address the scarcity of labeled data, we employ an active learning strategy through several uncertainty sampling techniques to iteratively select the most informative samples for model training. We also introduce weighted emoji handling to better capture semantic cues. Experimental results using the OSACT2022 dataset show that the proposed framework achieves a state-of-the-art macro F1-score of 85.42%, outperforming existing methods while using significantly fewer fine-tuning samples. The findings of this study highlight the potential of integrating MTL with active learning to efficiently and accurately detect offensive language in resource-constrained settings.</jats:p>

title: Development and Content Validation of a Self-Assessment Checklist for Electronic Medical Record Use Certification in Korea: Convergent Mixed Methods Study
container-title: JMIR Medical Informatics
f7bcf70cfcb107b154b2515e53f9c6d9423b48f9.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Electronic medical record (EMR) certification programs have traditionally focused on product-level requirements, such as interoperability, security, and core functionality. However, growing evidence suggests that many patient safety risks associated with EMRs arise after implementation and are closely related to system configuration, workflow integration, and real-world use. Despite the presence of a national EMR product certification system in Korea, a systematic evaluation of how certified systems are implemented and used in clinical practice is still lacking.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to develop and validate a self-assessment checklist for EMR use certification, focused on patient safety-critical functions, and to evaluate its content validity and expert-assessed practical applicability across health care institutions of different sizes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A convergent mixed methods design was used. A self-assessment checklist comprising 10 patient safety–related EMR functions was developed by adapting the US Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology self-assessment templates to the Korean EMR certification context. Content validity was quantitatively assessed using the Content Validity Index across 4 dimensions (relevance, usefulness, clarity, and importance) by a panel of 24 experts with experience in EMR implementation and certification. Qualitative feedback was collected through open-ended survey questions to examine feasibility, anticipated challenges, and differentiation between product and use certification across tertiary referral hospitals, general hospitals, and clinics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The overall Scale-Level Content Validity Index was 0.921, indicating strong content validity for the proposed checklist. Although most items demonstrated high agreement, lower ratings were observed for certain functions, particularly in clinic-level settings, reflecting structural and resource-related constraints rather than limited recognition of patient safety priorities. Qualitative findings highlighted challenges related to staffing, system governance, and the feasibility of assembling multidisciplinary assessment teams in smaller institutions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The self-assessment checklist demonstrated high content validity and was perceived as relevant for evaluating patient safety–critical aspects of EMR use. However, expert-assessed feasibility varied across health care institution types, particularly in clinic-level settings. Further empirical testing is needed to assess the checklist’s reliability, usability, and applicability in real-world certification processes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Digital Skills and Professional Judgment in AI-Driven Financial Decision-Making
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
fa94d39fbd808cc46e56a32eb78b60762c9d5124.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping financial decision-making by altering how information is analyzed, interpreted, and translated into professional judgment. This chapter examines the role of digital skills in determining whether AI strengthens or undermines the quality and accountability of financial decisions. Drawing on interdisciplinary literature, the chapter conceptualizes digital skills as cognitive–governance capabilities that extend beyond technical proficiency to include critical interpretation, calibrated reliance on AI, explainability, professional skepticism, and ethical judgment. Particular attention is given to automation bias, accountability risks, and the organizational conditions that shape human–AI interaction. The chapter concludes that responsible AI-enabled financial decision-making depends not on algorithmic capability alone, but on the alignment of digital competence, professional judgment, and effective governance.</jats:p>

title: From Financial Accountant to Digital Finance Architect
container-title: Digital Competencies and Skills for Future Finance Professionals
301bb7a811700c54a3c8f72796dd343a397ed320.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter analyzes the digital transformation of the finance function as a structural reconfiguration of processes, decision-making logic, and governance. It demonstrates how automation, artificial intelligence, sustainability, and RegTech are shifting traditional job profiles from process execution to the architectural design of digital financial systems. On this basis, the Digital Finance Competency Architecture (DFCA) is developed, integrating technological, data-analytical, governance-related, and strategic-cognitive competencies. The analysis illustrates that effective performance in digital finance environments requires systemic competence, i.e., the ability to translate data, models, and regulatory requirements into coherent decision-making architectures. Finally, implications for education, organization, and governance are discussed, and the Digital Finance Architect is established as a new professional role model.</jats:p>

title: The role of interferon-stimulated long non-coding RNA PKR-IT1 in the regulation of Zika virus and dengue virus replication and antiviral response
container-title: Microbiology Spectrum
cd94fcc28d752a838699b89fc7f13504f2018f34.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title/>
                    <jats:p>Interferon-stimulated genes play a critical role in the innate immune response against flaviviral infection. While recent studies have reported that interferon-stimulated lncRNAs participate in antiviral immunity, the functions of numerous lncRNAs in host-flavivirus interactions remain uncharacterized. Here, we demonstrate that the expression of lncRNA PKR-IT1 is induced by ZIKV and DENV infection. PKR-IT1 was induced by virus, poly(I:C), and IFNs in A549 cells, but this induction was largely abolished upon knockout of IPS-1 or IFNAR1 during viral infection. Additionally, PKR-IT1 overexpression inhibited viral production, whereas its suppression in A549, Huh7, and SH-SY5Y cells enhanced ZIKV replication. In PKR-IT1 knockout cells, viral replication also markedly increased compared with that in control cells. Interestingly, PKR-IT1 overexpression enhanced the activation of the JAK-STAT signaling pathway triggered by flaviviral infection and upregulated ISG expression. Conversely, PKR-IT1 deficiency decreased JAK1 and STAT1 phosphorylation levels, thereby impairing ISG expression. Mechanistically, the silencing of STAT1 in PKR-IT1-overexpressing cells partially restored ZIKV replication. Furthermore, PKR-IT1 directly bound PABPC1 and promoted its proteasome-dependent degradation. PABPC1 was found to bind to ZIKV RNA, while the inhibition of PABPC1 attenuated the levels of ZIKV protein, viral particles, and later viral RNA. Notably, the reintroduction of PABPC1 restored viral replication in PKR-IT1-overexpressing cells. Clinically, PKR-IT1 levels negatively correlate with fever duration and symptom number, and are lower in DENV-infected patients with severe leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. In summary, PKR-IT1 modulates flavivirus replication and JAK-STAT signaling, and may serve as a clinical correlate of dengue severity, offering insights for antiviral therapy development.</jats:p>
                    <jats:sec>
                      <jats:title>IMPORTANCE</jats:title>
                      <jats:p>Flaviviruses such as ZIKV and DENV pose significant public health threats, yet the roles of long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) in host antiviral immunity remain poorly understood. Here, we identified that PKR-IT1, as an interferon-stimulated lncRNA, not only suppresses flavivirus replication by binding PABPC1 to promote its proteasome-mediated degradation, but also enhances the activation of the JAK-STAT signaling cascade during flavivirus infection. Importantly, clinical correlations reveal that lower PKR-IT1 expression is associated with severe leukopenia and thrombocytopenia in DENV-infected patients, as well as longer fever duration and more symptoms. These findings establish that PKR-IT1 not only acts as a novel modulator of both flavivirus replication and the JAK-STAT signaling pathway, but also may serve as a correlate of dengue disease severity. By elucidating a previously uncharacterized lncRNA-mediated regulatory mechanism, this work provides a foundation for developing therapeutic strategies and prognostic tools against flaviviral infections.</jats:p>
                    </jats:sec>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Evaluating an AI-Powered Patient Simulator for Communication Skills Training: One-Year Randomized Controlled Trial
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
95a62b89e12f29ec2d10ee4b3bff78918b9670c6.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Clinical communication skills are a core yet complex competency in medical education and practice. However, early-stage medical students often struggle to apply communication frameworks in practice due to limited opportunities for structured simulation training. Generative AI (GenAI)–supported training has the potential to offer a scalable and innovative approach for clinical communication skills training.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examined the longitudinal development of medical students’ clinical communication skills over 1 academic year and investigated whether AI-powered simulation contributed to differential improvement relative to conventional training. In addition, the study explored motivational, behavioral, and affective mechanisms associated with communication skills development.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A nonblinded randomized controlled design was used at a medical school in the United Kingdom, with students assigned either to the control group (n=28, 56%) or to the AI group (n=22, 44%), who practiced with SimPatient, a patient-simulator chatbot accessed through a web browser. Communication skills performance was assessed using standardized objective structured clinical examinations (OSCE) scores relative to the pass marks to enable comparison across time points. Paired t tests and difference-in-differences (DID) analyses were conducted between groups and over time to examine changes in communication skills. Latent change score modeling was used to identify predictors of communication skills change. Sentiment analysis was conducted on 6120 comments from AI-student conversations. Finally, a system quality survey was used to assess participants’ feedback on the AI-powered simulator.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Latent change score modeling showed that gains in intrinsic motivation and behavioral learning were significant predictors of students’ communication skills change. The AI group showed a greater descriptive increase in communication skills than the control group, yet the between-group difference was not statistically significant. Within the AI group, consultations whose lexical tone trended more strongly toward resolution (consultation tone) were descriptively associated with communication skills improvement; given the small subsample (n=17), this finding is reported as exploratory. The AI group’s confidence level in AI use was negatively associated with communication skills improvement, while the group nevertheless reported a generally high level of satisfaction with the system.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this study, medical students’ clinical communication skills increased over the academic year, with this development most strongly associated with their motivation and behavioral engagement; the AI-supported group did not differ significantly from conventional training. The simulator responded appropriately and provided a usable environment for practicing foundational communication behaviors but was limited in capturing the affective complexity, vulnerability, and narrative unpredictability of real clinical encounters. In conclusion, this study suggests that GenAI holds promise for supporting foundational clinical communication training and providing positive practice environments, thereby fostering motivation and behavioral engagement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Generalizing equilibrium propagation to Lagrangian systems with arbitrary boundary conditions and equivalence with Hamiltonian echo learning
container-title: Neuromorphic Computing and Engineering
6aba435dd3046edb46583af3bca9f846866563f9.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Equilibrium Propagation (EP) is a learning algorithm that applies to Energy-Based Models (EBMs) on static inputs. It estimates loss gradients by contrasting two steady states of the same EBM, rather than resorting to explicit adjoint dynamics. EP originally appealed as a plausible learning theory for biological substrates and has more recently attracted interest for its amenability to analog hardware. Extending EP to time-varying inputs and outputs is a challenging problem, as the variational description must apply to the entire system trajectory rather than just its steady state. While the use of the action of a Lagrangian system as an energy function appears as a natural choice—which we herein refer to as
                    <jats:italic>Lagrangian Equilibrium Propagation</jats:italic>
                    (LEP)—careful consideration of boundary conditions was largely overlooked in prior studies although it becomes essential. It is also unclear how applying LEP to Lagrangian systems theoretically relates to applying
                    <jats:italic>Hamiltonian Echo Learning</jats:italic>
                    (HEL) algorithms—i.e. Hamiltonian Echo Backpropagation and Recurrent Hamiltonian Echo Learning —to Hamiltonian systems. In this work, we thoroughly revisit LEP and demonstrate that different learning algorithms can be obtained depending on the boundary conditions of the system, many of which are impractical to simulate—e.g. with a prohibitive memory or computational cost, or requiring explicit Jacobian computation. We also show that HEL algorithms, which are much easier to simulate, can be explicitly cast as a special case of LEP where the initial conditions can be picked arbitrarily. Building upon this connection enables the extension of LEP to a broader class of systems with dissipation terms. By filtering out intractable instantiations of LEP and building an explicit mapping between HEL and LEP algorithms, this work facilitates the simulation of self-learning Lagrangian systems as well as extensions of LEP to broader classes of physical systems.
                  </jats:p>

title: Utilizing machine learning and MALDI-TOF MS platform for rapid detection of ceftriaxone-resistant nontyphoidal Salmonella
container-title: Microbiology Spectrum
0007814d2a85a4f8ede0188bb91d2dc1d46494a3.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title/>
                    <jats:p>
                      Ceftriaxone (CRO) is a first-line antibiotic for pediatric nontyphoidal
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Salmonella</jats:italic>
                      (NTS) infections, but rising resistance threatens public health. Conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing remains time-consuming, delaying treatment. Although MALDI-TOF MS enables rapid microbial identification, it lacks inherent resistance detection. This study integrates MALDI-TOF MS with machine learning to predict CRO resistance in NTS. Using 472 isolates (1,414 spectra) from three medical centers, we developed and validated a model based on the Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LGB) algorithm. With only seven features, LGB achieved AUCs of 0.94 (training), 0.88 (internal validation), 0.79 (external validation 1), and 0.80 (external validation 2). We further deployed the model as an interactive Streamlit web interface to demonstrate its potential usability and facilitate future laboratory evaluation. This approach provides a proof-of-concept framework for rapid preliminary prediction of ceftriaxone resistance in NTS using routinely generated MALDI-TOF MS spectra. However, further large-scale, prospective, multicenter validation is required before this model can be implemented as a routine clinical susceptibility testing tool.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>IMPORTANCE</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The increasing prevalence of ceftriaxone-resistant nontyphoidal
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Salmonella</jats:italic>
                      in pediatric patients, particularly in cases requiring antimicrobial therapy, highlights the need for faster antimicrobial susceptibility testing. In this study, we developed a machine learning model integrated with MALDI-TOF MS to predict ceftriaxone resistance in NTS and deployed it as a web-based research-use interface. This proof-of-concept approach may support the future development of rapid adjunctive tools for antimicrobial resistance prediction.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Cost Learning and Strategic Inventory: Who Should Carry Inventory in a Vertical Supply Chain?
container-title: Manufacturing & Service Operations Management
813a51fae39625afc1d5b853031bf4579caa49be.abstract:
<jats:p>Problem definition: In a decentralized supply chain, the downstream retailer (he) may strategically carry inventory to induce lower future wholesale prices, triggering the upstream manufacturer (she) to raise the early-period wholesale price to deter such behavior. In the presence of cost learning, where future production cost declines with cumulative early-period production, the manufacturer faces a key trade-off. To accelerate cost learning, should she lower the early-period wholesale price to encourage larger retailer orders and downstream inventory carryover, or should she instead overproduce in the early period and hold inventory herself, bearing the holding cost? Methodology/results: We develop a game-theoretic model to capture such supply chain interactions in the presence of the manufacturer’s cost learning and the retailer’s strategic inventory. We characterize the conditions for different inventory-holding patterns in the supply chain, where only the manufacturer, only the retailer, both, or neither carries inventory. Countering the established notion that a manufacturer should hold inventory to enhance cost learning when her holding cost is low, our research reveals that she should abstain from holding any inventory, even at zero holding cost, when the retailer’s holding cost is sufficiently low. Further, we show that the manufacturer should completely refrain from holding inventory as an instrument to accelerate learning, irrespective of the retailer’s holding cost, when there is no uncertainty associated with cost learning or when the learning benefits are realized continuously. Managerial implications: Our results guide manufacturers experiencing cost learning to determine their inventory decisions based on cost-learning features and the retailer’s holding cost.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2022.0178 .</jats:p>

title: AI-Enabled Digital Health Tool Implementation in Clinical Practice Settings: Umbrella Review
container-title: JMIR AI
ed6b7c7bd88c542620745d58d7720ce6fb1ecaf8.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI has the potential to improve clinical decision-making, efficiency, and patient outcomes, yet adoption in routine clinical practice has been slower than anticipated. While prior studies have identified factors that influence AI implementation, a comprehensive synthesis grounded in implementation science frameworks is lacking.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to qualitatively and comprehensively describe barriers and facilitators to AI implementation in clinical care settings using an implementation science determinants framework, the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR), and to identify AI-specific determinants not fully captured by CFIR.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted an umbrella review of reviews examining determinants of AI implementation in clinical practice. In accordance with the PRIOR (Preferred Reporting Items for Overviews of Reviews) reporting guidance, we systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, and CINAHL for English-language reviews published between January 2013 and July 2025. Reviews were included if they addressed barriers to and facilitators of implementing AI-enabled digital health tools in clinical care settings. Determinants were deductively mapped to the updated CFIR and inductively analyzed to identify emergent AI-specific constructs. Review quality was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal checklist, and overlap among primary studies was evaluated using the GROOVE (Graphical Representation of Overlap for Overviews) tool.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twenty-two reviews published between 2021 and 2025 were included, encompassing studies conducted from 1990 to 2025. Reviews varied in design, including systematic, scoping, rapid, narrative, and literature reviews. Overall review quality was mixed, with 9 (41%) reviews rated at 100% quality and 4 (18%) at 50% or lower. Primary study overlap was slight, with a corrected covered area of 0.4%. Determinants of AI implementation were identified across all CFIR domains. Prominent barriers at the innovation level included limited evidence of clinical impact, poor interpretability, complexity, lack of adaptability, and insufficiently representative data. Facilitators included perceived relative advantage, co-design with clinicians, and evidence of local clinical benefit. At the implementer level, low AI literacy, limited confidence, time constraints, and concerns about professional displacement were common barriers, while training and technical support facilitated adoption. Inner setting barriers included inadequate infrastructure, limited resources, poor workflow compatibility, and weak governance structures. Outer setting barriers included unclear policies, laws, and liability frameworks, whereas partnerships and cross-sector collaboration were frequent facilitators. Inductively identified AI-specific determinants included transparency, trust, accountability, model bias, data governance, model maintenance, robustness, generalizability, existential threat, and concern about loss of the human element in care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI implementation in clinical settings is shaped by complex, multilevel, and AI-specific determinants that extend beyond traditional digital health considerations. Implementation science frameworks can be adapted to incorporate these constructs. Tailored, theory-informed strategies addressing technical, organizational, psychological, and regulatory factors are essential to support safe, equitable, and sustainable integration of AI into clinical care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Neglected Open-Globe Injury and Limb Amputation Following a Blast Explosion in a Pediatric Polytrauma Patient: An Observational Analytic Case Study on Delayed Ophthalmic Intervention, Ocular Trauma Score Dynamics, and Health System Barriers in Remote Eastern Indonesia
container-title: Bioscientia Medicina : Journal of Biomedicine and Translational Research
af23f88ee1aef2a17f2366f255f087df256c5e47.abstract:
<jats:p>Background: Blast-related ocular trauma in children in archipelagic developing regions is a devastating, multimechanistic emergency, often complicated by systemic polytrauma prioritization and geographical referral barriers.
Objective: To characterize the clinical trajectory, Ocular Trauma Score dynamics, and health-system barriers of a neglected pediatric open-globe blast injury with concomitant traumatic hand amputation in remote eastern Indonesia.
Methods: A 13-year-old boy presented 5 days after a homemade fish-bomb explosion. Evaluation used Birmingham Eye Trauma Terminology (BETT) classification, longitudinal biomicroscopy, acoustic B-scan ultrasonography, quantitative Ocular Trauma Score (OTS) and modified Pediatric OTS, and multi-level structural barrier assessment.
Results: At presentation (Day 5), right eye (OD) visual acuity was light perception with intraocular pressure of 7 mmHg, full-thickness superior eyelid margin laceration, total dark hyphema (Grade IV), and traumatic corneal scars, while the left eye (OS) maintained 20/20 vision with multiple corneal foreign bodies. Acoustic B-scan OD revealed complete funnel-shaped retinal detachment tethered to the optic disc and dense vitreous hemorrhage. OD calculated an OTS raw score of 12 (Category 1, 74% no-light-perception probability). Following surgical delays driven by maritime transit and BPJS insurance administrative bottlenecks, 1-week follow-up (Day 12) revealed fulminant corneal keratolysis with diffuse stromal melting, chemosis, and cicatricial eyelid notch, whereas OS achieved complete corneal re-epithelialization.
Conclusion: Neglected pediatric blast ocular trauma leads to accelerated enzymatic keratolysis and irreversible functional amaurosis when systemic polytrauma prioritizes limb salvage over sight. Integrating mandatory ophthalmic triage into rural disaster protocols is critical.</jats:p>

title: Beyond binary AI text detection: Partial authorship, source-text similarity, and an integrated threshold model of detectability
container-title: International Review of Applied Sciences and Engineering
acc924b3d1c0e2463fe1a308d503fda2a23b1d77.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    This study investigates AI text detection under conditions that more closely reflect real-world writing practices than conventional binary human-versus-AI benchmarks. Rather than treating authorship as a dichotomy, detectability is examined as a function of partial AI authorship, source-text similarity, and generator heterogeneity. Ten pre-LLM, human-written English scientific abstracts were used as reference texts, from which four authorship states (H100, AI50, AI75, and AI100) were constructed through controlled rewriting and paragraph-level mixing. AI-generated content was produced using four large language models: ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and LLaMA. Detection outputs from Turnitin and GPTZero were evaluated using non-parametric statistics, correlation analysis, and logistic threshold modeling. The results demonstrate that fully human and fully AI-rewritten texts are statistically distinguishable: median AI scores increased from 0 in H100 to 53 in AI100 for Turnitin (
                    <jats:italic>U</jats:italic>
                    = 49.5,
                    <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                     < 0.001) and from 0 to 11 for GPTZero (
                    <jats:italic>U</jats:italic>
                    = 61.0,
                    <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                    < 0.001), although AI-generated texts did not constitute a homogeneous class. Detectability also varied significantly across the four nominal authorship states for both Turnitin (H = 30.39,
                    <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                    < 0.001) and GPTZero (H = 21.77,
                    <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                    < 0.001), and systematically with source-text similarity and the generating model. Turnitin showed greater sensitivity than GPTZero to changes in nominal AI proportion and transformation intensity, particularly under mixed-authorship conditions. Significant generator-dependent differences were also observed, with Gemini outputs generally receiving higher AI-detection scores than ChatGPT or LLaMA outputs. The main methodological contribution is the Integrated Detectability Threshold Model (IDTM), which represents detection probability as a joint function of nominal AI proportion and transformation intensity. Within the present sample, the model identified a similarity transition range of approximately 63–66%, below which Turnitin-based detection became more likely than non-detection. These findings support a shift from binary AI classification toward a threshold- and risk-sensitive interpretation of AI text detectability.
                  </jats:p>

title: The Self as Aching Void
container-title: Seeing and Subjectivity
cfc3303b7e661e9e6d167d8fdd39abf9f4af5e0b.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>What should we say about the seeing subject as such, the one who stands as first relatum in a perceptual relation to actualities, absences, and artworks? Adapting an idea in William James, Bhattacharyya almost seems to call the I an ‘aching void’. Just as the solution to a puzzle is an unknown to which the various available clues point, so the I is a sought-for answer at the centre of a network of negations, an apophatic place-holder, a searched-out but otherwise indeterminate something pointed at by negations, the denotatum of ‘anti-descriptions’. So when I try to think about myself, it is as a search for the solution to a puzzle where the clues are: I am neither my material body, nor am I the flow of my sensation, nor yet am I a sense of self or feeling of being me. What, then, am I? Bhattacharyya gnomically writes that ‘introspection is not believing in the I: it is the I’; or, as Arvidson would later put it, ‘We do not attend to ourselves as having freedom, as if we were a substance to which adhered the quality of freedom. We attend to ourselves as freedom.’ This chapter suggests that the idea can more perspicuously be formulated within the framework developed in this book. It is that our subjectivity is already imminent in our perceptual experience. The very fact that my perceptual experience is reflective is enough, by itself, for me to be present to myself, free of any need for the identification of myself with any other thing, and so without myself becoming a focal object in experience.</jats:p>

title: PGP-FD: A Lightweight Phase-Guided Generative Graph Process for Resource-Efficient Edge Fault Pattern Recognition in Fire-Protection Valve Sensing Systems
container-title: International Journal of Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence
e8c77c8dfb0acb232d4d72b81bf0990419bebb53.abstract: <jats:p>Edge fire-protection sensing systems must recognize latent valve faults under limited computation, memory, and energy budgets, although fault samples are scarce and operational responses are strongly phase-dependent. This paper proposes PGP-FD, a lightweight phase-guided generative graph process for event-driven edge fault pattern recognition. Each valve operation or inspection is represented as a compact response window. A depthwise temporal encoder captures local dynamics, a monotonic phase gate models the ordered evolution of standby, actuation, transient, recovery, and settling phases, and a compact measurement graph learns hydraulic-mechanical coupling among pressure, valve motion, and event context. To reduce class imbalance, a fault-conditioned stochastic process generates rare events during training under range, phase-order, and valve-pressure consistency constraints. The training-only posterior and offline synthesis branches are removed during deployment, while confidence-uncertainty prefix inference avoids unnecessary continuous computation and retains full processing for difficult cases. Experiments on real fire-protection valve data show that PGP-FD improves recognition quality, response speed, and online model compactness over representative baselines. The results demonstrate a practical integration of lightweight pattern recognition and mechanism-consistent generative learning for resource-efficient industrial edge intelligence.</jats:p>

title: ATT-SV2-ES Net: Hybrid Deep Learning Features and Lightweight Attention-Based Model for Early Glaucoma Detection
container-title: International Journal of Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence
bc275378bb5009d7f256155d09bb39b3c0bf9888.abstract: <jats:p>Glaucoma is one of the main causes of permanent blindness. Timely intervention is ensured by its early and precise identification. This paper proposes a new hybrid approach, integrating handcrafted features with Deep Learning (DL), for reliable glaucoma identification and prediction on the G1020 dataset. Initially, pre-processing is conducted, which includes data augmentation to increase the diversity of images, Gaussian filtering to reduce image noise, Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE) to enhance local retinal contrast and then grayscale conversion to simplify retinal image representation. After pre-processing, the enhanced images were given to Depthwise Dilated Spatial Attention Mechanism (DDSAM)-based Glau-SegNet for optic disk (OD) and optic cup (OC) segmentation. From the segmented images, handcrafted features, such as Local Binary Patterns (LBPs) and fractal analysis, which describe complementary texture and structural information, are extracted. In parallel, the segmented images are processed by the Attention ShuffleNet V2 with Echo State Network (Att-SV2-ES Net) to obtain high-level deep feature representations. Then these deep features and handcrafted features are concatenated and fed to a fully connected layer with sigmoid activation to classify into the class for the prediction of glaucoma. This combined approach achieves a balance between high accuracy and scalability, addressing the growing need for accessible and reliable glaucoma screening solutions. The experimental results demonstrate the proposed system’s superior performance in detecting and predicting glaucoma. Furthermore, the findings demonstrate that the proposed model, which integrates DL features, outperforms all other models in terms of key performance metrics, including achieving 99.32% specificity, 99.43% sensitivity, and 99.37% accuracy.</jats:p>

title: Impact of Undertreated Antithrombotic Therapy on Adverse Patient Outcomes: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association
container-title: Circulation
3a18c6a0b841a8284e7aeed9f4eac96f66309d8f.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title/>
                    <jats:p>Antithrombotic therapy undertreatment includes omission, nonadherence, underdosing, and clinical circumstances that result in subtherapeutic antithrombotic levels. Antithrombotic undertreatment has profound implications for patient safety, public health, and healthcare costs. Due to deviation from evidence-based clinical practice, misperceptions of bleeding versus thrombotic risk, and inequities in healthcare access, many patients with atrial fibrillation, venous thromboembolism, or peripheral artery disease remain untreated or receive suboptimal anticoagulant dosing. Antithrombotic undertreatment has been shown to increase rates of ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, recurrent thrombosis, and mortality. Real-world data continue to highlight substantial gaps in care, which appear to be magnified in patients with inequity in social determinants of health. The emergence of antithrombotic stewardship, in concert with growing bodies of literature on antithrombotic agent underdosing, represents a transformative opportunity to address these gaps through structured, interprofessional, and evidence-based approaches. Through interdisciplinary collaboration, healthcare professionals are well positioned to enhance patient health and safety by recognizing and recommitting to reducing antithrombotic undertreatment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Self-Determination and the Value of Nationality
container-title: A Liberal Nationalist Theory of Secession
b4e70d62dde194ded1d0504e8f2453fec101933e.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In this chapter, the author develops and defends an account of the value of collective self-determination. The author argues that co-nationality is a relationship—like friendship and familial relations—that makes an intrinsic contribution to individual welfare. The chapter then sets out three arguments that move, cumulatively, from this claim to the conclusion that nations have a presumptive claim against interference in their affairs. The author argues that co-nationality is an intrinsically valuable relationship and presents a conditional argument in support of this claim. Specifically, the author contends that if one accepts that friendship and familial relationships can be intrinsically valuable, then one should also accept that co-nationality can be intrinsically valuable. The chapter then advances three arguments showing how the intrinsic value of co-nationality cumulatively grounds a strong presumption in favour of national self-determination. The author maintains that this presumption amounts to a presumptive claim to collective autonomy for nations. That is, nations have a claim-right to act in accordance with their collective decisions unless it can be demonstrated that doing so would result in wrongful harm. With this presumption established, the chapter turns to the question of whether it is always defeated—that is, whether unilateral secession by a national group necessarily involves wrongful harm.</jats:p>

title: Cross-regulation of iron and phosphate homeostasis by Fep1 and Pho7 in fission yeast
container-title: Microbiology Spectrum
44e525631c09f1c5fbd50fe50c83b5cfc052a77e.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title/>
                    <jats:p>
                      Iron and phosphate are essential micronutrients with partially interconnected homeostatic control; however, the underlying transcriptional mechanisms that integrate these signals in the fission yeast
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Schizosaccharomyces pombe</jats:italic>
                      remain unclear. Fep1 (GATA-type repressor) is a key regulator of iron-uptake genes, whereas Pho7 (Zn
                      <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                      Cys
                      <jats:sub>6</jats:sub>
                      -family transcription factor) drives phosphate starvation response. However, whether each of the two factors influences the target regulon controlled by the other remains unclear. We combined genome-wide chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing, RNA sequencing, and auxin-inducible degron-mediated acute depletion to define the joint Fep1–Pho7 transcriptional control and regulatory landscapes under defined iron and phosphate conditions. Unexpectedly, these analyses showed extensive overlap in chromatin occupancy between Fep1 and Pho7 at a subset of target promoters. Fep1 bound not only to canonical iron-uptake genes but also to the
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">pho7+</jats:italic>
                      locus and multiple phosphate-responsive promoters, whereas Pho7 showed association with a defined subset of Fep1 targets. Acute depletion experiments showed that Fep1 loss substantially increased Pho7 chromatin occupancy at iron-responsive promoters. Under iron-depleted conditions, Pho7 contributed to the transcriptional activation of specific Fep1 target genes (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">fio1+/fip1</jats:italic>
                      + and
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">str3+</jats:italic>
                      ), which indicated that Pho7 supports iron uptake gene expression when Fep1 repression is attenuated. Condition-dependent binding analyses showed that iron availability influences the relative regulatory contribution of the two factors at shared loci. These findings support a model in which Fep1 and Pho7 form a cross-regulatory module that converges on shared genes to enable iron-dependent redistribution of their influence. Together, these findings suggest a mechanistic framework for integrating iron and phosphate signals at the promoter level in fission yeast.
                    </jats:p>
                    <jats:sec>
                      <jats:title>IMPORTANCE</jats:title>
                      <jats:p>Iron and phosphate are essential micronutrients requiring balanced cellular levels for metabolism, redox control, and stress resistance. However, the transcriptional logic that integrates these signals remains unclear. Although fission yeast provides a powerful model for nutrient signaling, the iron-responsive factor Fep1 and the phosphate-responsive factor Pho7 have been treated as independent regulators. This study shows that Fep1 and Pho7 occupy promoters regulated by each other, supporting iron-dependent transcriptional cross-regulation. These findings suggest functional interplay between canonical iron- and phosphate-responsive pathways, although indirect metabolic coupling cannot be excluded. The iron-dependent shift in regulatory hierarchy between Fep1 and Pho7 at co-occupied promoters provides a mechanistic framework for understanding how cells can prioritize and integrate competing micronutrient demands. Therefore, cross-regulatory interactions between nutrient-specific transcription factors could indicate a general strategy for organizing multi-element homeostasis in fungi and may explain adaptation of pathogenic or commensal yeasts to fluctuating metal and phosphate environmental conditions.</jats:p>
                    </jats:sec>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Emotional Intelligence and Mental Well-Being in AI-Driven Hospitality
container-title: Experience Economy Insights on Human-Centric Hospitality 5.0
53a8b9399dccecdf1d6c3cc1543b58d05b5ccf4c.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, and digital service systems within the hospitality sector has ushered in an era known as Hospitality 5.0. While these advancements enhance efficiency, personalization, and guest satisfaction, they also increase emotional labor, psychological strain, and occupational stress among employees. This chapter analyzes, using major theories and frameworks, how emotional intelligence and mental well-being mediate sustainable workforce outcomes in AI-intensive hospitality. An original conceptual model, the Emotionally Sustainable Hospitality Workforce Model (ESHWM), is introduced, highlighting sustainable HRM as critical for maintaining emotional and psychological health amid digital disruption. The chapter summarizes empirical evidence linking AI adoption to increased workplace stress and shows how high emotional intelligence protects and boosts frontline hospitality worker performance. Practical implications are offered for managers, HR practitioners, and policymakers, aligning with UN SDGs 3, 8, and 9.</jats:p>

title: Parent Anxiety and Response to a Telehealth Intervention for Hypoglycemia Fear: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Trial
container-title: JMIR Pediatrics and Parenting
63971aa457c3894bb67c12122205a27ec79fdf93.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Parents of young children with type 1 diabetes (T1D) frequently report fear of hypoglycemia (FH), which can impact their diabetes management. REDCHiP (Reducing Emotional Distress for Childhood Hypoglycemia in Parents) is a telehealth-delivered cognitive behavioral intervention shown to reduce FH, but less is known about which parents benefit most.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This secondary analysis examined whether pretreatment parent anxiety moderated REDCHiP’s effects and explored responder patterns by intervention arm and pretreatment anxiety.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This was a secondary analysis of a large, randomized clinical trial comparing REDCHiP to an attention control condition (ATTN). We assessed outcomes before treatment (time 1) and 3 months after treatment (time 3). Our primary outcome was parental FH at time 3, adjusted for time 1 FH. The original trial used validated measures of parent FH and general anxiety. We evaluated parent anxiety at time 1 as both a categorical variable (clinically elevated or not) and a continuous variable (centered). We defined responders as parents achieving a reduction of ≥0.5 SDs in FH from time 1 to time 3. An analysis of covariance tested the treatment arm by anxiety interaction, with sensitivity analyses modeling anxiety continuously.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      There was no significant treatment arm by anxiety interaction when modeling parent anxiety as either a categorical or continuous variable (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      >.05). However, exploratory analyses found that the adjusted mean time 3 FH was numerically lower among REDCHiP parents than ATTN parents with clinically elevated anxiety. Among parents with elevated anxiety, 78.6% (22/28) of REDCHiP parents met our responder criterion compared with 47.4% (9/19) of ATTN parents. Among parents with elevated anxiety, the adjusted odds of meeting the responder criterion were higher for REDCHiP than ATTN parents (odds ratio 6.35, 95% CI 1.47‐29.00).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While time 1 parent anxiety did not significantly moderate treatment response, exploratory analyses suggested a potentially meaningful pattern among parents with clinically elevated anxiety. As telehealth-delivered behavioral interventions expand in pediatric type 1 diabetes care, secondary analyses of participant characteristics may help guide targeted implementation and enhance treatment benefit.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Nurturing an Understanding of Trustworthiness in Cross-Cultural Doctoral Research: An Autoethnography Exploring Active Learning in Higher Education
container-title: American Journal of Qualitative Research
844158052edc870e39e38da3681c44833688a5d8.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en"><i>University leaders, researchers, students, and policymakers frequently call for increased active learning in higher education. Within this context, novice scholars grapple with how to meaningfully nurture an understanding of trustworthiness throughout the doctoral research process. This study addresses that gap by examining how an innovative reflexive binning system, grounded in the ICAP framework and informed by multilayered reflexivity, can help novice scholars develop an understanding of trustworthiness in cross-cultural doctoral research. Using autoethnography combined with visual vignettes, the study traces the author’s development as a doctoral student learning to engage with qualitative inquiry in reflexive and relational ways. The study examines how developing a reflexive binning system served as a methodological tool for building an understanding of trustworthiness and how engagement with the system reflected progression across the modes of the ICAP framework. The reflexive bins system organizes data across literature, artifacts, experiences, and interviews while integrating structured generative questions and interactive dialogue. Multilayered reflexivity provides the analytic lens for examining how self, interpersonal, and collective dimensions of reflexivity shaped meaning-making across the research process. Two visual vignettes demonstrate how the system functions in practice, making visible the processes through which meaning is constructed, challenged, and refined. The manuscript suggests that reflexive bins foster a deeper understanding of trustworthiness by embedding active learning, reflexive engagement, and relational accountability throughout the research process. This study offers guidance to higher education professionals seeking to support doctoral students in strengthening their understanding of trustworthiness as they transition to independent scholars.</i></jats:p>

title: AI Scribe in Specialized Rehabilitation: Usability Study of Perceived Usability and Usefulness Among Physicians and Psychologists
container-title: JMIR Rehabilitation and Assistive Technologies
c5049fe9025dc797144b0755cc5c8f46a237bd87.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Clinical documentation in specialized, interdisciplinary rehabilitation is often time-consuming and complex and may contribute to clinician burnout and reduced time for patient interaction. AI-based scribes transcribe and summarize clinical notes and may reduce documentation burden; however, their usefulness and usability in specialized rehabilitation remain uninvestigated.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to assess the use of an ambient AI scribe tool among physicians and psychologists in specialized rehabilitation, focusing on perceived usefulness, usability, note quality, impact on patient interaction, perceptions of time spent on documentation, and documentation-related fatigue.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Over approximately 4 weeks, physicians and psychologists at 9 specialized rehabilitation centers used an ambient AI scribe during clinical consultations. Usability and user experience were assessed using the System Usability Scale (SUS) and a modified technology acceptance model (TAM). Participants rated an AI-generated note using a modified 8-item Physician Documentation Quality Instrument (PDQI-8) questionnaire to evaluate documentation quality. Additional questions explored perceived impact on patient interaction, documentation-related fatigue, and general attitudes toward AI technology.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Thirty-one clinicians (18 physicians and 13 psychologists) used the AI scribe over approximately one month and completed evaluation questionnaires. The mean SUS score was 78.3 (SD 10.4), with 86.7% of participants scoring above the usability threshold. Perceived usefulness (PU) and perceived ease of use (PEOU) were relatively high (mean PU score 5.65, SD 1.33; mean PEOU score 5.56, SD 1.17), and 87.1% expressed intention to use the AI scribe in future practice. Most participants (80.6%) agreed that using the AI scribe reduced time spent on documentation, while 66.6% reported a reduced perception of documentation-related fatigue. The quality of AI-generated notes was rated relatively high, with a mean modified PDQI-8 score of 4.3 (SD 0.3) out of 5. Comprehensibility received the highest rating (mean 4.6, SD 0.6), whereas thoroughness received the lowest rating (mean 3.9, SD 1.0) among the note quality variables. Overall, 71.0% of participants expressed some level of agreement that the AI scribe enhanced attentiveness during patient consultations, while a similar proportion (70.9%) agreed that it made active listening easier by reducing distractions associated with note-taking. A few participants reported that some notes were incomplete, lacked biopsychosocial details, and contained inaccuracies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study demonstrated broad acceptance of an AI-based ambient scribe among physicians and psychologists working in specialized rehabilitation. The AI scribe was generally perceived as valuable, easy to use, and clinically relevant. Most participants reported a reduced perceived documentation burden and improved attentiveness during consultations. These findings suggest that clinicians perceived the AI scribe as supporting more focused patient interactions. Some concerns were noted regarding completeness and occasional inaccuracies, highlighting areas for refinement. Future research should explore long-term implementation in routine rehabilitation settings and its effects on workflow, documentation quality, and patient experience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Performance of an infliximab precision-guided dosing tool from a capillary blood–based self-collection device in inflammatory bowel disease patients
container-title: Inflammatory Bowel Diseases
ba7c9959c1e845471dad967287ab15cc1b5f8976.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Aims</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Infliximab (IFX) trough concentrations are routinely measured to guide dosing and optimize efficacy. Bayesian forecasting tools may enable earlier prediction of trough concentrations, while patient-friendly capillary self-collection devices could improve access to precision-guided dosing (PGD). We evaluated the performance of the PredictrPK IFX platform in forecasting IFX trough concentrations by using serum collected with an upper-arm self-collection device and compared its performance with standard venous blood obtained by phlebotomy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) receiving IFX maintenance therapy were recruited from a single IBD center. Midcycle samples collected via an upper-arm self-collection device and via traditional venipuncture were compared. The IFX clearance was estimated by use of a nonlinear mixed-effects model with Bayesian priors and the predicted IFX levels were compared with measured trough concentrations obtained prior to infusions. Deming regression was used for statistical analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study included 57 patients (61% males, median age, 34 years). The median IFX dose was 10 mg/kg with a median interdose interval of 6 weeks. A total of 97 capillary and venous blood pairs were tested. Concentrations of IFX from venous and capillary blood samples demonstrated strong correlations (R2 = 0.987, Demings = 1.08). There was also a strong association between predicted IFX concentrations and measured IFX trough concentrations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>PredictrPK accurately predicted IFX trough concentrations. Capillary self-collection using an upper-arm device yielded results comparable to those from venous blood measurement, which may facilitate increased implementation and accessibility of PGD in clinical practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: The two-component system CrdRS mediates sub-inhibitory antibiotic-induced biofilm formation in Helicobacter pylori via bidirectional regulation of transporters PlpA and GlnP

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title/>
                    <jats:p>
                      Biofilm formation by
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Helicobacter pylori</jats:italic>
                      is a major driver of antibiotic tolerance and treatment failure, yet the signaling pathways that trigger biofilm development under sub-inhibitory antibiotic pressure remain poorly understood. Here, we show that sub-MIC levels of metronidazole, amoxicillin, and ciprofloxacin potently induce dense
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">H. pylori</jats:italic>
                      biofilms. Through transcriptomic and genetic analyses, we identify the two-component system CrdRS as a central signaling hub that orchestrates this response via the bidirectional regulation of two ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters. Phosphorylated CrdR binds to AC-rich promoter motifs to directly activate
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">plpA</jats:italic>
                      , which encodes a substrate-binding protein that drives exopolysaccharide secretion and matrix assembly. Concomitantly, CrdR represses
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">glnP</jats:italic>
                      , which encodes an inner-membrane permease, thereby relieving transcriptional inhibition of the L-asparaginase gene
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">ansB</jats:italic>
                      . This derepression triggers aberrant reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, which promotes oxidative stress-dependent biofilm maturation. Through phenotypic analysis of c
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">rdRS</jats:italic>
                      deletion mutants, phosphorylation-defective point mutants (CrdR
                      <jats:sup>D53A</jats:sup>
                      and CrdS
                      <jats:sup>H173A</jats:sup>
                      ), and exogenous hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) induction, we demonstrate that CrdRS is required for mediating antibiotic-induced stress responses in a manner genetically separable from ROS sensing. Collectively, our findings establish a dual-mechanism model in which CrdRS orchestrates antibiotic-induced biofilm formation by simultaneously controlling matrix production and intracellular ROS generation. Notably,
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">glnP</jats:italic>
                      expression was significantly lower in clinical multidrug-resistant isolates than in drug-sensitive ones, whereas
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">plpA</jats:italic>
                      showed the opposite trend. These findings provide a mechanistic foundation for developing CrdRS-targeted strategies to combat biofilm-associated
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">H. pylori</jats:italic>
                      infections.
