title: Beyond TAM: a mediated-moderated analysis of perceived anthropomorphism and technology trust as catalysts for AI adoption
container-title: Global Knowledge, Memory and Communication
f42fc18f511ad00f2591df2314c14dd596c3b3e4.abstract: Purpose This study examines customers’ adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the Jordanian telecommunications sector by extending the technology acceptance model (TAM). Specifically, it aims to investigate the effects of perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use and perceived anthropomorphism on actual use of AI, while testing customer intention as a mediator and technology trust as a moderator. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative approach was employed. Data were collected through self-administered questionnaires from customers of telecommunications companies in Jordan. Using stratified random sampling, 482 questionnaires were distributed, and 438 valid responses were analyzed. Partial least squares structural equation modeling using SmartPLS 4 was applied to assess the measurement model, structural relationships, mediation effects and moderation effect. Findings The results show that perceived ease of use and perceived anthropomorphism significantly and positively influence customers’ intention to adopt AI, whereas perceived usefulness has no significant effect. Customer intention significantly predicts actual AI use and mediates the relationships between perceived ease of use, perceived anthropomorphism and actual AI use. However, intention does not mediate the relationship between perceived usefulness and actual AI use. Technology trust significantly moderates the relationship between customer intention and actual AI use. Practical implications Telecom providers should design AI-enabled services that are simple, intuitive, human-like and trustworthy. Managers should also communicate the tangible benefits of AI more clearly to strengthen customers’ usefulness perceptions and encourage sustained usage. Originality/value This study extends TAM by integrating perceived anthropomorphism and technology trust into a mediated-moderated model of AI adoption in an underexplored Middle Eastern telecommunications context.

title: When AI takes control, who takes responsibility? Structural analysis of agentic AI risks in supply chains
container-title: Industrial Management & Data Systems
856fe8a0aa1ef33e7ac05c1632f3b6d6a499b839.abstract: Purpose Agentic AI systems execute procurement decisions, reroute shipments and renegotiate supplier contracts at speeds that preclude real-time human review. The existing literature offers limited analytical attention to the risks that arise when decision authority is delegated to agents. This paper develops a risk taxonomy for agentic AI in supply chains and traces the hierarchical dependencies and influence magnitudes among the identified risks. Design/methodology/approach A systematic review of literature, analyzed through theories–characteristics–contexts–methods framework, produces the risk taxonomy. A hybrid modified total interpretive structural modeling and fuzzy decision-making trial and evaluation laboratory methodology is then applied to structured expert judgments to establish the causal hierarchy and quantify inter-risk influence. Findings Three risks, namely workforce skill gap, data quality and reliability and ethical misalignment occupy the deepest level of the causal hierarchy. Lack of accountability and governance and data privacy emerge as terminal outcomes. All three analytical methods converge on a conclusion: agentic AI risks originate at the institutional layer, with technical risks acting as transmission mechanisms. Practical implications The findings indicate that effective governance requires that workforce capability, data integrity and objective-function alignment are addressed before deployment. The stratified agentic AI governance framework is proposed that translates hierarchical structure into a sequenced intervention architecture, providing practitioners with governance priorities organized by risk-propagation logic. Originality/value This paper contributes a systematically derived risk taxonomy and a causally weighted governance map for agentic AI risks in supply chains. Five propositions are derived from the causal structure and are advanced as a testable research agenda.

title: The AI augmentation gap: data richness, automation and business value
container-title: EuroMed Journal of Business
a9d4693b4aede355f90e6e8d3722e0aafd2cb720.abstract: Purpose Grounded in the resource-based view (RBV), this study examines how data richness, as an organisational resource, is associated with business value through two deployment processes, automation and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled augmentation, and whether they differ in their capacity to generate value. Design/methodology/approach Survey data from 366 Greek firms across four sectors were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) with bootstrapped mediation analysis and coefficient-difference tests; business value is measured as perceived value from digital technology. Findings Data richness is positively associated with both deployment processes. Automation is positively associated with business value and channels part of the association between data richness and value, whereas AI-enabled augmentation, the less developed process, shows no significant direct association; the difference is statistically significant, revealing an AI augmentation gap. Data richness also retains a significant direct association with value, and additional analyses suggest that the capability associations with value run through enacted digital transformation. Practical implications Firms should build a strategically governed data foundation, expand automation for near-term returns and develop augmentation as a longer-term capability built on skills, role redesign, validation and trust in AI-supported decisions; EuroMed policy instruments can be aligned with this sequencing. Originality/value Drawing on the RBV, the study shows that deployment processes of the same digital resource differ significantly in their association with value, a heterogeneity interpreted as reflecting the maturity of the complementary capabilities each requires, and provides evidence from a resource-constrained Mediterranean economy.

title: Architectural hedging capacity: preserving strategic optionality in AI provider relationships
container-title: Strategy & Leadership
1f10cf4b1b679b2084257feedf9f44642c6acab3.abstract: Purpose Firms increasingly depend on a small number of external providers for artificial intelligence (AI) models, yet that dependence is not only imposed by supplier concentration; it can also be reproduced by a firm’s own technology-integration decisions. This paper aims to examine how provider-specific integration progressively erodes a firm’s ability to switch providers, and what company leadership can do about it. Design/methodology/approach This paper is conceptual. Using resource dependence theory as its base, it draws on transaction cost economics, modularity and real options reasoning, organisational routines theory, and the attention-based view to develop a mechanism and an organisational capability, formalised in four core propositions, a typology matrix and a remedy audit. Findings The paper develops integration drift, a reinforcing process in which locally rational integration decisions cumulatively raise the cost of switching providers. It also introduces architectural hedging capacity (AHC), an organisational capability enacted through three recurring routines: governance-enforced modularity, rehearsed recalibration and sustained managerial attention. And lastly, the argument also identifies a boundary condition in resource dependence theory: where dependence is continuously reproduced through organisational integration, maintaining autonomy requires continuously reproduced exit capacity rather than a one-time remedy. Originality/value The paper extends resource dependence theory to settings where dependence is reproduced inside the firm through its own architecture, not only imposed externally. A typology and a remedy audit checklist give boards and managers a diagnostic for assessing and managing AI-provider dependence.

title: When AI signalling backfires: a threshold model of perceived firm innovativeness
container-title: Journal of Services Marketing
e7ff3a52b723ffba9e1d77084570515269cb1034.abstract: Purpose This study aims to interrogate the implicit monotonicity assumption in service-dominant logic by examining whether AI signalling intensity uniformly enhances perceived firm innovativeness (PFI) or exhibits threshold-dependent fragility. The study empirically validates relational coherence as a perception-level mediating state, thereby confirming its role as the integrator of AI-enabled capability inference, and specifies structural and demographic boundary conditions. Design/methodology/approach A two-study archival design tests the proposed threshold model. Study 1 exploits discrete AI capability announcements among 1,012 Asian service firms (2012–2024) using event-study difference-in-differences to identify dynamic shifts in customer text-based PFI. Study 2 estimates a dynamic panel system generalised method of moments model incorporating lagged PFI, non-linear AI intensity and relational coherence, addressing reverse causality and omitted capability shocks while computing turning points and moderated curvature. Findings AI signalling exhibits an inverted-U relationship with PFI: moderate intensity strengthens capability perception, whereas high intensity attenuates and reverses effects. Relational coherence mediates this relationship, with the indirect pathway weakening and becoming negative beyond a calculable threshold. The curvature steepens and the threshold occurs earlier in high-contact services and firms serving older customer segments. Originality/value The study advances service-dominant logic by introducing threshold-fragility into its resource-integration premise, repositioning technological operant resources as legitimacy-constrained rather than uniformly accretive. It conceptualises relational coherence as the perception-level integrator governing AI-enabled capability inference and embeds demographic and structural heterogeneity within a formally identified non-linear, dynamic analytical model structure.

title: The impact of explorative generative AI usage on construction project professionals' innovative work behavior: a technology affordance actualization perspective
container-title: Engineering, Construction and Architectural Management
d4b9feb8355cb976dddf7887f9e4fb88383051a9.abstract: Purpose This study attempts to investigate the influence of generative AI (GenAI) on construction project professionals' innovation, specifically by exploring how and under what contextual conditions the use of GenAI fosters innovative work behavior. Design/methodology/approach Grounded in the technology affordance actualization perspective, we identified explorative GenAI usage as the critical trigger of innovative work behavior, specifically by boosting knowledge acquisition, and organizational support as a buffer of the translating process. The theoretical model was empirically tested using the structural equation modeling approach with 239 valid responses from the Chinese construction industry. Findings The findings reveal that explorative GenAI usage acts as a critical actualization behavior that significantly enhances construction project professionals' knowledge acquisition, which subsequently empowers their innovative work behavior. Crucially, this study highlights that the positive effects of explorative GenAI usage are valid when organizational support is high, instead of low. Originality/value This study contributes to construction project management literature by deepening the understanding of the impact of emerging GenAI on micro-level individual behavioral patterns and provides valuable implications for construction managers in today's GenAI era.

title: AI-enabled lead temperature: a narrative review and five-dimension framework for machine-learning lead prioritization
container-title: Vilakshan - XIMB Journal of Management
bb5b053b4668bcaf446ce869d642767ec7b51679.abstract: Purpose This study aims to reconceptualize cold, warm, hot and sales-ready leads as dynamic states of sales-readiness and develops a five-dimension framework based on customer-profile fit, engagement, buying intent, authority and timing. Design/methodology/approach A narrative review integrates the original 47-source DOI-bearing peer-reviewed analytical corpus with a reviewer-directed verification and update of recent peer-reviewed evidence. The synthesis covers qualification/scoring, nurturing, marketing-sales handoff, CRM/pipeline governance, inside sales/follow-up and AI/predictive lead management, using explicit eligibility, coding and bias-mitigation procedures. Findings Lead temperature is a reversible, timestamped configuration rather than a fixed label or engagement score. The framework translates the five dimensions into four operational levels: cold, warm, hot and sales-ready. Machine-learning models can estimate or rank this state, but decision value depends on recency, calibration, explainability, data quality and managerial governance. Research limitations/implications The framework requires longitudinal, multi-firm validation across channels, industries and sales-cycle lengths. Practical implications RevOps, marketing and sales teams can use the model for routing, nurturing, response-time SLAs, downgrading stale leads and governing predictive scores. Originality/value The paper links practitioner lead-temperature terminology to machine-learning lead prioritization through an interpretable feature architecture and eight testable propositions.

title: Are you a positive or negative user of AI? Exploring the impacts of undergraduates' GenAI use
container-title: Journal of Research in Innovative Teaching & Learning
66831f84cd92159e84b218b9318c21fb4ab01adf.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are rapidly becoming commonplace in many academic environments; however, studies examining not just whether students use these technologies but how their usage patterns shape learning outcomes and academic integrity remain understudied. This study begins to address this gap by exploring undergraduates' patterns of constructive or problematic use of AI and their relation to academic and ethical behaviors. Design/methodology/approach This exploratory study used a cross-sectional design employing quantitative data collection methods. A correlation and multiple regression analysis were conducted with college students' (N = 110) self-reports of AI use, academic motivation and engagement, reliance on AI, and digital citizenship. Findings Negative and positive AI use were correlated with AI Reliance. Negative AI use also predicted stronger AI reliance with weaker digital citizenship skills, unlike positive AI use. Notably, positive and negative AI use were strongly correlated, suggesting that use patterns are not uniform on an individual level and may vary by context. Research limitations/implications Our results suggest that students may shift between different AI patterns. Future researchers should aim to clarify the causal mechanisms and recruit a larger and more diverse sample to validate and expand upon our findings. Originality/value To our knowledge, this paper is a rare empirical study that explores the relationship between specific student academic outcomes and AI use in distinctive usage patterns: positive and negative.

AI can automate bounded tasks, augment managerial judgement, or combine both roles across different decision stages. This conceptual paper develops an integrative framework explaining how AI adoption influences managerial decision-making and organisational performance through human–AI collaboration and decision implementation. Drawing on the automation–augmentation paradox, sociotechnical systems thinking, decision-making theory, and dynamic capabilities, the paper argues that AI creates value when analytical capabilities complement managerial contextual knowledge and are embedded in accountable routines. The framework proposes that AI adoption influences decision quality through information processing, option generation, and decision support; decision quality contributes to performance when decisions are implemented effectively. 08074844f49f8c91461c248324358c01be99a4bd.abstract: 高校武术普修课班额大、动作瞬时完成，教师凭肉眼难以逐人纠错，技术评价长期依赖主观印象。研究把动作识别定位为“形的测量仪”，而不是“功夫的裁判”，构建采集、识别、诊断、决策、反馈五层结构，以诊断、处方、复测三者的闭合程度界定教学精准。在某高职院校体育教育专业两个普修班（117人）开展16周准实验：实验班技能测评由68.4分升至86.1分，对照班由68.1分升至78.9分，后测组间差异有统计学意义（t=5.57，P<0.001，d=1.03，95%CI 0.66~1.44）；达标率89.8%对72.4%，课堂练习密度与课外自主练习时长同步上升；技能自我效能提高，理论测验未见差异。识别模块在5个动作上的分类准确率为90.2%，关节角平均绝对误差4.2°，与教师评分的相关系数为0.84。研究认为，动作识别的作用集中在诊断与反馈两个环节，其教学价值取决于处方是否可行、反馈是否撤得掉，而不取决于算法精度本身。

title: The challenge of AI dependence: exploring its impact on cognitive autonomy and elaboration in creative performance
container-title: Information Technology & People
a96bf40abb09f16316c20b255932ea6efe5dc15e.abstract: Purpose As artificial intelligence advances and its application scenarios continue to expand, human–artificial intelligence interaction grows increasingly close. While artificial intelligence brings convenience, it also raises concerns that it may weaken users' cognitive autonomy. To investigate this issue. This study aims to explore the composition of AI dependence and its impact on cognitive autonomy and specific aspects of creative performance. Design/methodology/approach This study draws on cognitive evaluation theory and the elaboration likelihood model to construct a dual-pathway model with instrumental dependence and affective dependence as core variables. The model explains the formation mechanisms of the two types of artificial intelligence dependence and their differential effects on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily examines their potential role in the elaboration dimension of creative performance. A two-stage mixed-method design was employed to test the model. Findings Study 1 found that perceived trust mainly had a positive effect on instrumental dependence. Different dimensions of interactivity differentially affected affective dependence and cognitive autonomy. Mediation analysis further confirmed the core mediating role of Dependence. Study 2, a small-sample exploratory experiment, re-tested selected hypotheses and found a possible negative effect of instrumental dependence on the elaboration dimension of creative performance. Research limitations/implications The main theoretical contribution of this study lies in revealing the dual-pathway formation mechanisms of artificial intelligence dependence and the reshaping effects of different types of dependence on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily explores the potential effects of dependence on elaboration performance. Originality/value The dual-pathway dependence model constructed in this study offers practical implications for understanding how long-term use of artificial intelligence affects cognitive autonomy.

title: Comparison of joint laxity measured using 60- and 80-N distraction forces and manual stress during robot-assisted total knee arthroplasty
container-title: Arthroplasty
84efe849a6fc664edadf8590d3d797d0f3125527.abstract: Abstract Background Appropriate intraoperative soft-tissue balance is essential for achieving successful outcomes following total knee arthroplasty (TKA). However, the optimal distraction force for evaluating joint laxity remains unclear. This study aimed to compare joint laxities measured using specific distraction forces with those obtained under manual varus-valgus stress and assess the interobserver variability. Methods A total of 55 bi-cruciate-stabilized TKAs were performed using a robotic system. Medial and lateral joint laxities were evaluated using a force-controlled tensioner device under a distraction force of 60 and 80 N at 10°, 30°, 60°, and 90° of flexion and under manual varus-valgus stress using the robotic system. To assess interobserver differences, all measurements were performed independently by the senior surgeon and one of the assistant surgeons. Results In the medial compartment, no statistically significant differences were detected between joint laxity under manual stress and that measured using a distraction force of 80 N at 10° and 30° of flexion. At 90° of flexion, no statistically significant difference was detected between JLR and JLT60N. In the lateral compartment, no statistically significant differences were detected between joint laxity under manual stress and that measured using 80 N at 10° and 90° of flexion, whereas joint laxity under manual stress was significantly greater than that measured using 80 N at 30° and 60° of flexion. Interobserver variability was greater in the lateral compartment than in the medial compartment, especially at higher flexion angles. Conclusions The differences between joint laxity measured under manual stress and that measured using a tensioner device varied depending on the compartment and knee flexion angle. The lateral compartment showed greater measurement variability, suggesting the need for careful assessment and standardization of intraoperative joint laxity evaluation during robot-assisted TKA.

title: AI Maturity
ae32042f98c7b540e945e2aa1658b2550f7460b9.abstract: This Element explores how generative AI transforms education, not only by requiring new forms of literacy but by demanding a framework of autonomy, responsibility, and epistemic virtues. Current AI literacy frameworks emphasize technical proficiency, yet remain incomplete without addressing the normative risks of AI immaturity. This Element argues that education must promote AI maturity: the ability to use AI without succumbing to cognitive offloading, algorithmic dependence, or epistemic heteronomy. It identifies key forms of AI immaturity and reconceptualizes prompting as a dialogical practice paralleling the Socratic method – the art of questioning, iterating, and critically engaging AI. Finally, it introduces a framework of epistemic virtues that enables students and citizens to resist disempowerment and cultivate epistemic autonomy. By bridging philosophy and pedagogy, the Element shows how generative AI can become a medium of epistemic autonomy, offering concrete guidance for curricula, assessment, and classroom practice.

title: Gate the claim, not the tool: verification for AI-accelerated research in nutrition
dd9fa223bdbefdfad63d94b84e859755f00b7874.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and agentic workflows can accelerate nutrition science across living systematic reviews, dietary assessment and cohort analyses, yet they have also fuelled a surge of formulaic papers mined from open datasets. Journals and funders have responded largely by restricting how AI may be used, especially in writing. Because AI use leaves no reliable trace in a single paper, such rules cannot be enforced; they drive use out of sight, penalize honest authors who disclose it, and fall out of date within months as models improve. A gate works only when what it checks is visible at submission. When three publishers stopped accepting unvalidated papers built on the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), their NHANES publications fell by 72% in the first nine months of 2026, showing that visible gates work, though a rule that blunt can also turn away sound epidemiology. Rather than policing the tool, nutrition science should use AI openly under human scientific judgement and hold every result to four verification gates scaled to its consequence: depositing data, code and agent logs so others can rerun the work; naming an accountable investigator who understands the study design and answers for each claim made; independently verifying findings that could change clinical practice or dietary policy; and disclosing what AI and humans did without penalty. As output grows, papers will likely become concise accounts for human readers resting on machine-auditable records, shifting prestige from the journal name to whether a claim matters when verified.

title:
Extracellular
Polymeric Substances Govern Horizontal
Gene Transfer of Antibiotic Resistance Genes: Mechanisms, Pathway
Specificity, and Research Gaps
container-title: Environmental Science & Technology
dd5819bc7f31237b41afbcc3f39449dce0a245b5.abstract: Abstract The dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in environmental systems is recognized as being shaped by local matrix conditions, yet the pathway-specific role of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), the dominant matrix of biofilms, sludge flocs, and granules, remains poorly resolved. In this Review, we develop a mechanism- and pathway-resolved perspective for evaluating how EPS govern horizontal gene transfer (HGT) of ARGs. Current evidence indicates that conjugation is the most directly supported pathway, with EPS facilitating or restricting transfer through effects on donor–recipient contact, matrix organization, and transfer-related physiology. For transformation, EPS-associated extracellular ARGs constitute reservoirs, but EPS–DNA binding can both preserve genetic material and limit its immediate bioavailability. By contrast, EPS involvement in phage-mediated transduction and vesicle-mediated transfer remains mechanistically plausible but insufficiently validated. We identify five interconnected mechanisms: physical retention and spatial organization, DNA adsorption and bioavailability, regulation of intercellular contact, modulation of cell physiology and transfer competence, and community-scale mobilome coupling. By clarifying evidence boundaries across pathways, this Review moves EPS–HGT research from correlation-based interpretation toward mechanism-informed assessment of ARG mobility. We conclude by outlining research needs, including standardized EPS definition and extraction, component-resolved characterization, pathway-resolved causal assays, and validation in realistic environmental aggregates.

title: I don’t want AI in my online search. What options do I have?
Hybrid Metaheuristic–AI Modeling for Accurate Prediction of CO₂ Solubility in Amine–Ionic Liquid Hybrid Solvents
container-title: Journal of Machine Learning Advances
f0da3f283f341e35ffb770eb130dbb72ee495848.abstract: Reducing CO₂ emissions from fossil-fuel-based processes requires accurate and reliable predictive tools for designing advanced solvent systems for post-combustion carbon capture. In this study, an extensive experimental database of CO₂ solubility in hybrid amine–ionic liquid (IL) solvents was compiled and modeled using four hybrid metaheuristic–machine-learning frameworks: Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting combined with the Multi-Verse Optimization Algorithm (HistGBoost-MVOA), Tabular Neural Network combined with the Moth-Flame Optimization Algorithm (TabNet-MFOA), Support Vector Regression combined with the Improved Whale Optimization Algorithm (SVR-IWOA), and Extreme Learning Machine combined with the Jellyfish Optimization Algorithm (ELM-JFOA). The input variables included temperature, amine concentration, IL concentration, molecular weights of the amine and IL, and CO₂ partial pressure, while the CO₂ mole fraction in the liquid phase (xCO₂) was considered the target variable. To ensure robust model development, outlier detection was performed using the Isolation Forest algorithm, followed by Robust Scaling for data normalization. Model performance was evaluated using repeated 10-fold cross-validation and independent testing based on R², RMSE, MAE, MAPE, and PBIAS, together with Taylor diagrams, centered RMSE (cRMSE), SHAP-based interpretability analysis, and bootstrap uncertainty quantification. All developed models demonstrated excellent predictive capability (testing R² > 0.96), with SVR-IWOA consistently achieving the highest prediction accuracy and the narrowest uncertainty intervals. SHAP analysis identified the molecular weight of the ionic liquid and temperature as the most influential variables governing CO₂ solubility. The proposed modeling framework provides a robust and interpretable data-driven approach for accurately predicting CO₂ solubility and supports the design and optimization of hybrid amine–ionic liquid solvents for carbon capture applications.

title: Can Generative AI Preserve Tail-Risk Networks? Evidence from Cryptocurrency Markets
d603bfb118d128d5d27946a454b3b2d03b3a6ed8.abstract: Abstract Generated financial scenarios inform risk estimation and portfolio decisions, but agreement with standard distributional diagnostics does not show that a generator preserves the structure a decision depends on. We evaluate generated scenarios in three layers: conventional distributional and risk diagnostics; preservation of a conditional lower-tail network, judged against the sampling uncertainty of the empirical network; and realised outcomes of an allocation rule that uses the network’s node rankings. Using hourly data for ten cryptocurrencies over 2020–2025, we compare a stationary bootstrap, a GARCH-t copula model and a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM). The layers yield different conclusions about these generators. The discrepancy between the aggregated GARCH-t network and the observed network exceeds the bootstrap reference band at all 16 evaluation refits, yet overall distributional discrepancy stays within its band in 96 of the 157 GARCH-t panels that fall outside both the conventional-diagnostic and network bands. DDPM meets the joint conventional-diagnostic criterion in no panel but meets the single-panel network criterion in 120 of 160. Network differences change allocation weights and volatility exposure. After ex ante risk matching, differences in daily expected shortfall relative to the historical-network rule range from −0.09 to −0.02 percentage points, and every paired 95% interval contains zero. Controlled simulations show when ranking errors are costly: if tail hubs differ mainly in asymmetric downside dependence, a correlation-matching copula reverses the hub ranking and raises population expected shortfall by 3.1% relative to the true-network benchmark. Conventional diagnostics, network preservation and allocation outcomes give distinct assessments of these generators. JEL classification: C45 · C58 · G11 · G32

title: Mapping data privacy at the intersection of AI and the digital economy: a bibliometric review, taxonomy, and research agenda
container-title: Electronic Commerce Research
a2d35586dccf8bad42e327afbba39dfaa480e28f.abstract: Abstract The rapid integration of artificial intelligence and related emerging technologies has intensified data privacy challenges across the digital economy. Although scholarship has grown substantially, it remains fragmented across technical, legal, ethical, and sector-specific domains, limiting a clear view of the field’s structure and development. This study presents a bibliometric analysis and thematic mapping of 434 peer-reviewed articles published between 2016 and 2026 in the Web of Science Core Collection. It identifies seven thematic clusters and finds that applied and privacy-preserving technical work dominates, while business strategy, trust, and public-sector governance remain underdeveloped. The study extends this mapping with a multi-dimensional privacy taxonomy and a TCCM (theory, context, characteristics, and methodology) synthesis, moving beyond the topic- and domain-specific scope of prior reviews to diagnose where the field is structurally weak. It argues that privacy remains under-theorized as an economic and behavioral phenomenon despite its centrality to digital commerce and sets out a research agenda of economically grounded questions derived from these gaps.

title: Integrating AI General Education with Digital Literacy Cultivation and Cognitive Construction in Industry-Specific Universities
container-title: Communications in Humanities Research
fd9b89ad8c965d3d4be7255a513cbbde498f584e.abstract: Artificial intelligence has evolved into a general-purpose technology that permeates nearly every corner of knowledge production and social governance. This transformation is pushing college students' digital literacy far beyond the traditional "digitization" benchmark toward what this paper terms "intelligent-digital" literacy. For industry-specific universities—institutions committed to serving specific industries and cultivating application-oriented talents—the significance of AI general education is perhaps even greater than for other types of universities, because their graduates directly enter the industrial chain. Taking the practice of Moutai Institute as a concrete case, this paper elaborates on the internal logic, practical challenges, and feasible pathways for integrating AI general education into students' digital literacy cultivation and cognitive construction. The core argument of this paper is that such education should be anchored in industrial scenarios rather than abstract theory, and that cultivating compound talents equipped with digital literacy, industrial awareness, and social responsibility requires simultaneously grasping three main threads: technological empowerment, value guidance, and cognitive construction. On this basis, this paper proposes a trinity integration framework and offers actionable strategies from four dimensions: curriculum system, teaching model, faculty development, and evaluation mechanism. This paper aims to provide theoretical reference and practical insights for general education reform in industry-specific universities.

title: Lightweight AI Fundus Image Model for Early Screening of Diabetic Retinopathy
container-title: Theoretical and Natural Science
556ac020ee769b611e2a4b32ad6c7c3900e2da47.abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is now the main cause of preventable blindness in working-age adults worldwide. With the rising prevalence of diabetes, the need for DR screening is becoming increasingly urgent. Traditional DR screening requires professional ophthalmologists; thus, there are problems of a shortage of expert resources, uneven distribution, and lengthy manual interpretation. Most of the current deep-learning models have too many parameters and are computationally expensive; therefore, they are not suitable for deployment on edge devices. To solve the problem of deployment bottlenecks, the development of lightweight artificial intelligence models for fundus images has become necessary. This paper systematically reviews the recent developments in lightweight artificial intelligence models for DR screening based on fundus photographs. Custom image pre-processing, a lightweight network design, advanced model compression techniques and interpretability mechanisms are employed to reduce both the number of parameters and computational cost substantially without losing the sensitivity to early retinopathy. The model's diagnostic reliability and computational resource consumption have been examined. Ablation studies and visual analyses show the respective contributions of each module to the model's performance and efficiency. Additionally, to improve the interpretability of the model and boost clinical trust, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) is introduced. Future research will enhance the adaptability of cross-device and cross-domain applications, expand the scope of clinical verification, and integrate multimodal clinical data for reliable and fair ophthalmic AI deployment.

title: Discursive Manipulation of National Security and Industrial Competitiveness in U.S. AI Regulation: Domestic Contestation and the Fragmentation of Global AI Governance
container-title: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences
5b9bad9832926449f0558ab0f8883de617f95edd.abstract: Against the backdrop of generative AI emerging as a core strategic asset for major powers, the rhetorical tropes of national security and industrial competitiveness are subject to strategic manipulation by divergent domestic actors. The deregulatory camp within the White House invokes industrial competitiveness to roll back security-focused executive orders; the security faction in Congress expands chip export controls in the name of national defense; state-level authorities counter federal overreach through consumer protection mandates; and Silicon Valley deploys a two-pronged lobbying strategy. Taking the 2023-2026 policy pendulum and BIS chip regulations as its analytical case, this paper demonstrates that domestic contestation spills over globally through transmission channels. This has produced a global AI governance landscape defined by fragmentation, hollowed-out soft law processes, and a three-bloc divide across the U.S., the EU, and China, while the shortening commitment half-life of U.S. policy positions has inflated the costs of multilateral cooperation. The study also identifies limited positive spillover effects. In response, the paper puts forward targeted strategies. The conclusion argues that U.S. internal regulatory divisions constitute a mechanism that externalizes domestic political costs as global governance uncertainty. Understanding this mechanism is a prerequisite for reshaping the multilateral AI order.

title: Substitution Boundaries of AI Agents in Team Collaboration: An Empirical Analysis Based on Front-Line Employees' Perceptions
container-title: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences
71bc2c105cada90065e781ec3cb0f5bf07fa26ab.abstract: With AI agents increasingly involved in teamwork, whether AI can substitute human collaboration has become a heated topic in academia. Large-model-driven agents are now capable of participating in team brainstorming, task coordination, and collaborative problem-solving, and knowledge-intensive industries are beginning to form a large number of human-machine hybrid teams. Existing research mostly relies on theoretical reasoning and lacks empirical perceptual data from front-line practitioners. Drawing on a questionnaire survey of 158 employees with cross-industry teamwork experience, this paper explores practitioners' perceptions regarding the substitution of human collaborative behaviors by AI. The results show that AI can only partially substitute procedural and rule-oriented collaborative tasks, whereas social-emotional communication, conflict mediation and value judgment remain irreplaceable human strengths. Position, work experience and AI familiarity jointly shape individual perceptions of the substitution boundary. Most practitioners regard AI as an auxiliary tool rather than a leader of team collaboration. This study provides a practical reference for enterprises applying AI collaboration tools.

title: Selecting Cooling Architectures for High-Density AI Data Centres
container-title: Applied and Computational Engineering
c7292bec74b9afb41909c2d2dff915b29ccb6fc0.abstract: Rising power concentration in artificial intelligence servers has made cooling architecture a primary design constraint for high-density data centres. This paper compares recent peer-reviewed studies of air cooling, direct-to-chip cold plates, single- and two-phase immersion, and their environmental effects. The findings show that liquid cooling expands the thermal operating envelope of high-power hardware, although the size of the benefit depends on the measurement boundary. Direct-to-chip systems can retain a substantial air-side load, warmer coolant may increase server power, and immersion performance varies with flow distribution, fluid properties, and hardware design. Facility-level outcomes also depend on climate, electricity supply, water source, coolant production, and equipment lifetime. Cooling options should therefore be compared under a common workload and system boundary. Optimised air remains suitable for moderate-density or legacy facilities, direct-to-chip cooling provides a practical route for many high-density racks, and immersion is best suited to cases where exceptional heat density and purpose-built infrastructure justify changes to hardware and maintenance.

title: AI-Assisted Adaptive Interface Design for Lowering Entry Barriers in Real-Time Strategy Games
container-title: Applied and Computational Engineering
b96e88edfc1c92bcf1001b7d05c7e708a1e29bb9.abstract: Real-time strategy (RTS) games require players to make strategic decisions while executing numerous commands. This paper presents a qualitative synthesis of recent academic research on game accessibility, human–Artificial Intelligence (AI) assistance, interface design, and community content. Six design directions are examined against accessibility, strategic depth, long-term engagement, and practical value. A layered control model is proposed with beginner, traditional, and competitive profiles sharing the same strategic rules. Routine automation requires player approval and remains visible and reversible, while tutoring uses information available to the player. Cooperative practice, hybrid interactions, and community content are considered as supporting design contexts. A conceptual mission walkthrough examines how the model could separate repeated operations from consequential decisions. The analysis yields design requirements and testable hypotheses; no prototype or new participant experiment was conducted. Controlled player studies, including unassisted transfer tasks and return-session measures, are needed to determine whether the model lowers entry barriers while preserving strategic depth.

title: Efficacy of AI in the diagnosis of oral squamous cell carcinoma from clinical images: A systematic review and meta-analysis
container-title: Annals of the Academy of Medicine Singapore
dd0241c5bbfb7b9858123b244bbc03902330ab07.abstract: Introduction: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is a common malignancy that is frequently diagnosed at advanced stages, partly because of limitations in conventional diagnostic approaches. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of artificial intelligence (AI) models in detecting OSCC from clinical images. Methods: PubMed, ScienceDirect, the Cochrane Library, and Embase were searched from January 2000 to September 2024. Studies assessing the diagnostic accuracy of AI models for OSCC using clinical images were included. Studies that did not involve clinical images, were not specific to OSCC, or were not published in English were excluded. In accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, study selection was performed independently by 4 reviewers, with disagreements resolved through consensus. Subsequently, diagnostic accuracy data were extracted, risk of bias was assessed using Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies using AI, and thematic analysis was performed by 2 reviewers. Where appropriate, a random-effects meta-analysis was conducted. Results: Nine studies comprising 47,987 oral clinical images were included, with 6 studies in the meta-analysis. AI models demonstrated a pooled sensitivity of 0.94 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.87–0.97), specificity of 0.95 (95% CI 0.86–0.98), and an area under the curve of 0.975 (95% bootstrap CI 0.911–0.986). AI systems generally achieved higher diagnostic accuracy than general practitioners and performance comparable to specialists under controlled study conditions. Conclusion: AI models show strong diagnostic performance for OSCC detection from clinical images. However, current evidence is largely derived from retrospective and heterogeneous datasets without external validation. Prospective and blinded studies are required to determine their role as decision-support tools in real-world settings.

title: National AI Strategies and the Green Transition: Cross-Country Evidence from Staggered Difference-in-Differences and Double Machine Learning
container-title: Applied and Computational Engineering
f7a88b0cc7e88902ba5d6838c0f50b249a7e41dd.abstract: National artificial intelligence (AI) strategies have proliferated since 2017, yet whether they advance the green transition remains unknown. We exploit the staggered adoption of national AI strategies by 59 countries within an 85-country panel over 2000–2021, combining two-way fixed effects (TWFE), Callaway–Sant'Anna difference-in-differences, and double machine learning (DML). Strategy adoption raises the renewable energy share of consumption by 1.87 percentage points in fixed-effects estimates and by 1.47 points in dynamic event-study aggregation, and reduces the CO₂ intensity of GDP (−0.026 kg per 2017 PPP dollar), a result corroborated by a significant decline in CO₂ emissions per capita. In contrast, we find no robust effect on the share of environment-related patents: pre-trends are rejected and point estimates switch sign across estimators. Green-patenting effects are concentrated, albeit imprecisely, in high-income economies, and carbon-intensity reductions are larger where renewable endowments are high. DML estimates for green patenting are sensitive to the choice of learner. National AI strategies appear to green the energy mix before they green the innovation base.

title: From EEG Classification to Personalized Neurofeedback: An Explainable AI Framework for Alzheimer's Disease
container-title: Applied and Computational Engineering
dd746e4d727e24716dbdb4c75f98ad2248c582a4.abstract: This study developed an explainable machine learning (ML) framework for Alzheimer's disease classification using resting-state EEG-BCI recordings from the OpenNeuro ds004504 cohort, which consists of 36 patients with AD and 29 Healthy Control (HC). Four EEG biomarkers and a normative-deviation score are integrated with feature weighting and logistic classification, while SHAP, gradient saliency, and layer-wise relevance propagation provide complementary explanations of model predictions. The performance of the framework was evaluated using stratified 5-fold cross-validation and a locked 15-subject holdout set (8 AD, 7 HC). The model achieved a mean cross-validated area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.823 ± 0.095 and a holdout ROC-AUC of 0.929. The Explainable AI (XAI) feature attribution identified posterior alpha power, alpha peak frequency, and frontal theta/beta ratio as significant discriminators between AD and HC (p < 0.05), with posterior alpha power showing the strongest association with classification (p < 0.001). Posterior alpha power alone achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.900 ± 0.074. These results demonstrate the feasibility of using explainable AI to extract important spectral features that can distinguish AD from healthy controls and may inform the future development of adaptive neurofeedback protocols tailored to individual brain patterns. However, a larger and more diverse data set is needed for future studies of real-time, personalized neurofeedback applications.

title: Based on Personalized Content: Addressing Homogenization in AI-Supported Learning Through the Smart Mistake Solver
container-title: Applied and Computational Engineering
01abd366176d65a2f7562b993bb6f09b597ae8be.abstract: The adoption of artificial intelligence allows for an advancement in personalized learning, since the development of diverse types of learning materials and content may not succeed in always developing highly personalized experience. This article will explore personalized learning in relation to the homogeneity of a course program design based on an example of the Smart Mistake Solver program, an artificial intelligence learning assistance tool, which detects and corrects students' mistakes while dealing with math problems. The process of error detection, student model created with the help of Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) and development of personalized content are crucial aspects of the artificial intelligence support in learning. The conceptual analysis of Smart Mistake Solver demonstrates the limitations of artificial intelligence in enhancing personalized learning, which are conditioned by the necessity to use a list of predestined errors and measurable performance metrics. In conclusion, it was found that meaningful personalization should occur with respect to the specific needs of each learner within a learning experience along with distinction of learning materials; these cannot be fully met in all cases with the help of artificial intelligence.

title: When Caution Blocks Learning: Justifying the Non-Adoption of Medical AI
141cfb5eb3fda21a6a2ff717b8ebde5f8ec56ee2.abstract: Abstract A healthcare institution may reasonably decline to introduce an artificial intelligence (AI) system because evidence of its local safety and value is insufficient. A different question arises when that institution also controls, and declines to permit, a proportionate means of addressing the uncertainty. This article examines the justification of that second decision. It builds on established accounts of AI underuse, adoption-dependent learning, and institutional duties within learning healthcare systems; the dependence of evidence on use is not presented as a new discovery. Through a hypothetical medication-review example, I argue that a reason sufficient to withhold routine clinical use does not automatically justify closing a decision-relevant learning pathway. Where an institution has a relevant care-governance responsibility, controls necessary access, and can make a fair contribution to ethically permissible inquiry, refusing that contribution requires an action-specific justification. This requirement does not establish a duty to adopt the system, compel patient participation, or undertake every informative study. Nor does institutional responsibility for missing evidence make an unvalidated system safer. An institution can remain right to withhold clinical use while being answerable for having obstructed reasonable inquiry. The practical implication is to evaluate the present deployment decision and the maintenance of its evidential basis separately, with responsibility for restoring justified learning opportunities rather than automatically relaxing safety standards.

title: Generative AI Misuse and Rule Compliance Among University Students in Bhutan: Implications for Assessment and Institutional AI Policy
container-title: Journal of Education and Learning Reviews
803b74b5cc2e0e79e1abc6b3b1070e03ff677b5b.abstract: Background and Aim: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) use is expanding in Bhutanese universities while institutional policies remain under development. Guided by an extended Theory of Planned Behavior, this study examined factors associated with unauthorized AI use and intention to comply with institutional AI policies. Materials and Methods: An anonymous, cross-sectional survey was conducted in June 2026 among a convenience sample of 713 Bhutanese university students. Seven-point Likert-type responses were analyzed using factor analyses, reliability assessments, correlations with false discovery rate correction, multiple and moderated regression, and bootstrapped indirect association tests. Robustness checks included robust standard errors and demographic controls. Results: The models explained 24.5% of variance in AI misuse and 19.6% in compliance intention. Approximately 29% of respondents endorsed at least one misuse item. Misuse was associated with misuse acceptability, AI familiarity, academic pressure, moral rationalization, rule clarity, subjective norms, and learning impact. Compliance intention was associated with subjective norms, rule clarity, behavioral control, productive AI use, institutional enforcement, and moral rationalization. Institutional enforcement showed a small independent association with compliance intention (β = .086). Compliance intention was inversely associated with misuse (B = −0.10, p = .004). All six indirect associations were small, with bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero. Demographic adjustment preserved findings; academic level showed no significant moderation. Conclusion: Findings support evaluating assignment-specific AI guidance, coordinated workloads, classroom discussion of misuse rationalizations, and communicated institutional policies. Cross-sectional data preclude causal inference, and convenience sampling limits generalizability. These associations provide a basis for evaluating approaches to responsible AI governance.

title: Operating regimes of quarter-turn-aware frontier-based coverage path planning
container-title: Frontiers in Robotics and AI
7840491ba039ccd1b052fae108ae8047dcb4116c.abstract: Introduction The practical question in turn-aware coverage planning is when reduced angular travel compensates for extra distance and overlap. Methods We study that question with TURN-F, a deliberately simple deterministic frontier planner that searches cell–heading states and charges angular travel in 90 ° units. Its normalized motion-cost index is J β = L + β Q , where L is path length, Q is the number of quarter turns, and β exposes grid pitch, platform speed, and a rotation-to-translation power ratio; it is not measured battery energy. The main evaluation combines 178 public layouts, 4 distance-only baselines, and 2 heuristic turn-aware comparators re-planned at every β . Results At β = 1 , TURN-F reduces quarter turns by 21.2% relative to GREEDY but travels 6.1% farther and increases overlap from 0.154 to 0.192, yielding a small 1.25% mean advantage (108 wins in 178 grids) that the rank-based post hoc test does not separate. A β = 0 same-code control provides no detectable evidence that state representation or tie-breaking explains that advantage ( + 0.18 % in J 1 , 95% CI [ − 0.22 , 0.56 ] % , p = 0.20 ). The corpus-mean crossing is β * = 0.82 (grid-bootstrap 95% interval 0.74–0.89). For β > 0 , an exploratory geometry-conditioned model improves grouped-CV prediction over a β -only model, but leave-one-family-out validation fails on HouseExpo, and calibration varies by family. On 20 seeded-random non-overlapping windows from five real-robot laser logs, TURN-F is 3.21% lower at β = 1 (17 wins); the five-source test is statistically inconclusive ( p = 0.0625 ) . The result remains TURN-F-favoring for boundary-rich, low-boundary, all-candidate, and 2,000 repeated random selections. Under a rest-to-rest acceleration model, predicted completion time is 4.5%–9.7% lower, but no controller execution or energy measurement was performed. Discussion The contribution is therefore a reproducible analysis of a turn–travel trade-off and its limitations, not a universal planner ranking or a hardware-validated energy claim.

title: Comparative evaluation of ResNet-Based AI models for breast cancer detection in digital mammography and digital breast tomosynthesis
container-title: Frontiers in Systems Biology
b5cd32e8397df1843cd74bcffa6248924139b1ea.abstract: Introduction Early detection of breast cancer is crucial for better treatment options; however, physicians usually encounter challenges when reading breast mammograms because some tissues can overlap or look similar. New computer technologies can help by highlighting areas that may contain cancer. In this study, we assessed computer systems to identify whether a breast image is normal, benign or malignant and compared their performance on standard digital mammography (DM) and digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) images. Methods This retrospective study included 31 (100 after augmentation) images with malignant breast lesions, 175 with benign findings, and 475 normal images. We developed a deep learning convolutional neural network (CNN) model to classify images using ResNet-18 and ResNet-50. We trained the model via 10-fold cross-validation and Holdout validation. Performance was measured for each model. We computed performance metrics on original (non-augmented) images from 10-fold cross-validated predictions, with 95% confidence intervals from a stratified patient-level bootstrap (2,000 replicates), precision–recall analysis with average precision (AP), and paired DeLong and exact McNemar tests with Holm correction. We increased the malignant class from 31 to 100 images in the training set via data augmentation for the stage-2 classifier. Validation used non-augmented images. Results In normal versus abnormal classification (679 original images per view; ResNet-18, 10-fold cross-validation), DM CC, DM MLO and DBT MLO achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.995 (95% CI 0.991–0.998), 0.984 (0.975–0.992) and 0.994 (0.989–0.998), sensitivity of 95.1%, 95.6% and 95.1%, and specificity of 96.6%, 94.1% and 98.5%, respectively. DBT had significantly higher specificity than DM in selected comparisons (ResNet-18 vs. DM MLO and ResNet-50 vs. DM CC; Holm-adjusted p ≤ 0.002), with no significant AUC-ROC differences between modalities or architectures (all Holm-adjusted p ≥ 0.13). In benign versus malignant classification (131 original images, 31 malignant), AUC-ROC ranged from 0.977 to 0.999 and AP from 0.946 to 0.996, with no significant differences between DM and DBT or between ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 (all Holm-adjusted p ≥ 0.50). The detection and classification of malignant, benign, and normal images in DBT and DM using an artificial intelligence (AI) training model achieved comparable performance to the medical field. Conclusion Computer systems can detect and classify breast findings with high accuracy, helping to reduce errors and support physicians’ decisions. The original number of malignant images was relatively small (n = 31), which may affect the model’s generalizability and highlights the need for validation on larger, multi-institutional datasets. These findings may encourage more use of computer-assisted detection in breast imaging and contribute to developing better tools for early breast cancer diagnosis.

title: Investigating the impact of generative AI on academic integrity in universities student attitudes, ethical challenges, AI-assisted plagiarism, and institutional responses
container-title: Perspectives in Social Sciences
855e32a3120a9cd40b45cb459b808616e4102978.abstract: This study aimed to explore the influence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) on academic integrity within Pakistani universities, examining students' perceptions, ethical dilemmas, the role of AI in plagiarism, and institutional measures. A mixed-methods research approach was employed to draw out students' experiences and institutional views of academic use of generative AI. The targeted population consisted of students of undergraduate and post graduate level in public and private universities of Pakistan. The sample size for quantitative analysis was 350 students while for qualitative analysis, the students, lecturers and academic administrators were sampled. A structured questionnaire and interview questions were used to discuss the use of AI, ethical awareness, academic dishonesty, and institutional policies. Overall, the findings indicated that students were positive about the use of generative AI as an educational tool, particularly for writing assistance, research, and information retrieval. However, issues arose about AI-assisted plagiarism, dependence, originality, and the trustworthiness of AI-generated information. The findings also revealed that the policies in universities were not consistent, and students' awareness of AI was not high, which made it hard to implement responsible AI. The study highlighted the importance of establishing institutional policies, promoting AI literacy, transparency in disclosure, and adjusting assessment systems to maintain academic integrity and stimulate technological innovation in higher education in Pakistan.

title: Fail-Closed Authorization for Tool-Using AI Agents: A Capability Contract and Case Study
732fc9ee0d24c7cb1bcb0899e1e4272b04f11159.abstract: Abstract For tool-using LLM agents the decisive question is whether a concrete tool call is authorized before it executes. We describe the Agent Security Contract (ASC), a deny-by-default, pre-execution gate for agent and MCP tool calls. An ASC policy pins a SHA-256 digest of the approved tool catalog, declares per-agent tool allowlists with argument constraints, marks high-impact tools that require out-of-band approval, and bounds call rates; each decision (ALLOW, BLOCK, REQUIRE_APPROVAL) is emitted as an integrity-checked (unkeyed) JSON evidence envelope, and every error path we enumerate and test resolves to BLOCK. We evaluate the open-source implementation on static, recorded tool-call traces only; no live agent is run. Bypasses of the v0.1.0 demo policy found in review were fixed in v0.2.0; on a 60-case adversarial probe, allowed attacks fall from 32 to 1 (a policy gap), at the cost of 3 new benign over-blocks. On the author-constructed 66-scenario v0.2.1 corpus, designed around these checks, ASC returns the expected verdict in 66/66 cases; tool-name RBAC (Python and OPA/Rego) admits 30 of its 33 attacks by construction, and mutation testing shows the corpus exercises few policy constraints (8 of 62 single-constraint mutants killed). As a held-out check we replay 132 AgentDojo v1.2 ground-truth traces under policies frozen beforehand. With tool-level approval policies, 25 of 26 non-empty attack traces but also 60 of 97 benign tasks are held for approval. v0.2.0's strict-argument rule makes these unadapted policies block 94 of 97 benign tasks. Policies derived mechanically from AgentDojo's tool signatures first hit v0.2.0's lack of optional arguments (31 benign blocks); with v0.2.1 they reproduce the tool-level verdicts on all 132 traces, with no blocks and no newly admitted attack, so type-only declarations add no protection here. Median in-process latency is about 38 us per trace.

title: Superpower Competitiveness in the 4IR: AI, FinTech
container-title: Frontiers of Finance
3251c76328c511578625b2ebd589e40943676381.abstract: This study compares the competitiveness of the USA, EU, China and India over 2017–2025, using verified international indices (GII, GTCI, NRI) and descriptive indicators of AI, FinTech, human capital and innovation. Three exploratory propositions, motivated by endogenous growth in 4th Industrial Revolution, dynamic comparative advantage, and institutional theory, are examined. Innovation scores converge modestly relative to incomes per head. Talent competitiveness (GTCI) and Global innovation (GII) move together in levels, but initial talent does not predict later gains. Risk-based regulation is not associated with higher FinTech adoption: the EU records the lowest adoption, China the highest, the USA leads in capitalization. A Network Readiness Index (NRI) integrating talent, infrastructure, capital, regulatory complexity is partly computable. Three qualitative 2030 scenarios, with multipolar specialization most plausible, are exploratory, not forecasts. Policy implications (prioritizing human-capital investment, adaptive governance, infrastructure complementarity, open knowledge flows against costly technological decoupling) are hypotheses for testing on larger samples.

title: Perceived Usefulness and Willingness to Consider AI Legal Assistants for Preliminary Guidance in Bangladesh
966f4c0ed2ba0d2d8ed062df52cf7b13a947ac4d.abstract: Abstract AI legal assistants may expand preliminary information access, but perceived usefulness and willingness to consider a service should not be equated with improved access to justice. This study examines their alignment using 385 adult, consenting, AI-aware responses from Bangladesh, collected through a mixed online and in-person questionnaire approach. The legally oriented sample includes 227 law students. Low internal consistency across four questionnaire blocks motivates item-level analysis rather than composite mediation. Methods combine full response distributions, paired endorsement contrasts, joint response patterns, rank correlations and adjusted binary and ordinal models. Basic access, time saving and convenience have identical means of 3.85, yet 44.9% of respondents differ in endorsement between time saving and basic access. Willingness to consider preliminary AI guidance is endorsed by 63.9%; 30.4% jointly endorse time saving, convenience and willingness. The conditional statement that transparent explanations increase willingness receives 87.5% endorsement, exceeding general willingness by 23.6 percentage points. No focal coefficient survives multiplicity correction in the primary adjusted binary model; the nominal barrier-reduction association also does not persist in ordinal sensitivity analysis. The findings reveal broadly favourable marginal evaluations without a reliably established individual pathway from perceived benefits to willingness. The contribution is to distinguish informational convenience, prospective consideration and justice outcomes, while showing how similar averages conceal different respondent configurations. Implications favour task-specific information support, verifiable sources and human referral, evaluated through comprehension and completed service pathways. The results concern perceptions within a legally oriented sample, not demonstrated improvements in legal assistance, procedural fairness or dispute resolution.

title: CardioTwin-AI: development and internal validation of a digital twin-based adaptive risk-aware learning framework for heart disease prediction
container-title: Frontiers in Digital Health
ad124e367bd9776c8ecde4d8d57bbe7082beaa2f.abstract: Heart disease is one of the most common causes of death in the world and early identification of individuals at elevated cardiovascular risk requires reliable risk-assessment methods that can support clinical decision-making. Many conventional machine-learning models focus primarily on disease classification or risk prediction and do not explicitly provide patient-specific virtual representations. This study introduces CardioTwin-AI, a Digital Twin-based Adaptive Risk-Aware Learning Framework (ARLF) to predict the presence or absence of heart disease. We propose a data-driven, patient-specific Digital Twin representation based on clinical attributes, in which the patient state is mapped to a corresponding virtual state and evaluated using state-level synchronization measures, including Twin Simulation Error (TSE) and Twin Fidelity Score (TFS) to quantify representation consistency. The deep feature representations are generated by feature engineering process based on autoencoder, and then analysed by the ARLF prediction model to estimate the probability of the presence of heart disease. It achieved high patient-state representation consistency between the source clinical state and its virtual representation, with a Twin Fidelity Score of 99.76% and a Twin Simulation Error of 0.002402. The proposed ARLF model achieved accuracy of 90.21%, precision of 90.32%, recall of 94.11%, F1-score of 92.18%, and ROC-AUC of 95.13% in the fixed held-out evaluation. The results indicate the potential of CardioTwin-AI for predicting the presence or absence of heart disease and assessing patient-state representation consistency, subject to further external validation and prospective clinical evaluation.

title: Gender-differentiated effects of motion-enhanced AI-generated images in instructional videos: a mixed-process study using TAM-related perceptions and cognitive load theory
container-title: Frontiers in Psychology
6c320926fe075b32b1922147c5b572f0252164bf.abstract: With the widespread adoption of online educational technologies, instructional videos have become a pivotal tool for flexible and efficient learning. The integration of visual aids, such as animations and dynamic elements, aims to enhance the learning experience; however, their effectiveness remains debated. This study examined learning performance and subjective experience when instructional videos presented static AI-generated images or manually animated versions of those images. A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted with 40 undergraduate participants ( n = 10 per cell), comparing static versus motion-enhanced presentation conditions across male and female participant groups. Stable Diffusion XL generated the base images, and CapCut was used to add motion; the motion itself was not AI-generated. Participants viewed a 140-s mobile video on mortise-and-tenon structures, completed a 10-item accuracy test, and rated willingness to continue learning, preference, acceptability, ease of understanding, and mental effort. The ANOVA results provided no statistically significant evidence of a main effect of motion on learning accuracy. Differences across gender groups were observed for several subjective outcomes. For acceptability, the gender × motion interaction was statistically significant, but Bonferroni-adjusted simple-effect tests supported a gender-group difference only in the static condition. For mental effort, the interaction was also statistically significant; adjusted simple-effect tests indicated higher mental effort among female than male participants in the dynamic condition and higher mental effort in the static than dynamic condition among male participants. Given the small sample and multiple outcomes, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory.

title: SynForge-Cardio: a unified multimodal synthetic dataset generation framework for privacy-preserving cardiovascular AI
container-title: Frontiers in Digital Health
53d7a1f04e63b97105e6928eb46809e02c7207b9.abstract: Multimodal cardiovascular AI systems benefit from jointly available chest radiographs, 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs), and structured electronic health record (EHR) variables. In practice, multi-institutional model development is constrained by privacy regulations, institutional data silos, and class imbalance for less common findings. Existing open-source synthetic data tools are largely modality-specific: tabular libraries such as Synthetic Data Vault (SDV)/Conditional Tabular Generative Adversarial Network (CTGAN), image generators based on latent diffusion, and time-series methods such as Time-series Generative Adversarial Network (TimeGAN) each require its own setup, configuration, and validation. This study presents SynForge-Cardio, a multimodality orchestration framework for prompt-driven synthetic dataset generation across chest X-ray (CXR), 12-lead ECG, and EHR modalities. Rather than introducing a new generative backbone, SynForge-Cardio coordinates established components—latent diffusion with optional low-rank adaptation for CXR; parametric and bounded morphology-preserving augmentation (with an optional TimeGAN path) for ECG; and size-aware routing among jitter augmentation, Gaussian copula, and CTGAN/Tabular Variational Autoencoder for EHR—behind a shared clinical prompt interface, a rule-based router, and a postgeneration quality/privacy reporting layer. The three modalities were generated independently from separate datasets; the framework does not perform patient-level joint synthesis and makes no claim of anatomical or physiological consistency across modalities. This system is implemented as a FastAPI backend with a React frontend and can run on a single workstation GPU. Herein, we formalize the orchestration objective, specify modality-wise models and metrics [Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), dynamic time warping (DTW), power spectral density similarity, Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistics, correlation preservation, and distance-to-closest-record privacy screening], and describe an evaluation protocol on public corpora (NIH Chest X-ray14, PTB-XL, and the UCI Cleveland Heart Disease dataset), including a four-regime train-on-synthetic/test-on-real (TSTR) utility analysis with five random seeds. On the framework alone, we measured 94.6% modality-routing accuracy, 100% direct-vs.-routed generation equivalence on the evaluated cases, 59 unnecessary generator calls avoided, and 100% validation/reporting completeness (1,105/1,108 tests pass, 3 skipped). Downstream-utility results were mixed: augmenting a 25%-real training set with synthetic data changed the held-out AUROC by −0.041 to +0.050 across three CXR tasks (none significant at five seeds); by +0.019 for ECG MI-vs.-NORM [produced by mode B (bounded real-waveform augmentation, whose synthetic samples can be matched to their true source recording at top-1 ≈ 42.7–43.4%, and hence, mode B is not an independently learned generative model)]; and by +0.017 for EHR heart disease classification, which is not evidence of benefit given the 61-record hold-out set (the test-set bootstrap 95% CI for the difference includes zero). Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV acquisition was not completed because credentialed access was unavailable; all reported EHR results were UCI-based. SynForge-Cardio is intended as a practical, reproducible research framework for privacy-conscious cardiovascular data augmentation and prototype development.

title: From cognitive relief to motivational enhancement: associations between perceived Agentic AI Capability and student engagement in systems development courses
container-title: Frontiers in Psychology
27aafbc2fd89ad8063440234ea6febf14a27bb85.abstract: Generative AI agents are increasingly emerging as important learning partners for supporting complex problem-solving in higher education; however, the psychological processes associated with student engagement remain insufficiently understood. Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines how perceived Agentic AI Capability is associated with students' extraneous cognitive load, academic self-efficacy, and overall student engagement in systems development courses. An empirical study was conducted among undergraduate students majoring in e-commerce who participated in systems development-related courses. The results indicate that perceived Agentic AI Capability is negatively associated with extraneous cognitive load and positively associated with academic self-efficacy. Extraneous cognitive load is negatively associated with academic self-efficacy and student engagement, whereas academic self-efficacy is positively associated with student engagement. The indirect associations through academic self-efficacy and the sequential pathway are statistically significant. The findings provide evidence on cognitive and motivational correlates of AI-supported learning while, given the cross-sectional design, not establishing causal or temporal relationships. This study extends the application of Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory to human–AI collaborative learning environments and provides theoretical insights and practical implications for integrating generative AI into systems development education.

title: PhageLysData: an evidence-aware and AI-ready dataset of phage lytic enzymes and depolymerases
container-title: Frontiers in Bioinformatics
8b0c08ff820626b15401ffaa2d0fca3d450f7f1f.abstract: Bacteriophage lytic enzymes and depolymerases are relevant to phage biology, antimicrobial development, and protein engineering, but their sequence and annotation data remain dispersed across general databases, specialized resources, genome-centred collections, and prediction-oriented datasets. We present PhageLysData, an evidence-aware and AI-ready resource constructed through reproducible multisource integration, provenance tracking, and exact-sequence consolidation. The release integrates 807,366 source observations from seven primary resources into 759,105 unique exact-sequence entities, comprising an evidence-supported Core of 11,867 entities, a Prediction Extension of 745,092 prediction-only candidates, and 2,146 Context entities retained for provenance and reference. This architecture preserves broad sequence-space coverage while maintaining a clear distinction between non-predictive and prediction-derived support. Core entities are enriched with harmonized biological annotations, physicochemical properties, independent InterProScan-derived functional annotations, mapped PDB and AlphaFold DB structural assets, and reusable numerical representations. For 11,259 eligible Core sequences, PhageLysData provides embeddings from 11 protein language models together with one-hot encoding under a common representation contract. Release-facing examples demonstrate latent-space exploration, unsupervised clustering, supervised classification, and evidence-aware candidate retrieval without defining a universal predictive benchmark. PhageLysData provides a traceable, versioned, and computationally accessible foundation for protein retrieval, comparative analysis, task-specific dataset construction, and machine-learning applications involving phage lytic enzymes and depolymerases.

title:
Beyond AI Productivity: Enterprise AI Systems,
Human–AI Responsibility, and the Future of Work
0de0d9ca1f0ef63e0d4a49798cbf60ef60b57dd8.abstract: Abstract A prior U.S. review, Enterprise AI at the Decision Point, established that enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) as-sistants have task-dependent productivity effects and that public evidence does not identify an independent financial return or a complete chain from AI cost to verified workforce replacement. The human side of that productivity record, and any organiza-tional consequences of workforce change, were left open. This study examines responsibilities, training, job insecurity and well-being, human oversight, and performance after U.S. enterprise AI adoption from November 2022 through September 2026. The design is a critical integrative review. Firms that report a task effect most often report exclusive augmentation. Frequent AI use is associated with greater fear of job loss. In one worker panel, displacement concern, rather than use frequency itself, is associated with lower engagement and higher burnout. The contribution is a responsibility-transfer framework with five constructs and four testable propositions. A proposed computa-tional specification of that framework, Human–AI Responsibility-Aware Workflow Optimization (HARWO), places verification and accountability on the workflow graph. Gross task-time savings are separated from net employee time. HARWO is not solved or estimated in this paper. The evidence gap reflects a measurement disconnect: existing studies separately examine task productivity, workforce changes, and employee well-being, but the evidence examined here does not adequately link these outcomes within the same organizations over time. Consequently, whether AI-driven efficiency gains reduce human workload or redistribute responsibilities remains unresolved. The U.S. record is consistent with the separation of task change from employment change, and with anticipatory strain. The performance of organizations that combine AI with workforce reduction remains unmeasured, and the propositions are not empirically validated.
