title: Cognitive Metaphors as a Means of Persuasive Influence in Texts of Various Genres
container-title: Journal of Management Practices, Humanities and Social Sciences
82422fddc0741ef8edb2c1df403a0499c983b067.abstract: The present research is dedicated to the effectiveness of cognitive metaphors as a means of persuasion in political, media, and artistic discourses. Even though numerous studies have already been conducted on metaphorical conceptualization in particular discourse types, comparisons of metaphor structure, function, and audience reactions are rare. In the present study, 30 English texts (published between 2020 and 2024) belonging to the genre of political speech, media, and art (10 texts in each genre) were selected among materials from political databases, English-language magazines and literary journals. 90 people aged 20-35 (M = 26.2) evaluated metaphorical messages using C. Osgood’s semantic differential, questionnaire about the effectiveness of persuasive message and free answers. Content analysis and contextual-semantic analysis, along with descriptive statistics and one-way ANOVA were used to identify some patterns. The major source domains in political discourse include: WAR, PATH, MECHANISM, BODY and GAME, in media discourse: ELEMENT, DISEASE, THEATER, ORGANISM, and WEAPON, in artistic discourse: NATURE, LIGHT/DARKNESS, JOURNEY, BODY, and EVERYDAY LIFE. The research revealed the following: political metaphors have a tendency to be normative and rationalizing; media metaphors are critical-evaluative and disturbing; artistic metaphors show better emotional appeal and symbolism. The distinctive feature of the research is a combination of conceptual, pragmatic, and recipient-based analysis of cognitive metaphors. The findings of the research contribute to the development of cognitive metaphor theory by providing evidence concerning the persuasive and emotive effects of metaphor usage.

title: AI Anxiety, Digital Overload, and Technostress in a Polycrisis Context: A Moderated Mediation Study of Emotional Exhaustion and Psychological Well-Being Across Four Industry Sectors
287811c3d509c854883b0a89f89875e174e3e465.abstract: Abstract Background : The concurrent occurrence of AI-induced disruption, rapid post-pandemic digitalization, and macroeconomic instability has fundamentally reshaped the psychological demands of modern work, creating a polycrisis. Staff members in digital work environments experience rising AI anxiety, digital overload, and technostress, but how such polycrisis-related demands impact PWB through these mechanisms and the extent to which personal resources may act as a shield against such an effect has not been comprehensively understood yet. Based on the assumptions of the Job Demands-Resources model, the present study examines a model of moderated mediation, wherein emotional exhaustion mediates the demand-PWB association, and psychological capital (PsyCap) moderates and strengthens PWB. Methods: Cross-sectional surveys using six psychometric scales were conducted among 340 full-time workers from sectors such as IT, Health care, Education, and Banking/Finance. Hypotheses regarding the structure were validated using CB-SEM with 5,000 bias corrected bootstraps whereas sector-specific MGA and fsQCA identified configurations related to lower PWB. Results: All three job demands were able to predict emotional exhaustion: AI anxiety (β = 0.396, p < 0.001), digital overload (β = 0.333, p < 0.001), and technostress (β = 0.318, p < 0.001), explaining 32.1% of the variance. Emotional exhaustion fully mediated the influence of all three variables on PWB (β = -0.434, p < 0.001) through bootstrapped indirect effects. PsyCap had a significant direct effect on PWB (β = 0.460, p < 0.001) for all four sectors. Through MGA, sector-specific differences emerged with regard to AI anxiety, which was more important in the IT sector, digital overload in Healthcare and Banking/Finance, and technostress in the Education sector. In fsQCA, digital overload was found as a necessary condition for low PWB (consistency = 0.909), where there were three configurations, each required low PsyCap as a boundary condition (solution consistency = 0.841, coverage = 0.573). Conclusions: Demands resulting from polycrisis are linked to low PWB mainly because of emotional exhaustion, and demand salience differs significantly across sectors. Low PsyCap functions as a universal boundary condition for low levels of well-being. Organisations should prioritise PsyCap development as an industry-invariant approach in addition to demand management, which takes into account the characteristics of the job.

title:
How Much Should Artificial Intelligence Do Without a Physician?
An Autonomy Scale for AI Agents in Solid Organ Transplantation.
70f263f55880c20a80acd3b4a4d6e6cdd9d0b4c1.abstract: Abstract Background: Artificial intelligence in surgery and transplantation is moving from tools that give a single output toward software agents that retrieve data, plan several steps, use other tools, and take actions. Existing autonomy classifications and device frameworks address physical autonomy and fixed-function outputs well, but they do not specify oversight for systems whose behavior depends on intermediate decisions and tool use. Methods: We developed a governance framework by combining Yang and colleagues’ six-level autonomy scale with an agentic overlay covering tool use, data access, action scope, and persistence. We mapped the framework against current U.S. guidance for AI-enabled devices and the American Medical Association’s 2026 framework for agentic AI. We illustrated its application with four worked examples from solid organ transplantation: donor procurement, machine perfusion, and post-transplant monitoring with cell-free DNA and donor-specific antibodies, assigning each plausible agent function a level and governance tier and identifying the controls that apply. Results: The framework assigns each agent function to one of four governance tiers based on autonomy level, reversibility, and consequence. Tier A (levels 0 to 1) requires accuracy testing and query logging. Tier B (level 2) requires bounded limits, full action logs, and drift monitoring. Tier C (level 3) requires clinician approval of each consequential action, prospective evaluation, and named accountability. Tier D (levels 4 to 5) is not recommended for high-consequence decisions in the current evidence period. In the transplant example, the organ-acceptance decision is assigned to Tier C with clinician decision authority, allocation pairing is excluded from agent action, and a protocol-defined perfusion-time limit is enforced deterministically outside the model. Across the four examples, clinicians approve each consequential action, no viability marker drives acceptance alone, and automatic immunosuppression changes are excluded. Conclusions: Oversight of agents in transplant care should scale with autonomy, reversibility, and consequence rather than with product category. Binding rules should be enforced in deterministic code rather than left to model reasoning. Prospective evaluation is required before any agent in a high-consequence transplant decision advances beyond Tier C.

title: Prospective associations between diet quality, frailty and incident cognitive impairment in the health and retirement study
container-title: BMC Global and Public Health
80417bcdac85d08136be021ebebfe83d3bb6e56b.abstract: Abstract Background Diet quality is a modifiable determinant of healthy aging, potentially influencing physical and cognitive functioning through inflammatory and metabolic pathways. Although healthier dietary patterns have been linked to reduced frailty and cognitive decline, findings remain inconsistent. The interrelationships among diet quality, physical frailty, and incident cognitive impairment, including potential modification by specific dietary components, remain poorly understood. Methods We analyzed 1,636 cognitively normal participants in 2016 from the Health and Retirement Study, a longitudinal study of adults in the United States (U.S.), with diet assessed in 2013, frailty in 2016, and cognitive follow-up through 2022. Cognitive impairment was assessed with cognitive tests and used the Langa–Weir classification; diet quality was measured using the Healthy Eating Index–2015 (HEI-2015); and physical frailty used a modified Fried phenotype. Survey-weighted regression, Cox models, four-way decomposition, competing-risk and multistate models, and additive Bayesian network (ABN)–informed generalized structural equation models (GSEM) were applied. Results Higher HEI-2015 scores were associated with lower frailty (β = −0.13, P < 0.001), but not with incident cognitive impairment. Frailty was associated with higher cognitive risk in minimally adjusted models (Hazard Ratio (HR) = 2.27, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.56–3.32), with attenuation after full adjustment. Exploratory analyses identified 13 nominally significant food-item associations with composite cognitive impairment, including higher risks associated with selected dairy products, processed meats, and beverages, and an inverse association with red wine (HR = 0.77, 95% CI: 0.66–0.89). None survived FDR correction. Five dietary associations with probable dementia alone survived FDR correction but remained exploratory. Four-way decomposition provided limited evidence of dietary mediation or interaction, while sensitivity analyses supported attenuation of frailty–cognition associations. Conclusions Higher diet quality was associated with lower physical frailty but not independently with incident cognitive impairment. Food-specific associations were heterogeneous and largely did not survive multiple-testing correction. Findings warrant replication before drawing dietary recommendations for cognitive health.

title: Please Forward this Postdigital Feminist Chain-Letter on Living with AI in Higher Education
container-title: Postdigital Science and Education
97107e75549a7b1d23b73a701cdc9f4ca9237854.abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) enters higher education within established hierarchies of knowledge and expertise, becoming entangled with judgments about who sounds authoritative and which forms of writing carry weight. Those judgments were gendered, long before GenAI arrived. Drawing on feminist postdigital inquiry and collaborative, experimental approaches to knowledge production, this article reports a chain-letter experiment. Thirteen academics who identify as women or gender-diverse, from nine countries, write in relation to the letters preceding their own. The chain letter produces knowledge through response, so that each letter is partial and the argument accumulates between them. Read together, the letters describe a persistent need to defend expertise within a field shaped by masculine norms of authority, and the frustration and exhaustion this produces. Authors variously report work intensifying rather than easing, critique of GenAI tools being reframed as failures of individual users, and a sense that AI-assisted writing diminishes what makes teaching and research pleasurable. Their positions differ, with some refusing these tools while others work closely with them. At the same time, the exchange brings solidarity, hope and relief, and the discovery that these difficulties are structural as well as personal. The letters suggest that GenAI makes long-standing, gendered questions about expertise and working conditions more pressing, and that these remain shared and unfinished. The article closes with an open invitation to join a feminist and postdigital conversation about GenAI in research and education.

title: A Teacher's Concerns about AI in Primary School: Critical Thinking, Personal Data and the Fear of Cognitive Dependence
container-title: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
48daf9f5949effd20204e7775dffc33ae168a630.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is already part of pupils' everyday lives and of school life. Written from the perspective of a primary school teacher and principal, this perspective paper examines three interrelated concerns of the author herself. These concerns arose from a wish to protect her pupils and led her to study the topic for her own professional development and to help her colleagues make teaching safer and better. They concern developing critical thinking towards AI-generated answers, protecting the personal data of minors, and the fear that excessive assistance from AI will weaken pupils' thinking. Drawing on a narrative, non-systematic review of recent research on cognitive offloading, the European and Greek regulatory framework, and illustrative examples from the author's own teaching practice and lesson scenarios for primary school, it argues that the fear of cognitive dependence is a plausible concern rather than an established finding for primary school pupils. The available evidence, which comes mainly from adolescents and adults, suggests that the form of AI support (whether it replaces the learner's effort or scaffolds it) may be an important factor. AI is regarded throughout as a valuable tool; the risk lies mainly in the way it is used. The classroom examples come from ordinary lessons whose only purpose was to teach pupils to question AI answers and to protect themselves when using AI. They were not planned as research, no research data were collected, and they are offered as the author's practitioner reflections, not as findings. The author's classroom experience illustrates that such activities can be implemented in ordinary primary school lessons, but their effects on pupils' critical thinking have not yet been evaluated. The paper relates the three concerns to long-standing educational principles, in particular Socratic questioning, Dewey's reflective thought and Vygotskian scaffolding. On this basis, it proposes a simple, as yet untested three-step classroom protocol (``think -- ask -- check''), age-appropriate data protection rules, and a role for school leadership, and outlines questions for future research.

title: Slip Detection for Robotic Grasping with LSTM and TCN: Edge AI Evaluation on Embedded Platforms
container-title: Journal of Intelligent & Robotic Systems
6055ae5b60252dbfa2a2679fdf1a98b6863dffdc.abstract: Abstract Reliable object grasping is essential for robotic manipulation in real-world environments, such as manufacturing and assembly. Undetected slips can lead to task failure, while effective slip detection enables robots to adapt their grip in real time, improving robustness and safety. In earlier work, we showed that Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks can be deployed on edge devices for real-time slip detection, but that study used a manually labelled dataset and reported only accuracy and F 1 scores, which limited comparisons of model–hardware combinations. In this work, we collect a large slip detection dataset using a Fin Ray-inspired soft gripper with tactile Force Sensing Linear Potentiometers (FSLPs), a Time-of-Flight (ToF) sensor, and an encoder, to generate slip and no-slip labels from automatically estimated ArUco marker poses. We design and evaluate lightweight LSTM and Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) architectures trained on sensor sequences and compare their performance on a held-out test set. We then deploy the selected models on several embedded platforms, including Nvidia Jetson AGX Orin, Google Coral Dev Board Micro, ESP32, and Arduino Nicla Sense ME, and benchmark accuracy, F 1 score, average inference time, and estimated average energy per inference. The results show that accurate slip detection is feasible even on constrained microcontroller- class hardware, and provide a more comprehensive comparison of model and hardware choices than previous work.

title: The personal side of cognitive effort
container-title: Translation, Cognition & Behavior
Translation, Cognition and Behavior
ae01894e5cbb76871e2d262fad88c10d8b1365d0.abstract: Abstract This study investigates whether the Need for Cognition (NFC), an individual’s inclination to engage in mentally challenging tasks, predicts cognitive effort in translation and moderates how effort scales with text readability. Twenty-one native Arabic-speaking translators completed the 18-item NFC scale and translated six English texts of varying readability; eight eye-tracking and keylogging indicators captured their effort. Robust linear mixed-effects models showed limited direct effects of NFC, with marginal positive associations with character insertions and source-text reading time. NFC played a clearer role as a moderator. On the second-hardest-to-read text, high-NFC translators made more deletions and insertions and had longer production times than low-NFC peers. On the hardest-to-read text, high-NFC translators spent longer reading the source text. These findings suggest that translation process research accounts of effort should incorporate stable motivational dispositions alongside source-text demands. Given the modest sample, the findings are exploratory and require replication.

title: Learning mathematics in rural and urban schools
container-title: Australian and International Journal of Rural Education
24079e646f3a74e57ec036c3c45114583c0fa9da.abstract: Students’ mathematical problem solving is influenced not only by curriculum and instruction but also by the territorial contexts in which schools operate. This study examines how school typology—Rural, Urban, and High-Diversity Urban—relates to primary students’ performance and cognitive processing in arithmetic word problems. A total of 2,306 students from Grades 1–6 in Castellón (Spain) completed problem-solving tasks for this study using AWPSolver, a digital environment that captures detailed indicators of reading behaviour, problem-solving actions, and efficiency. We analysed success rates, reading and solving times, and efficiency indices using generalized linear models for performance, non-parametric tests for processing times, and correlations between speed and accuracy. Results revealed clear developmental improvements across grades, with older students showing higher success rates and shorter reading and solving times. Rural students tended to show favourable patterns of success and efficiency in several comparisons, particularly in the upper grades, whereas High-Diversity Urban students showed lower estimated success probabilities in some grades and stronger associations between processing time and performance in the upper grades. By integrating outcome and process-based measures, this study provides new insight into how territorial educational contexts are associated with the cognitive dynamics of mathematical problem solving. The findings suggest that school typology relates not only to achievement outcomes, but also to students’ reading and problem-solving processes. These results contribute to research on rural–urban educational differences and offer implications for designing context-sensitive instructional strategies that account for students’ social, territorial, and linguistic environments.

title: Associations of white matter microstructural damage with both cross-sectional and longitudinal cognitive decline in cerebral amyloid angiopathy and non-CAA mild cognitive impairment
container-title: Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience
33bb561edbd24eebc6e8ee0e2d3d40cb2d0139e4.abstract: Background Peak width of skeletonized mean diffusivity (PSMD) is an automated diffusion marker that captures white matter microstructural damage more sensitively than conventional small vessel disease markers. We investigated the cross sectional and longitudinal associations of PSMD and amyloid β (A β ) burden with cognition, and whether concomitant cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) modifies these relationships in mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Methods A total of 124 MCI patients were included from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, classified as CAA-MCI or non-CAA MCI by Boston criteria version 2.0. Cross-sectional and longitudinal associations between baseline PSMD, amyloid burden, and cognitive outcomes were assessed using linear regression, linear mixed-effects models, and Cox proportional hazards models. Results PSMD showed strong cross-sectional associations with processing speed and executive function, however this association was not modified by CAA status. No significant difference for longitudinal cognition changes between CAA and non-CAA groups. Within CAA-MCI, higher PSMD correlated with lower A β burden but not with cognition. Over 4 years, PSMD did not predict decline after correction for multiple comparisons in both CAA and non-CAA groups. Greater A β burden predicted multi- domain decline and dementia conversion in both groups, and the A β -associated decline in global cognition was steeper in CAA-MCI. Conclusion PSMD indexed current processing speed and executive function rather than subsequent change, independently of conventional small vessel disease markers and of CAA, whereas A β burden drove longitudinal decline and dementia conversion. The two biomarkers therefore appear to capture processes unfolding on different time scales. Whether concomitant CAA modifies amyloid-related decline requires confirmation in larger cohorts.

title: Prophylactic oxytocin infusion rate and adequate uterine tone in repeat cesarean delivery: a randomized dose-response trial
container-title: Frontiers in Medicine
b31e043f2239bb5798dac8983381fd2e75bb43de.abstract: Background The dose-response relationship of an infusion-only prophylactic oxytocin regimen in women undergoing repeat cesarean delivery remains uncertain. We evaluated adequate uterine tone at six dose levels (saline placebo at 0 IU/h and five active infusion rates of 4–20 IU/h) and estimated the originally targeted ED90. Methods In this single-center, randomized, double-blind dose-finding trial, 120 women aged 21–34 years undergoing elective repeat cesarean delivery before labor were assigned to saline placebo (0 IU/h) or oxytocin infusion at 4, 8, 12, 16, or 20 IU/h immediately after fetal delivery, without an initial bolus. The primary outcome was adequate uterine tone (score ≥ 7 on a 0–10 scale) at 3 min, assessed before rescue uterotonics. Logistic regression was the primary dose-response model; probit regression, an asymmetric complementary log-log model, isotonic regression, and assumptions for the two missing primary outcomes were examined in additional analyses. Results Primary outcome data were available for 118 women. The observed adequate-tone rate increased from 5.3% (1/19) in the placebo (0 IU/h) group to 90.0% (18/20) at 20 IU/h. In the primary logistic analysis, the estimated ED50 was 9.92 IU/h (95% confidence interval [CI], 7.72–12.09 IU/h), and the post hoc ED80 was 16.62 IU/h (95% CI, 13.93–20.80 IU/h). The logistic model-estimated ED90 was 20.54 IU/h (95% CI, 17.00–26.50 IU/h), with a point estimate above the highest tested rate of 20 IU/h. The requirement for rescue oxytocin decreased with increasing infusion rate ( P &lt; 0.001). Estimated blood loss and recorded potential oxytocin-related adverse events did not differ significantly among groups; this trial was not powered for hemorrhage or uncommon adverse events. Conclusion In this selected population, adequate uterine tone increased across the tested dose levels of 0–20 IU/h. The model-estimated ED90 point estimate lay outside the tested range and depended on extrapolation. An infusion rate around 20 IU/h should be viewed as a candidate for further evaluation, not a definitive recommended dose. Findings should not be extrapolated to bolus-plus-infusion regimens or laboring and emergency cesarean deliveries. Clinical Trial Registration https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=39583 , Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR1900023469, registered on May 30, 2019.

title: AI in communication education: a sociotechnical perspective on algorithmic automation and human mediation in Ecuador
container-title: Frontiers in Political Science
e87192d8e8ba84d92a7130d3881f914a8186cbc2.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence is transforming higher education and professional communication, creating a tension between technological automation and human critical thinking. In teaching communication, this tension highlights the need to rethink the skills students should develop as AI becomes increasingly integrated into academic and professional practice, especially the ability to use AI strategically without losing human judgment, ethical reasoning, and decision-making in their context. Methodology The study uses an exploratory-descriptive, cross-sectional, mixed-methods design combining quantitative and qualitative evidence to explore how students and program directors in Ecuador perceive AI integration in communication education. It surveyed 230 students across seven institutions and conducted 12 semi-structured interviews with directors. Survey analysis identified AI usage patterns, while thematic analysis of interviews focused on benefits, barriers, ethics, and priorities. Initially, Pearson's chi-square test examined associations with sociodemographics, but it was unreliable due to low expected cell counts. Findings are presented as descriptive patterns, not inferential or population-level conclusions. Results Students report using AI mainly for communication (28.70%), trend prediction and audience analysis (13.04%), and segmentation (9.57%). Four AI applications were identified: operational efficiency, strategic analysis, audience management, and digital optimization. The gender-based chi-square test was inconclusive ( χ 2 = 12.728; df = 14; p = 0.548), with over 50% of cells having fewer than 5 responses. Among directors and coordinators, common uses included content generation, assisted writing, research, data analysis, and audience engagement. The thematic analysis revealed four patterns: operational efficiency, decision-making, automation vs. human judgment, and training needs. Discussion and conclusions Communication students in Ecuador mainly use AI to improve efficiency and effectiveness, with key applications in trend prediction, audience analysis, and segmentation. Program leaders see AI as useful in content creation, research, and audience engagement. The study identifies four AI use areas: operational efficiency, strategic analysis, audience management, and digital optimization. The study highlights tension between automation and human judgment, stressing the continued importance of critical thinking, creativity, ethics, and context. It proposes a framework balancing AI automation with human input to support strategic communication decisions.

title: From emotional comfort to relational investment in generative AI companionship: evidence from SEM and fsQCA
container-title: Frontiers in Psychology
6c8384f16783c106639bef8d6d4125fd000ef3d8.abstract: With the rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI), chatbots are evolving from instrumental assistants into emotionally responsive companions. This study develops a low-friction relational process model to examine the relationships linking generative AI companionship with emotional relief and positive social investment. AI emotional responsiveness, non-judgemental interaction, and memory-based continuity were conceptualized as interaction conditions, while perceived being understood, deep self-disclosure, and synthetic attachment were specified as psychological mechanisms. Structural equation modeling (SEM), bootstrap mediation analysis, moderation analysis, and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) were employed to analyse 765 valid responses from generative AI chatbot users. The SEM results show that non-judgemental interaction exhibits the most consistent pattern of associations with perceived being understood, deep self-disclosure, synthetic attachment, emotional relief, and positive social investment. Perceived being understood and synthetic attachment show relatively stable mediating patterns, whereas deep self-disclosure is significantly associated with emotional relief but shows a less consistent association with positive social investment. Perceived AI safety and self-disclosure habit play differentiated moderating roles. The fsQCA findings reveal three configurations for high emotional relief and four configurations for high positive social investment, complementing the SEM results. This study provides a systematic account of generative AI companionship and offers implications for safer and relationship-oriented AI design.

title: Audience appraisal of AI generated visual media across viewers and scenes
container-title: Frontiers in Psychology
bfe9ed4d52f73ab8b93caff7355f18ed32b05f34.abstract: How do audiences relate the authenticity, emotional meaning, trustworthiness, and acceptability of AI-generated visual media? For cultural exhibitions and other uses of reconstructed pasts, emotional appeal and perceived credibility need not coincide, and audience responses may differ across scenes. We examine these questions through an appraisal-oriented account of AI-generated reconstructions of urban everyday life. Study 1 ( N = 513) used Mode-A composite PLS-SEM with 24 items representing eight constructs to estimate viewer-level evaluation associations. Ten of eleven hypothesized paths were supported. Nostalgic response was associated with acceptance intention, but its hypothesized positive association with trust was not supported after perceived authenticity and AI traces were considered. Study 2 independently compared baseline and treated versions of 12 scenes using a nonrandomized design (primary N = 780). The overall perceived-authenticity difference was not significant (0.010, 95% CI [−0.033, 0.052], p = 0.656). Perceived AI traces were higher in the treated group in the fixed-scene analysis (0.060, 95% CI [0.025, 0.096], BH-adjusted p = 0.007), but the interval crossed zero in a post hoc scene-level condition random-slope model (0.060, 95% CI [−0.098, 0.219]). Condition-by-scene interactions were significant for all eight constructs. Together, the studies show why the appraisal of AI-generated pasts should distinguish emotional reception from trust and examine particular proposed scenes rather than rely on a single average authenticity rating.

title: Generative AI feedback use and deep cognitive engagement in university EFL writing: a mixed-methods study of autonomy, self-regulated learning, and AI literacy
container-title: Frontiers in Psychology
afb75769dc989373555c79649418b5d149ca608a.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to obtain feedback in English as a foreign language (EFL) writing, but its educational significance depends on how learners interpret and regulate that feedback. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory and self-regulated learning theory, this explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examined an AI-supported motivated self-regulated learning framework using a cross-sectional survey of 486 university EFL students and follow-up interviews with 20 students. Structural equation modeling identified a positive direct association between reported AI feedback use and deep cognitive engagement, together with a positive indirect statistical association through learning autonomy and self-regulated learning. The AI feedback use–autonomy association was stronger at higher modeled levels of AI literacy. Interview accounts described feedback-related control, critical evaluation, and awareness of AI limitations, alongside contrasting experiences of rapid polishing and careful evaluation despite limited familiarity with AI. Integration of the two strands highlighted variation in how learners evaluated and incorporated feedback. These self-report findings do not establish temporal ordering or causal effects. They identify learner agency, strategic regulation, and critical evaluation as relevant considerations for future investigations of AI-supported writing.

title: Information overload, cognitive fatigue, and postgraduates’ intention to use generative artificial intelligence for English academic writing: the role of lower-order cognitive offloading
container-title: Frontiers in Psychology
44519a3982b4f3a7618933a7c685ba32b093e792.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) returns large amounts of information that postgraduates must judge and integrate when they write in English. The stressor-strain-outcome framework suggests that such overload strains cognitive resources and weakens plans for further use. This study tested whether cognitive fatigue links perceived information overload with later behavioral intention to use AI for English academic writing. It also tested whether lower-order cognitive offloading, such as having AI summarize papers, conditions the overload-fatigue association. Methods In total, 475 Chinese master’s and doctoral students who used AI for English academic writing completed three surveys at two-week intervals. Overload and offloading were measured at Time 1, fatigue at Time 2, and intention at Time 3. A moderated mediation model adjusted for baseline fatigue, baseline intention, and AI-use frequency. Results Higher perceived information overload accompanied higher cognitive fatigue 2 weeks later and weaker behavioral intention 4 weeks later, net of baseline levels. Cognitive fatigue was associated with weaker later intention and carried part of the overload-intention association. The overload-fatigue association was weaker at higher levels of lower-order cognitive offloading. Among the most frequent offloaders it was not statistically significant, which does not indicate its absence. The indirect association through fatigue was likewise weaker at higher offloading. These patterns held with additional covariates, a competing interaction with AI-use frequency, and shortened scales. Conclusion In this sample, cognitive fatigue accompanied the prospective association between overload and weaker plans to use AI. This pathway was weaker among postgraduates who delegated foundational tasks more often. Writing programs can teach students which foundational tasks to delegate, and tool developers can limit output overload.

title: Atherogenic index of plasma and cognitive recovery trajectories after ischemic stroke: a retrospective longitudinal cohort study
container-title: Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience
d6dc75817dcb14a78d909c9e414016fb939ed79e.abstract: Background Early cognitive recovery after ischemic stroke is heterogeneous. We examined global cognitive recovery trajectories and their associations with the atherogenic index of plasma (AIP) during and after inpatient rehabilitation. Methods This retrospective longitudinal cohort included 210 patients with imaging-confirmed ischemic stroke and available cognitive assessments at rehabilitation admission, discharge, and approximately 3 months after discharge. AIP was calculated from triglyceride and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol concentrations in the same first fasting blood sample collected within 24 h after rehabilitation admission. Latent class mixed models characterized Chinese Mini-Mental State Examination (CMMS) trajectories. Secondary, exploratory analyses examined AIP associations with trajectory membership and longitudinal CMMS and Modified Barthel Index (MBI) scores. Trajectory-membership analyses accounted for classification uncertainty using two-stage joint likelihood estimation with 1,000 parametric bootstrap draws. Results Three trajectories were identified: moderate-baseline marked-improvement (94 patients [44.8%]), higher-baseline modest-improvement (69 [32.9%]), and low-baseline persistently low (47 [22.4%]). In the fully adjusted model, each 1-SD higher AIP was associated with greater odds of the low-baseline persistently low trajectory versus the moderate-baseline marked-improvement trajectory (odds ratio, 1.85; 95% CI, 1.16–2.96; nominal p = 0.0095), but not versus the higher-baseline modest-improvement trajectory. Each 1-SD higher AIP was associated with 0.77 points less CMMS improvement from admission to follow-up (95% CI, −1.09 to −0.44; nominal p &lt; 0.001). There was no clear association with longitudinal MBI recovery. Conclusion Early global cognitive recovery followed heterogeneous patterns. Higher rehabilitation-phase AIP was associated with less CMMS improvement and with the persistently low rather than the marked-improvement trajectory. These exploratory findings require independent replication; their clinical importance and prognostic utility remain uncertain.

title: Trustworthy AI for multimodal load-response modelling in team sports: a scoping review and full-text validation audit
container-title: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
92eda9136a55028de3d61b3243328292f5ffe5c2.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI), machine-learning and conventional statistical prediction methods are increasingly used in team-sport athlete monitoring, but it remains unclear whether current studies are validated and reported in ways that support trustworthy prospective use. This scoping review mapped predictive-modelling studies in team-sport athlete monitoring and multimodal load-response modelling and audited their validation and reporting practices. Methods Searches were conducted in OpenAlex, PubMed, Scopus and SPORTDiscus for records published from 2010 to 2026. After deduplication, screening and updated OpenAlex rerun screening, 258 studies were included and audited from full text. Systematic duplicate screening was not performed; full-text eligibility assessment and original audit coding were completed by a single reviewer. Data were extracted on publication characteristics, sport context, data modalities, modelled outcomes, model families and validation practices. A 10-domain trustworthy-AI audit assessed prediction context, temporal validity, repeated-observation independence, external validation, leakage control, calibration, class-imbalance handling, interpretability, uncertainty reporting and deployment/actionability. Bibliometric and NLP analyses provided complementary field mapping. A second reviewer independently assessed 45 studies from the original 223-study audit subset across all ten audit domains. Results The literature expanded rapidly after 2021, with performance modelling and injury-risk prediction as the dominant applications. Studies frequently used GPS/GNSS, session-RPE/internal load, wellness/sleep, HR/HRV, neuromuscular testing, IMU/accelerometry and video-derived features. Random forests, logistic/linear models and gradient boosting were the most common model families. Deployment-relevant validation remained limited. After targeted reassessment and updated-search incorporation, temporal validity was strongly documented in 28 studies (10.9%), while independent external validation was strongly documented in one study (0.4%) and partially documented in one additional study (0.4%). Leakage control, calibration, repeated-observation independence and model-level uncertainty reporting were also uncommon. Pre-correction exact agreement in the independent audit subset was 65.3% overall and varied substantially across domains. Discussion Predictive modelling in team-sport athlete monitoring is expanding, but model development has advanced faster than trustworthy validation practice. Future studies should define the intended decision context, preserve temporal and player-level data structure, prevent leakage, report calibration and uncertainty, validate models under realistic deployment conditions and translate outputs into practitioner-facing decision support.

title: A study on the synergistic effects of teacher–student interaction patterns and an AI-based emotional feedback system in secondary school chemistry laboratory classes: an intervention experiment grounded in inquiry-based instruction
container-title: Frontiers in Education
96b6b86b3b878503d2576ece5930fa96e5fb585b.abstract: While prior research has examined how teacher-student interaction influences student learning in conventional chemistry laboratory instruction, few studies have systematically disentangled the synergistic mechanisms that connect dynamic patterns of teacher-student interaction with AI-driven emotional feedback systems-and, critically, how these interactions jointly shape educational outcomes in AI-integrated chemistry laboratory classrooms. This gap constrains the evidence-informed design of emotion-responsive, intelligent chemistry pedagogy. This study employed a mixed-methods design integrating a quasi-experimental intervention with qualitative thematic analysis. A semester-long intervention was implemented with two cohorts of ninth-grade students: an experimental group ( n = 40) receiving inquiry-based chemistry laboratory instruction augmented by an AI-powered emotional feedback system, and a control group ( n = 38) receiving equivalent inquiry-based instruction supported solely by conventional teacher-student interaction. The study comparatively analyzed students' emotional experiences across the two instructional conditions. Distinct emotional trajectories emerged between the groups. The AI-supported experimental group exhibited a statistically significant increase in chemistry laboratory anxiety over the semester, with no meaningful improvement in subjective achievement. In contrast, the control group maintained stable anxiety levels and demonstrated consistent growth in perceived achievement. Moreover, the control group outperformed the experimental group in procedural compliance and the rigor of hands-on laboratory operations. No statistically significant intergroup differences were observed for other affective indicators-including sense of accomplishment and willingness to collaborate. These findings advance the theoretical understanding of human-machine collaborative pedagogy within intelligent learning environments. Empirically grounded, they yield actionable insights for the design of chemistry laboratory instruction in AI-integrated settings-particularly in developing learner-centered, emotion-aware frameworks for human-AI co-teaching.

title: Association between any informal helping and cognitive function among older adults: a propensity score study
container-title: Frontiers in Public Health
712173a9caa4ceb9a02f08a748588bf6e858bce8.abstract: Objectives Whether everyday informal helping is associated with cognitive function in later life, particularly among older adults recruited from healthcare and residential care institutions, remains insufficiently characterized. This study examined the association between any informal helping and cognitive function and explored the cross-sectional statistical indirect association through depressive symptoms. Methods Using a multicenter cross-sectional design and non-probability convenience sampling, we recruited adults aged 60 years or older from seven healthcare and residential care institutions in Hubei Province, China, between June 2025 and June 2026. To reduce baseline differences between participants who did and did not provide any informal helping, seven propensity score (PS) approaches were applied, including inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) and overlap weighting (OW). Depressive symptoms were assessed using the 10-item Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D-10), and an exploratory cross-sectional mediation analysis was conducted to estimate the statistical indirect association through depressive symptoms. Finally, sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the consistency of the observed associations across alternative estimators and outcome definitions. Results Among 864 participants, the median age was 69.00 (64.00–74.00) years; 474 (54.86%) were men, and 214 (24.77%) reported any informal helping. Although several baseline covariates were imbalanced before PS adjustment, adequate balance was achieved afterward. The estimated mean differences from PS matching, stratification, and IPTW were 2.214 (95% CI, 0.987–3.440), 3.519 (95% CI, 2.614–4.424), and 3.588 (95% CI, 2.742–4.433), respectively. The direction of the association was consistent across alternative analytical approaches. An exploratory cross-sectional mediation analysis identified a statistical indirect effect through depressive symptoms (estimate = 2.122, 95% CI, 1.638–2.691; p &lt; 0.001). Conclusion Any informal helping was associated with higher cognitive function scores among older adults. An exploratory analysis also identified a cross-sectional statistical indirect association involving depressive symptoms. These observational findings require further investigation in longitudinal studies.

Subsequent high-temperature annealing produces the coarser microstructures required for martensitic phase development. High-purity aluminum and copper strips were combined with silver particles as the starting materials. The aluminum level was kept constant at 15[Formula: see text]wt.%, while the silver content was adjusted to 2.5, 5, and 7.5[Formula: see text]wt.%. After ARB processing, the multilayered composites were annealed for one hour at 700–[Formula: see text]C and then quenched to room temperature. The study focuses on how silver concentration and annealing temperature influence the resulting microstructure. All processed samples developed refined grains and elevated dislocation densities. Heat treatment produced new intermetallic compounds. Alloys containing 2.5[Formula: see text]wt.% Ag mainly formed Cu 9 Al 4 , whereas those with 5–7.5[Formula: see text]wt.% Ag stabilized orthorhombic Cu 3 Al martensite. The presence of martensite increased strength and microhardness at room temperature. The highest martensite content appeared in the 900–[Formula: see text]C annealing range. The annealed and quenched composites demonstrated strong shape memory performance at ambient conditions.

Fractional time-derivative h-curves and residual measures are used as finite-order sensitivity and equation-satisfaction diagnostics rather than as proofs of convergence or stability. The influence of fractional memory is examined for fractional orders from [Formula: see text] to 1. At [Formula: see text], the transition-front position changes from [Formula: see text] in the classical case to [Formula: see text] at the lowest fractional order considered, whereas the transition width and maximum spatial slope vary by less than approximately [Formula: see text] and [Formula: see text], respectively. In the classical limit, the sampled maximum error decreases from [Formula: see text] at the first truncation order to [Formula: see text] at the fourth. Independent validation using a fully implicit [Formula: see text] finite-difference scheme gives maximum discrepancies of [Formula: see text] for the principal fractional case and [Formula: see text] for an additional test case. These results indicate that, for the parameter regime examined, power-law memory primarily delays wave-front propagation while largely preserving the transition shape. title: Noun memory advantage drives sentence internal primacy and recency at clause boundaries
4c0f1815f12341b53fff8ba4c7ef1b2cf187d3d5.abstract: Classic research in psychology has shown that comprehenders in recall tasks ‘chunk’ word lists in order to facilitate later retrieval. Here we ask how chunking mechanisms apply in grammatically structured sentence stimuli. How do comprehenders make use of this grammatical structure to guide chunking of a sentence’s component words in memory? In previous studies of multi-clause sentence recall, many researchers have argued that chunking is clause-based, as evidenced by scalloped serial accuracy curves in which primacy and recency effects are observed within each clause. Here we suggest that these previous findings may have been driven by the correlation of sentence boundaries with nouns, a lexical class known to demonstrate an independent accuracy advantage in recall. Using immediate serial recall of naturalistic biclausal English sentences and manipulating noun placement, we find evidence that nouns indeed confer a large accuracy boost at the internal clause boundary that can explain prior results. We discuss the difficulty of applying serial position logic to highly structured representations such as those that underlie sentence forms.

title: Trust Modulates Speech Entrainment: Enhanced Cortical Tracking for Low-trust Speakers
container-title: Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience
93efb8d8a2efd6ac00960e2f7910f482c84055f4.abstract: Abstract Trust is a critical component of human communication, providing a foundation for understanding, information exchange, and social coordination. Much of the research on trust in speech communication has focused on how vocal characteristics impact perceived trustworthiness. However, little is known about how trust in a speaker affects the neural processing of speech. Here, we demonstrate a two-stage experimental framework to study that question using noninvasive EEG. First, participants engage in a trust-building stage, where they play an investment game with fictional characters, each paired with a distinctive voice and trustworthiness level (i.e., frequency and magnitude of lies). Next, participants engage in a story-listening stage, in which they are presented with stories from the same characters. Data acquired from 20 young adults confirm a statistically significant correlation between the perceived and actual trustworthiness of the fictional characters. Cortical speech tracking was quantified using a temporal response function analysis on the EEG data. We found that the trustworthiness established during the trust-building stage influenced the cortical tracking of speech in the subsequent story-listening stage, with lower trustworthiness corresponding to a stronger cortical tracking of speech. Interestingly, trustworthiness selectively modulated tracking strength, with no statistically significant changes in the spatial and temporal temporal response function dynamics.

title: Distributed Neural Dynamics Underlie the Shift from Movement Preparation to Execution
container-title: Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience
7a79083e41e8564c05cef0c9e6a1179e83f26049.abstract: Abstract Understanding how neural population activity supports the transition from movement preparation to execution remains a central challenge in systems neuroscience. Invasive recordings in nonhuman primates indicate that motor preparation and execution occupy orthogonal subspaces within the primary motor cortex (M1), yet how these neural dynamics evolve across broader networks and support skilled, memory-guided action remains poorly understood. We used source-resolved magnetoencephalography during a memory-guided finger-sequence task to track population dynamics across a cortico-hippocampal network. Manifold trajectories and decoding revealed that preparation and execution of movement sequences occupy distinct, yet not fully orthogonal, neural subspaces—a separation that generalized across all regions but was most pronounced in motor regions. Crucially, we identified a hierarchical spatio-temporal transition across the brain: The state shift originated in the hippocampus via theta-band modulations and rippled through the pre-SMA, SMA, and lateral premotor areas before culminating in M1 via broadband activity. This progression follows the functional hierarchy of descending motor pathways, with M1 shifting last, 160 msec before the first button press. Although sequence identity could be decoded from all areas during execution, only the hippocampus and M1 maintained predictive representations of upcoming sequences during preparation. These findings demonstrate that the initiation of complex motor sequences relies on a well-timed integration of hippocampal memory systems with primary motor output, rather than being a process localized to the motor cortices alone.

title: Sequential Sampling from Memory Underlies Perceptual Decisions Unyoked from Actions
container-title: Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience
a917d6aa52f462098a3786e8e5c48f2839ba057f.abstract: Abstract Perceptual decision-making refers to the class of decisions in which sensory evidence is used to categorize percepts and guide actions. Conventionally, categorical decisions are thought to precede motor actions. However, recent studies in nonhuman primates challenge this assumption—when perceptual decisions were uncoupled from the actions they bear upon, animals postponed the decisions until relevant response options were revealed. To determine whether this postponement stems from cognitive limitations unique to nonhuman primates, we conducted a similar experiment with human participants. Naive participants viewed a random dot motion (RDM) stimulus that was difficult to categorize. After a delay period following the RDM, two choice targets were presented and participants decided which target lay closer to the perceived motion direction. Decision accuracy varied across participants, reflecting individual differences in ability to integrate motion evidence. Notably, participants with higher decision accuracy showed prolonged deliberation after choice-target presentation. Furthermore, the time they took to report their decisions depended on the strength of the motion evidence. This pattern of accuracy and decision reporting time could be accounted for by a bounded diffusion model in which participants sequentially sample stored sensory information from memory during the target selection phase. When the RDM was challenging to categorize, the subsequent appearance of the targets provided a framework to interrogate stored evidence and render a decision. Our results reveal a strategic feature of working memory of retaining information based on its future utility. This observation opens new avenues for investigating how memory and decision-making interact.

title: Confounds in Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging—Part III: Auxiliary Data
container-title: Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience
7ebbf91cc1104ca6a325a8fc4b3255a08d3c579e.abstract: Abstract In the first part of this series, we reviewed the pathways that bring about confounding nuisance signals in fMRI. Then, in the second part, we considered how human factors can modify these pathways. In this, the third and final part, we review auxiliary data that may allow researchers to identify and perhaps correct for nuisance signals and their modifiers. We consider three broad categories of data: (1) measures that can be collected synchronously with the fMRI, (2) other MRI scans that either capture trait information or attempt to define the state that exists during an fMRI scan in the same session, and (3) non-MRI measures that can be collected before or after the scan and that also capture trait or relevant state factors influencing the fMRI. We conclude with some recommendations on ways to improve fMRI experiments going forward.

title: Group Counseling Using Cognitive Restructuring Techniques to Improve Self-Confidence in Students Experiencing Body Image Dissatisfaction
container-title: Urwatul Wutsqo: Jurnal Studi Kependidikan dan Keislaman
7431be1e125079182ebbbdf9ee795afaa40c31f7.abstract: This study aims to systematically examine the implementation of cognitive restructuring techniques in group counseling to enhance secondary school students’ self-confidence, investigate the relationship between body image dissatisfaction and self-confidence, and identify factors influencing counseling outcomes. A qualitative Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted using the PRISMA 2020 guidelines and SPIDER framework. Relevant publications from 2017 to 2026 were retrieved through Google Scholar and GARUDA. Ten primary studies met the inclusion criteria, comprising seven intervention studies and three correlational studies. Methodological quality was evaluated using the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tools, followed by thematic synthesis. The findings indicate that cognitive restructuring generally involves identifying negative thoughts, developing rational alternatives, practicing positive self-statements, and evaluating behavioral changes. Intervention studies consistently reported improvements in students’ self-confidence, although methodological limitations restrict causal conclusions. Student participation and supportive environments facilitated implementation, whereas embarrassment, hesitation, and fear of criticism constituted barriers. Correlational studies demonstrated significant positive relationships between body image and self-confidence without establishing causality. Importantly, none of the reviewed intervention studies specifically examined students experiencing body image dissatisfaction. This review contributes by integrating previously separate research findings and identifying an important evidence gap. Further controlled studies are recommended to evaluate cognitive restructuring interventions specifically among students experiencing body image dissatisfaction.

title: The Effect of ChatGPT Use on Students’ Reflection on Pancasila and Citizenship Education Learning Materials
container-title: Journal of General Education and Humanities
050236c7b96190ddf97fb7b818f89a0295355ad4.abstract: The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) into education has created new opportunities to support reflective learning; however, empirical evidence regarding the relationship between ChatGPT use and learning reflection in Pancasila and Citizenship Education remains limited. This study examined the relationship between ChatGPT use and students' learning reflection among Grade XI students. A quantitative correlational design was employed involving 56 Grade XI students selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using validated questionnaires comprising 15 items measuring ChatGPT Use and 12 items measuring Learning Reflection. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and simple linear regression. The results demonstrated a positive and statistically significant relationship between ChatGPT use and learning reflection (R² = 0.813, p < 0.001). Descriptive analysis indicated that ChatGPT Use (M = 54.21, SD = 3.57) and learning reflection (M = 42.77, SD = 4.38) were classified as being in the "Good" category. These findings suggest that ChatGPT can support reflective learning when integrated into well-designed pedagogical activities under teacher guidance. This study contributes empirical evidence regarding the educational use of Generative AI in Pancasila and Citizenship Education and provides practical implications for promoting reflective and responsible learning.

title: Chatgpt Acceptance among Students: An Information Systems Perspective in the Era of Generative
container-title: International Journal of Accounting and Business Finance
4d2ed33e753ae8bdeeee6ea7126abccc732273ad.abstract: This study investigates the factors influencing university students’ acceptance and use of ChatGPT from an information systems perspective in the context of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). As AI technologies become more common in society, their adoption within higher education has been rapidly increasing․ Students are utilizing tools such as ChatGPT for a variety of purposes, including information retrieval, writing support, and comprehension of complex academic topics․ Despite their educational potential, concerns about academic integrity, accuracy, and their effect on students' critical thinking have been raised. This study adopts a quantitative approach using a survey method to collect data from 650 undergraduate students of the Faculty of Management Studies and Commerce at the University of Jaffna (UOJ), Sri Lanka․ This study is based on information systems success theory and technology acceptance model․ This model depicts the impact of information quality, system quality, service quality, trust in service and self-confidence on system use, user satisfaction, and student achievability, as well as the effect of on student perceived benefits․ In order to test the relationships above, the data was analyzed using the Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) approach via the SmartPLS software․ Furthermore, system quality, service quality, trust, and self-confidence significantly influence user satisfaction and system use. Student achievability and user satisfaction were found to have a strong positive impact on perceived student benefits․ However, information quality did not significantly influence system use, satisfaction, or achievability. Overall, the findings underscore the importance of both technological and psychological factors in shaping students' experiences and attitudes towards generative AI tools, providing valuable insights for educators and institutions interested in utilizing these technologies responsibly and effectively in higher education contexts․

title: Longitudinal cognitive and functional outcomes after hemorrhagic stroke in patients with preserved consciousness: a prospective observational study
container-title: Frontiers in Neurology
a6dcd096c328872c19fc7e51efbe7313a5031202.abstract: Introduction Cognitive impairment is a common consequence of stroke but may be underrecognized in patients with preserved consciousness. This study evaluated longitudinal changes in neurological, cognitive, and functional outcomes during the first 6 months after hemorrhagic stroke and identified baseline predictors of unfavorable outcomes. Methods A total of 74 patients with hemorrhagic stroke and preserved consciousness [Glasgow Coma Scale ≥13; mean age, 57.9 ± 10.1 years: 36 women (48.6%)] were prospectively enrolled between July 2020 and July 2024. Cognitive and functional outcomes were assessed at the initial assessment and at 1, 3, and 6 months using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR), Basic Activities of Daily Living (BADL), and Instrumental Activities of Daily Living (IADL). Longitudinal changes were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models, and logistic regression was performed to identify predictors of unfavorable outcomes at 6 months. Results Cognitive measures improved significantly over time, with increases in MoCA scores ( p &lt; 0.001) and reductions in CDR scores ( p = 0.028). In contrast, BADL and IADL showed trends toward improvement without statistical significance. At 6 months, 25.7% of patients had unfavorable cognitive or functional outcomes. Older age, lower educational level, and previous stroke were independently associated with unfavorable outcomes. Conclusion Patients with hemorrhagic stroke and preserved consciousness showed gradual cognitive improvement over 6 months, although a substantial proportion experienced unfavorable cognitive or functional outcomes. These findings highlight the potential importance of early cognitive assessment even in patients with relatively mild neurological presentations. Given the modest sample size and exploratory nature of the analyses, larger prospective studies are warranted to validate these findings and further investigate predictors of post-stroke cognitive and functional recovery.

title: The effectiveness of AI-based cognitive behavioral therapy chatbots for anxiety and depression symptoms: a systematic review and meta-analysis
container-title: Frontiers in Public Health
12ee7b8b941ec1f9692a230d0f570c757b2ca9ce.abstract: Background AI chatbots are increasingly being used to provide accessible psychological support. However, the effectiveness of chatbot-delivered cognitive behavioral therapy for anxiety and depressive symptoms remains uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of artificial intelligence chatbot-based cognitive behavioral therapy on anxiety and depressive symptoms. Method A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, PsycINFO, Cochrane Library, CNKI, VIP, Wanfang, and CBM databases was conducted from their inception to July 8th, 2025. Updated search on August 25, 2026. Meta-analysis was conducted using Stata version 18.0 and RevMan version 5.4. The ES for the treatment effect was calculated using the SMD . Results Ten studies involving a total of 1,301 participants. The results of the meta-analysis showed that the CBT of AI chatbots could significantly improve depressive symptoms at the end of the intervention ( d = −0.40, 95% CI : −0.62 ~ −0.17, P = 0.0005). In contrast, the intervention did not significantly improve anxiety symptoms ( d = −0.029, 95% CI : −0.145 ~ 0.087, P = 0.623), with no substantial heterogeneity detected ( I 2 = 0%). The subgroup analysis for depressive symptoms indicated significant effects were observed in participant age stratification, intervention Duration, and Control group intervention. However, some subgroup estimates were based on a small number of studies, so the data should be interpreted with caution. Conclusion This meta-analysis emphasizes that AI-based chatbots for CBT may have great potential in contributing to the alleviation of depressive symptoms. Given the small number of included studies and the high heterogeneity, the results should be interpreted with caution. More high-quality RCTs are needed in the future to further validate these findings and explore their long-term benefits. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251089835 .

title: Latent profiles of teachers’ beliefs about drama pedagogy and children’s social–emotional, linguistic-communicative, and cognitive performance
container-title: Frontiers in Psychology
fc22ad1429c406f8e34509d938a4185b73190323.abstract: Introduction Although drama pedagogy is widely used as a participatory educational approach, less is known about how teachers organize their beliefs about its developmental value. The present study examined teachers’ beliefs regarding the contribution of the drama-pedagogical approach to children’s social–emotional, linguistic-communicative, and cognitive functioning. More specifically, it examined the internal structure of these beliefs, the identification of latent belief profiles, and the association of these profiles with teachers’ demographic and professional characteristics. Methods The study involved 571 primary education teachers who had previous training and teaching experience with drama-pedagogical practices. Data were collected through an adapted online questionnaire designed to capture teachers’ perceptions of the developmental functions of drama pedagogy. The analyses included an examination of the factor structure, assessment of internal consistency, latent profile analysis, and investigation of the association between profile membership and demographic and professional characteristics. Results The results provided qualified support for a three-factor organization of perceptions into social–emotional, linguistic-communicative, and cognitive dimensions, with strong positive correlations among the dimensions and satisfactory internal consistency. The latent profile analysis identified three belief profiles: a strong developmental beliefs profile, a moderate profile, and a comparatively lower profile. The profiles differed mainly in the overall intensity of beliefs and less in distinct combinations of dimensions. Profile membership was associated mainly with teaching grade or educational setting and, to a lesser extent, with gender. Discussion The findings indicate that teachers make sense of drama pedagogy as a multidimensional developmental practice, with differences in the intensity of their beliefs. The findings may inform the design of more targeted professional development programs, adapted to the teaching context and to teachers’ belief profiles.

title: Cognitive load detection using hyper-learning dragonfly optimization for feature selection
container-title: Frontiers in Physiology
5a453798221500241d3cfe550feba897cab0c822.abstract: Introduction Cognitive load detection is essential for understanding brain responses to mental effort and cognitive demands. Electroencephalogram (EEG) signals provide valuable information about neural activity and offer a non-invasive approach to identifying cognitive load. However, accurate detection and the identification of brain regions with superior discriminative capabilities remain important challenges. Methods This study proposes an EEG-based cognitive load detection framework using empirical Fourier decomposition (EPFD), entropy-based feature extraction, and the hyper-learning binary dragonfly feature selection algorithm (HLBDA). EEG signals recorded from each brain lobe over four-second intervals were decomposed into 10 intrinsic mode functions (IMFs). Entropy-based features were extracted from the IMFs, and the most informative features were selected using HLBDA. The selected features were classified using machine learning (ML) classifiers. The proposed framework was evaluated on the MAT, STEW, and MLR datasets. Additionally, lobe-wise cognitive load detection was performed on the MAT and STEW datasets to investigate the discriminative capabilities of five individual brain lobes. Subject-wise leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) was employed to prevent data leakage. Results The proposed framework achieved classification accuracies of 97.13%, 96.48%, and 98.2% on the MAT, STEW, and MLR datasets, respectively, using the K-nearest neighbors (KNN) classifier for MAT and STEW and the ensemble subspace KNN (ESSK) classifier for MLR. In the lobe-wise analysis, the frontal lobe demonstrated superior discriminative capability for cognitive load detection, achieving accuracies of 96.7% and 96.6% on the MAT and STEW datasets, respectively, using the ESSK classifier. Discussion The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed EPFD–HLBDA-based framework for EEG-based cognitive load detection across multiple datasets. The superior performance of the frontal lobe suggests its potential as a particularly informative region for distinguishing cognitive states. Furthermore, the use of subject-wise LOOCV strengthens the evaluation by reducing the risk of data leakage. Compared with recently reported methods, the proposed framework demonstrates competitive classification performance and highlights the potential of lobe-specific EEG analysis for reliable cognitive load assessment.

title: Association between plasma homocysteine levels and post-stroke cognitive impairment: a pooled analysis of 564 patients from two independent cohorts
container-title: Frontiers in Nutrition
7c0af70c2e569550b83f2b9dcf508c44c859fffb.abstract: Introduction Post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) affects one-third of stroke survivors, but early biomarkers are lacking. We tested whether plasma homocysteine (Hcy) independently predicts PSCI. Methods Two acute ischemic stroke cohorts were merged (564 patients). PSCI was defined as a Montreal Cognitive Assessment score ≤ 23 at 3–6 months. Associations were tested with multivariable logistic regression, restricted cubic spline, sensitivity, subgroup, and mediation analyses. Results PSCI occurred in 36.9%. Hcy was higher in PSCI (21.99 vs. 15.87 μmol/L, p &lt; 0.001) and associated after adjustment (OR = 1.019 per μmol/L, 95% CI 1.002–1.037, p = 0.030); in Cohort B, where age, sex, education and infarct laterality were recorded, the association remained significant after full adjustment (OR = 1.034, 95% CI 1.011–1.057, p = 0.004). The association was graded, with the steepest relative increase at lower Hcy levels and a plateau at higher levels (restricted cubic spline; non-linearity p = 0.054, borderline), and was not statistically significant at Hcy ≥ 20 or ≥ 25 μmol/L. Combining Hcy with Lp-PLA2, NIHSS, and β2-MG improved discrimination (AUC = 0.748, an apparent estimate that was not externally validated). In an exploratory counterfactual mediation analysis the proportion mediated was small (≈ 4% via NIHSS and ≈ 2% via Lp-PLA2). Discussion Elevated Hcy is associated with PSCI in this pooled analysis, and the association persisted in Cohort B after adjustment for age, sex, education and infarct laterality. The relationship was graded rather than sharply thresholded. As an observational finding, and given the absence of folate, vitamin B12 and renal-function data and the neutral results of B-vitamin trials such as VITATOPS, Hcy is best regarded as a risk marker rather than a proven causal target; dedicated trials are needed before any clinical recommendation.

title: A Cognitive Predictive Model of Air Traffic Controller’s Mental States
ce05181c1ef1dba04d9ea2ac5526e526b2ee6786.abstract: This paper presents the development and implementation of a psychological model aimed at predicting the mental states of air traffic controllers (ATCOs). The proposed model aims to advance human–machine collaboration in air traffic management by enabling the precise prediction of critical operator cognitive and affective states, including mental workload, fatigue, stress, and attentional engagement. By formally integrating core cognitive processes—namely perception, comprehension, and decision-making—within its architecture, the model provides a principled framework for the continuous monitoring and real-time adaptation of support systems. Such adaptive capabilities are intended to optimize the allocation of assistance provided by artificial agents, thereby strengthening human–system coordination and contributing to enhanced operational safety and efficiency within the complex and highly dynamic environment of air traffic control. To estimate the parameters of the model, several air traffic simulations were conducted with expert controllers. In these simulations changes to traffic situations were introduced. Those changes could affect the controllers' mental states. The results of these changes were observed in the measured verbal and psychophysiological dependent variables. This paper presents results that partially validate the initial parameters of the models. These results will contribute to a future improvement of the model by refining the parameters of the proposed formulas for calculating mental workload, fatigue, stress, and vigilance in the air traffic control task.

title: Memory and Time-Varying Activity in Batch Microbial Growth: A <em>ψ</em>-Fractional Monod Model Tested on Substrate–Biomass and Open Growth Data
446b7c2a4e47663f693889137401f6d02236fc5a.abstract: Batch cultures often show features that the Monod model cannot reproduce: lag phases, residual substrate and loss of cellular activity. Fractional-order extensions are increasingly proposed to capture such effects, but they are rarely tested against data. We formulate a ψ-fractional Monod model in which the order θ represents memory of the cells’ physiological history and a parameter β represents a time-varying activity. The model conserves mass, keeps concentrations positive, contains Monod kinetics as a special case and, without cell decay, predicts residual substrate if and only if activity declines (β > 0). We compare it with the Monod, Baranyi–Roberts, Weibull and tailing models on synthetic substrate–biomass data, a tequila batch fermentation and 43 open growth and survival curves, using information criteria, profile likelihoods and forecasting. With joint substrate–biomass data, the model recovers memory and deactivation where the Monod model returns biased kinetic constants. In the tequila fermentation, which stalls with 5.5% of the sugar unconsumed, it reproduces the stall with an identifiable order (θ = 0.54; 95% interval 0.40–0.67), but Monod kinetics with ethanol inhibition is equally supported. With biomass data alone, the order is not identifiable and the Baranyi–Roberts model forecasts better. We conclude with practical guidelines for model selection.
