title: Peer Review Report For: Omnichannel retailing, service quality, brand trust, and customer brand engagement as drivers of brand advocacy in Indonesian health care services: A cross-sectional PLS-SEM study [version 1; peer review: 1 approved, 1 approved with reservations]
Cognitive Metaphors as a Means of Persuasive Influence in Texts of Various Genres
container-title: Journal of Management Practices, Humanities and Social Sciences
82422fddc0741ef8edb2c1df403a0499c983b067.abstract: The present research is dedicated to the effectiveness of cognitive metaphors as a means of persuasion in political, media, and artistic discourses. Even though numerous studies have already been conducted on metaphorical conceptualization in particular discourse types, comparisons of metaphor structure, function, and audience reactions are rare. In the present study, 30 English texts (published between 2020 and 2024) belonging to the genre of political speech, media, and art (10 texts in each genre) were selected among materials from political databases, English-language magazines and literary journals. 90 people aged 20-35 (M = 26.2) evaluated metaphorical messages using C. Osgood’s semantic differential, questionnaire about the effectiveness of persuasive message and free answers. Content analysis and contextual-semantic analysis, along with descriptive statistics and one-way ANOVA were used to identify some patterns. The major source domains in political discourse include: WAR, PATH, MECHANISM, BODY and GAME, in media discourse: ELEMENT, DISEASE, THEATER, ORGANISM, and WEAPON, in artistic discourse: NATURE, LIGHT/DARKNESS, JOURNEY, BODY, and EVERYDAY LIFE. The research revealed the following: political metaphors have a tendency to be normative and rationalizing; media metaphors are critical-evaluative and disturbing; artistic metaphors show better emotional appeal and symbolism. The distinctive feature of the research is a combination of conceptual, pragmatic, and recipient-based analysis of cognitive metaphors. The findings of the research contribute to the development of cognitive metaphor theory by providing evidence concerning the persuasive and emotive effects of metaphor usage.

title: Does the Fama–French Five-Factor Model Explain Excess Returns? Evidence from non-Financial Firms in Sri Lanka
container-title: International Journal of Accounting and Business Finance
a79074a62fdd79b6733ef34fbebefc95a68f6253.abstract: This study examines whether the Fama–French Five-Factor model explains variation in expected excess returns of non-financial firms listed on the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) in Sri Lanka. The primary objective is to determine whether the five risk factor proxies: market risk premium, size, value, profitability, and investment significantly explain variations in the excess returns. The sample consists of 80 non-financial firms observed over the period 2020–2024. Quarterly data were obtained from company financial reports and the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE). The dependent variable is excess return, while the independent variables are market risk premium, size, value, profitability, and investment factor. Descriptive statistics show negative mean, maximum, and minimum values for both excess returns and market risk premiums during the study period, reflecting adverse market conditions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and Sri Lanka’s economic crisis. This highlights increased market volatility and reduced investor confidence. The panel dataset was analyzed using econometric techniques, including descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and panel regression modeling. The Hausman test was used to determine the appropriate model specification, confirming that the Fixed Effects model is the most suitable for addressing unobserved heterogeneity. The model explains 58.64% of the variation in excess returns, indicating considerable explanatory power. The market risk premium and size factors have a statistically significant positive effect on excess returns, while value, profitability, and investment factor do not show statistically significant relationships. This suggests that these characteristics may be underpriced in the CSE. The findings indicate that market beta and firm size are key determinants in equity portfolio strategies. Policymakers are encouraged to strengthen corporate transparency and disclosure practices to improve market efficiency and ensure that stock prices more accurately reflect firms’ underlying fundamentals. Overall, the study demonstrates the partial applicability of the Fama–French Five-Factor model in Sri Lanka’s emerging market and suggests future research directions, such as incorporating liquidity risk and macroeconomic variables to further enhance asset pricing models.

title: A Capacity-Constrained Spatial Equilibrium Model for Electric Vehicle Community Charging on Local Street Networks
container-title: Networks and Spatial Economics
c0bfcb914a5b7ee5a0cff28183dbc6acbd720808.abstract: Abstract Community charging places electric vehicle (EV) chargers in communal spaces such as shopping malls, public parking, and activity centers embedded in local street networks. It creates a spatial equilibrium problem with an access and coupling structure that corridor charging along freeways does not exhibit. Multiple origin–destination pairs and routes converge on the same community charger via overlapping local arterials, so charger waiting times depend on the aggregate inflow from many paths and a single hardware capacity simultaneously constrains feasible flow for many travelers. On the physical network, these features make the generalized link costs non-separable across the links feeding a shared station. We formulate community charging as a capacity-constrained spatial equilibrium with station-level capacity side constraints, and we show it is exactly a Beckmann program with arc-capacity side constraints on a station-expanded network, restricted to range- and access-feasible paths. The capacitated user-equilibrium theory therefore applies, while the community-charging structure lies in the admissible paths and in the queueing origin of the station cost and capacity. We prove the cross-link symmetry that certifies the potential on the physical network, characterize the KKT solution as a generalized user equilibrium with endogenous station prices, and establish uniqueness of equilibrium flows under strict convexity. To solve the program, we develop a primal–dual decomposition: an outer augmented-Lagrangian loop adjusts station-level shadow prices on capacity, and an inner column-generation loop solves parallelizable path-flow subproblems for each OD pair under the current prices. Numerical experiments on a toy network, the Sioux Falls network, and two real-world community-charging networks show that the proposed method consistently attains equilibrium (to the reported tolerances) and outperforms a path-based interaction-ignored algorithm and a link-based interaction-aware Frank–Wolfe algorithm in computational efficiency.

title: Prospective associations between diet quality, frailty and incident cognitive impairment in the health and retirement study
container-title: BMC Global and Public Health
80417bcdac85d08136be021ebebfe83d3bb6e56b.abstract: Abstract Background Diet quality is a modifiable determinant of healthy aging, potentially influencing physical and cognitive functioning through inflammatory and metabolic pathways. Although healthier dietary patterns have been linked to reduced frailty and cognitive decline, findings remain inconsistent. The interrelationships among diet quality, physical frailty, and incident cognitive impairment, including potential modification by specific dietary components, remain poorly understood. Methods We analyzed 1,636 cognitively normal participants in 2016 from the Health and Retirement Study, a longitudinal study of adults in the United States (U.S.), with diet assessed in 2013, frailty in 2016, and cognitive follow-up through 2022. Cognitive impairment was assessed with cognitive tests and used the Langa–Weir classification; diet quality was measured using the Healthy Eating Index–2015 (HEI-2015); and physical frailty used a modified Fried phenotype. Survey-weighted regression, Cox models, four-way decomposition, competing-risk and multistate models, and additive Bayesian network (ABN)–informed generalized structural equation models (GSEM) were applied. Results Higher HEI-2015 scores were associated with lower frailty (β = −0.13, P < 0.001), but not with incident cognitive impairment. Frailty was associated with higher cognitive risk in minimally adjusted models (Hazard Ratio (HR) = 2.27, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.56–3.32), with attenuation after full adjustment. Exploratory analyses identified 13 nominally significant food-item associations with composite cognitive impairment, including higher risks associated with selected dairy products, processed meats, and beverages, and an inverse association with red wine (HR = 0.77, 95% CI: 0.66–0.89). None survived FDR correction. Five dietary associations with probable dementia alone survived FDR correction but remained exploratory. Four-way decomposition provided limited evidence of dietary mediation or interaction, while sensitivity analyses supported attenuation of frailty–cognition associations. Conclusions Higher diet quality was associated with lower physical frailty but not independently with incident cognitive impairment. Food-specific associations were heterogeneous and largely did not survive multiple-testing correction. Findings warrant replication before drawing dietary recommendations for cognitive health.

title: A Teacher's Concerns about AI in Primary School: Critical Thinking, Personal Data and the Fear of Cognitive Dependence
container-title: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
48daf9f5949effd20204e7775dffc33ae168a630.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is already part of pupils' everyday lives and of school life. Written from the perspective of a primary school teacher and principal, this perspective paper examines three interrelated concerns of the author herself. These concerns arose from a wish to protect her pupils and led her to study the topic for her own professional development and to help her colleagues make teaching safer and better. They concern developing critical thinking towards AI-generated answers, protecting the personal data of minors, and the fear that excessive assistance from AI will weaken pupils' thinking. Drawing on a narrative, non-systematic review of recent research on cognitive offloading, the European and Greek regulatory framework, and illustrative examples from the author's own teaching practice and lesson scenarios for primary school, it argues that the fear of cognitive dependence is a plausible concern rather than an established finding for primary school pupils. The available evidence, which comes mainly from adolescents and adults, suggests that the form of AI support (whether it replaces the learner's effort or scaffolds it) may be an important factor. AI is regarded throughout as a valuable tool; the risk lies mainly in the way it is used. The classroom examples come from ordinary lessons whose only purpose was to teach pupils to question AI answers and to protect themselves when using AI. They were not planned as research, no research data were collected, and they are offered as the author's practitioner reflections, not as findings. The author's classroom experience illustrates that such activities can be implemented in ordinary primary school lessons, but their effects on pupils' critical thinking have not yet been evaluated. The paper relates the three concerns to long-standing educational principles, in particular Socratic questioning, Dewey's reflective thought and Vygotskian scaffolding. On this basis, it proposes a simple, as yet untested three-step classroom protocol (``think -- ask -- check''), age-appropriate data protection rules, and a role for school leadership, and outlines questions for future research.

title: “The promise with respect to Ethiopia cannot fail”
container-title: Journal of Language and Politics
8974a7dc2c3776156a6947a2de4c2c5cf97473c4.abstract: Abstract This study investigates biblical allusion in Joseph Jenkins Roberts’ inaugural addresses through the Entrenchment-and-Conventionalization Model. In accordance with this model, allusion is considered as a phenomenon that emerges out of the interaction of the intentional activation on the part of the speaker — through linguistic markers of any length — of a network of entrenched associations and regularities of linguistic behavior assumed to be shared with the audience. This definition is applied to the corpus of inaugural speeches delivered by Roberts during his first and second tenure as the President of Liberia. The findings show that Roberts utilizes entrenched associations and conventionalized conformity profiles that, together, make biblical allusions accessible and recognizable to his audience. These allusions plot a narrative that becomes an organizing principle for the self-understanding of a people, from the foundation to the fiery trial of exile, from deliverance to the eschatological fulfilment of Ethiopia.

title: The personal side of cognitive effort
container-title: Translation, Cognition & Behavior
Translation, Cognition and Behavior
ae01894e5cbb76871e2d262fad88c10d8b1365d0.abstract: Abstract This study investigates whether the Need for Cognition (NFC), an individual’s inclination to engage in mentally challenging tasks, predicts cognitive effort in translation and moderates how effort scales with text readability. Twenty-one native Arabic-speaking translators completed the 18-item NFC scale and translated six English texts of varying readability; eight eye-tracking and keylogging indicators captured their effort. Robust linear mixed-effects models showed limited direct effects of NFC, with marginal positive associations with character insertions and source-text reading time. NFC played a clearer role as a moderator. On the second-hardest-to-read text, high-NFC translators made more deletions and insertions and had longer production times than low-NFC peers. On the hardest-to-read text, high-NFC translators spent longer reading the source text. These findings suggest that translation process research accounts of effort should incorporate stable motivational dispositions alongside source-text demands. Given the modest sample, the findings are exploratory and require replication.

title: Managing impressions, mediating conflict
container-title: Journal of Language Aggression and Conflict
05c5f778cfe465712da48b1a7d1017c2235f3c16.abstract: Abstract Using critical discourse analysis, this study examines how mediators in China’s aging family conflicts use impression management strategies to construct professional authority in the setting of televised mediation, and reveals the cultural-ideological underpinnings of this practice. The research finds that mediators manage their impressions as a safe third party and moral-technical authority through a composite strategy system of emotional foundation, authoritative intervention, and boundary maintenance. The core mechanism of their practice lies in acting as cultural-ethical translators, reframing modern rights-based claims on support and property into sentiment-reason issues aligned with indigenous ethics like filial piety and family harmony. The study indicates that while this culturally embedded impression management model can effectively facilitate reconciliation, it may also moralize individual responsibility for structural intergenerational contradictions, producing a depoliticization effect. Theoretically, this study expands impression management theory by situating it within the high-emotion, relationship-intensive, and semi-institutionalized context of televised family mediation, and through dialogue with mainstream value-neutral models, argues for the cultural embeddedness of mediation practice and its inherent normative tensions.

title: The Contribution of Artificial Intelligence to the Functions of the Project Portfolio Manager
container-title: International Business Research
c883aecdbbf9e0d59266659ed87e70b72ffddeb3.abstract: Project Portfolio Management (PPM) occupies a strategic position in organizations, which must select, prioritize, and manage initiatives aligned with their objectives. However, increasing business complexity, uncertainty, resource pressure, and project proliferation make the portfolio manager&rsquo;s role particularly demanding. Portfolio managers must analyze large volumes of data, anticipate risks, optimize resource allocation, and support strategic decision-making. Faced with these growing responsibilities and information volumes, organizations are increasingly turning to technological solutions capable of supporting, automating, or improving some of these functions, particularly artificial intelligence (AI). The integration of AI into PPM, however, raises challenges that extend beyond technology and may influence its ability to reduce managerial workload. This study explores the contribution of AI to decision-making in project portfolio management and examines how it can support portfolio managers. Following a PRISMA selection process, fifteen publications were retained for a critical literature review examining contributions, limitations, and conditions for successful AI integration into PPM. The analysis examines recurring themes, methodological approaches, proposed solutions, developed tools, points of convergence and divergence, and common limitations. Based on this synthesis, the study proposes an integrated conceptual model linking organizational preconditions, AI capabilities, PPM functions, managerial effects, and human oversight and governance. Practical recommendations are also formulated to help organizations strengthen decision-making capabilities, improve portfolio management processes, and responsibly use AI to support portfolio managers.

title: Penerapan Artificial Intelligence dan Big Data dalam Akuntansi: Sebuah Tinjauan Literatur Sistematis atas Peluang, Risiko, dan Agenda Riset Masa Depan
container-title: ABIS: Accounting and Business Information Systems Journal
106dba1fb4be766e2878afdbe3fece74c738565a.abstract: Artikel ini mengkaji transformasi mendasar dalam praktik akuntansi dan keuangan akibat integrasi Artificial Intelligence (AI) dan Big Data. Digitalisasi telah mengubah sistem keuangan konvensional dari pendekatan manual menuju otomatisasi cerdas dan pengambilan keputusan berbasis data, sehingga penting dikaji bagaimana AI dan Big Data mentransformasi praktik akuntansi tradisional serta peluang dan tantangan apa yang dihadapi profesi akuntan dalam mengadopsinya. Kebaruan penelitian ini terletak pada pendekatan tinjauan literatur sistematis yang mengintegrasikan berbagai domain aplikasi AI dalam akuntansi, mulai dari audit, pelaporan keuangan, deteksi fraud, hingga perpajakan, serta mengidentifikasi kesenjangan penelitian yang belum banyak dieksplorasi, khususnya dalam konteks negara berkembang seperti Indonesia. Penelitian menggunakan metode tinjauan literatur sistematis mengikuti protokol PRISMA, dengan menganalisis artikel peer-reviewed berbahasa Inggris yang dipublikasikan antara tahun 2018 hingga 2025. Data diperoleh dari database Scopus dan Web of Science, difokuskan pada artikel jurnal, tinjauan, dan prosiding konferensi yang membahas aplikasi AI dan Big Data dalam akuntansi. Hasil tinjauan menunjukkan AI secara signifikan meningkatkan kualitas audit, mengurangi biaya, dan memperkuat deteksi fraud melalui analisis data komprehensif. Big Data Analytics memungkinkan pemrosesan data real-time yang meningkatkan akurasi peramalan keuangan dan pengambilan keputusan strategis. Namun, tantangan seperti biaya implementasi tinggi, kekhawatiran privasi data, bias algoritma, dan kesenjangan keterampilan tetap menjadi hambatan signifikan. AI dan Big Data memiliki potensi transformatif untuk merevolusi praktik akuntansi, namun adopsi yang efektif memerlukan penanganan tantangan struktural, etis, dan pendidikan. Akuntan masa depan perlu bertransisi dari peran pencatat transaksi menjadi analis strategis dan pengawas sistem AI.

title: Designing the Future: Leadership and AI
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
48d1a912943fae642bf3d6ccadf6945742236023.abstract: This chapter explores the evolving, reciprocal relationship between leadership and augmented/artificial intelligence (AI) across individual, team, organizational, and societal levels. While we use the term AI throughout in recognition of its widespread usage, we acknowledge the growing preference for augmented intelligence – a framing advanced by leaders in human–machine teaming, such as Paul G. Kaminski (2020), which emphasizes cognitive extension and human–AI partnership. Just as leadership helped shape – and was reshaped by – the Agricultural, Industrial, and Information Ages, the emerging Age of AI demands a renewed focus on human values and moral courage. Far from a neutral tool, AI reflects the intentions of its designers and the integrity of its leaders, and in turn, transforms how we work, relate, and lead. Grounded in authentic and moral leadership theory, systems thinking, and sociotechnical design, we examine how leaders can engage AI in ways that safeguard human dignity, foster trust, and advance ethical innovation. Through a multilevel lens, we explore how AI influences self-awareness, interpersonal responsibility, team dynamics, and global leadership strategies. We extend prior work on efficacy-performance spirals to the AI context, showing how trust, learning, and adaptation can reinforce or erode across levels over time. Drawing on work published in Organizational Dynamics, this chapter also applies the TRUST, COACH, and CARES frameworks to AI leadership. As AI reshapes decision-making and connection, the defining force will not be technology itself, but the authenticity, trustworthiness, and moral imagination of those who lead it.

title: Digital Transformation 2.0: Integrating AI and Empowering People for Sustainable Growth in the Future of Work
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
cd295fcbb5cd4820a5d40948a004a94d7d35cbec.abstract: The digital era has reached a new inflection point, accelerated by artificial intelligence (AI) and organizations’ need to adapt to dynamic, technology-driven conditions. This chapter examines the legacy of Digital Transformation 1.0—highlighting failures and their causes—and defines the imperatives of AI-infused Digital Transformation 2.0. Drawing from relevant case studies, research, and executive interviews, it emphasizes the critical shift from episodic digitization to sustained AI-embedded digitalization. Leaders must enable systems-level transformation across people, process, and technology while aligning cultural, ethical, and operational domains. Digital Transformation 2.0 demands coordinated iterative design over monolithic strategy, requiring organizations to reimagine work as a fluid mix of tasks rather than fixed roles. Human–AI collaboration is a new reality that depends on psychological safety, AI literacy, and digital dexterity across the blended human-AI workforce. Successful transformation hinges on new leadership behaviors that elevate trust, agency, and adaptability while modeling and encouraging the use of new tools. The piece explores decentralized workforce models, the urgency of building AI-ready cultures, and a new social contract. It examines how agile frameworks, value mapping, and upskilling efforts create coherence amid complexity, making change tangible and participatory. The Future of Work is framed not as a fixed destination, but as a dynamic system requiring deliberate, ongoing leadership to combine machine capabilities with uniquely human capabilities. Ultimately, this work calls for defining or reframing organizational purpose and progress: AI can multiply what we value, but it is up to us to define what we value—and how we lead with it.

title: A Cautionary Tale: When AI Outpaces Character in Leadership Development
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
0b2e9c41561f67c0653a2cb28c371eb88152dc74.abstract: This chapter, A Cautionary Tale, explores the risks and unintended consequences of pursuing leadership development and organizational transformation without grounding efforts in ethical discernment, evidence-based practice, and human-centered design. Drawing from decades of experience in the military, higher education, and executive coaching, the chapter highlights how well-intentioned initiatives often falter when leaders prioritize efficiency, image, or short-term outcomes over trust, character, and sustainable growth. Through illustrative narratives and applied research, it examines how misplaced reliance on tools, trends, or unchecked authority can erode organizational culture, diminish performance, and compromise individual well-being. The cautionary perspective emphasizes that leadership is not merely the accumulation of skills or the exercise of influence but a continual process of reflection, humility, and responsibility. Practical insights are offered for leaders navigating high-pressure contexts, including the importance of aligning purpose with practice, cultivating resilience, and embedding feedback loops that elevate both performance and values. Ultimately, the chapter argues that the true cost of neglecting character in leadership is not only organizational inefficiency but also the erosion of human dignity and trust – resources far more difficult to restore than financial capital. By reframing leadership as a moral as well as strategic endeavor, A Cautionary Tale serves as both a warning and a guide for leaders committed to building organizations that endure and uplift.

title: Agents of Change: Teamwork and Collaboration with AI at the Table
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
dcfd8d7ff89f9b704d69b63c67897d2290b5f515.abstract: This chapter explores the transformative implications of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technologies as a “teammate” in leading virtual and hybrid teams. The growing prevalence of GenAI tools and the shift toward remote and hybrid work create a critical need to reexamine how leaders demonstrate essential leadership competencies in these environments. Framed by discussions on GenAI as both a collaborator and a tool, this chapter considers the ethical dilemmas, pedagogical innovations, and practical strategies for integrating GenAI into team leadership. Building on the authors’ previous work in exploring leadership competencies for leading at the virtual table, it investigates how GenAI reshapes trust, collaboration, and productivity in diverse teams while balancing human agency and technological capabilities. Through critical questions, a case study reflection, and practical takeaways, the chapter offers a roadmap for fostering GenAI literacy (LeaderAIcy), managing ethical and technical considerations, and leveraging GenAI for meaningful leadership and teamwork in global, hybrid contexts.

title: Using AI Tools for Leader Development and Assessing Competencies
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
6670b996a20df16f557191ac8831733fc9abb418.abstract: This chapter explores how the United States Air Force (USAF) leader development course (LDC) used artificial intelligence (AI)/sentiment analysis (SA) for leader development and assessing leader development competencies that support learning objectives and course outcomes. A narrative format is first used to describe the engaged practice with key stakeholders and the staged approach process that underlaid the development of how innovation is driving change for leaders, assessing performance specific to selected competencies in mixed reality scenarios, and offering ways of strengthening leader development. A five-phased qualitative structure is used along with content analysis, design thinking, and a grounded theory approach. After coding data using thematic analysis from phases 1 to 4, a grounded theory approach is used to better understand the findings and discoveries with literature related to innovation development, AI technology associated with immersive learning environments, design thinking and change, performance and competency assessment, and leader development. A new theory (AI-augmented leader development theory) and a new model, emotionally tuned competency assessment model (ECAM), emerged as well as emphasis on the power of using dialogic development in virtual contexts to train, assess, and develop leaders. Theoretical and practical implications, as well as recommendations are provided for improving how AI tools can be used for leader development.

title: AI as a Catalyst for Change: Transforming Human Resources in Educational Institutions
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
93d2ee78452d2d36780fedbbf08d870e031b50d3.abstract: This chapter delves into the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and the human resources (HR) function within a public school district, offering a detailed case study of its implementation. It examines how AI tools were leveraged to streamline recruitment, enhance employee engagement, and support data-driven decision-making. The chapter highlights key challenges and opportunities, focusing on trust building and change management strategies essential for the successful adoption of AI tools. Ethical considerations are explored, including the need to mitigate algorithmic bias, ensure fairness in automated processes, and uphold data privacy and security standards. Recommendations emphasize the importance of transparent communication, reengaging employees through inclusive practices, and building trust in AI systems while reskilling and upskilling employees. By combining practical insights with emerging trends in digital transformation, this chapter provides a roadmap for educational leaders and HR professionals seeking to responsibly leverage AI in their organizations.

title: Leading Inclusively: Universal Design Principles in the Age of AI
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
ce20000e654b8aeff35b1155111a8b38d1312b8b.abstract: Modern organizational leaders increasingly encounter artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in their workplaces, creating both opportunities and challenges for inclusive leadership. This chapter introduces Universal Design for Learning (UDL) as a framework for navigating these technological changes while maintaining human-centered approaches to inclusion. UDL’s three core principles – multiple means of representation, engagement, and action/expression – provide leaders with practical strategies for creating flexible workplace systems that benefit all employees. When thoughtfully implemented, AI technologies can support these principles through personalized learning experiences, enhanced accessibility features, and improved communication tools. However, the chapter cautions leaders to ensure that technology is amplifying rather than replacing human judgment and cultural competence. The chapter addresses critical considerations for leaders, including the risks of algorithmic bias, the limitations of automated solutions in complex interpersonal situations, and the importance of maintaining employee agency and choice. It examines common implementation barriers – from cost concerns to misconceptions about technology as a cure-all for inclusion challenges – while demonstrating that UDL principles require minimal investment and generate significant returns. Through examination of both opportunities and pitfalls, leaders learn to distinguish between technological applications that enhance inclusion and those that may inadvertently create barriers. The chapter provides actionable guidance for implementing UDL principles in technology-enhanced environments, positioning inclusive leadership capabilities as essential competencies for organizational success regardless of technological context.

title: Generative AI Powered by Large Language Models for Leadership Development: Between Epistemic Responsibility and the Future of Innovation
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
2befe576d22df3abb8f03a51478516f11ce0d40c.abstract: This chapter examines language-based generative AI, particularly large language models (LLMs), as active epistemic agents in leadership development. Moving beyond their perceived neutrality, the authors argue that LLMs serve as mirrors of dominant assumptions, co-constructors of leadership meaning, and framing devices of legitimate knowledge. The sources highlight how these systems reinforce prevailing Euro-American managerial ideals, often marginalizing diverse leadership paradigms such as Indigenous, collectivist, or spiritual frameworks, thereby amplifying structural and cultural biases. Through epistemic feedback loops and personalization, LLMs can subtly shape leadership identity and constrain developmental horizons, leading to adaptive standardization or performative conformity. The chapter emphasizes the critical need for epistemic responsibility in innovation leadership, advocating for leaders to interrogate system framings, reflect on their influence, and cultivate design awareness. This involves fostering inclusive data practices, participatory design methodologies, and culturally responsive AI governance to ensure AI-mediated innovation ecosystems are just, inclusive, and reflect pluralistic worldviews. Ultimately, the chapter calls for leaders to reclaim framing power and engage AI dialogically to foster an innovation leadership that is reflexive, ethically grounded, and attuned to human complexities.

title: The Influence of Generative Artificial Intelligence on K–12 Educational Leadership
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
2e16eaf81aea3695e6f9f9b263f8c5764ccfa4cb.abstract: This chapter examines the transformative influence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) on K–12 educational leadership after the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. The rapid adoption of remote learning technologies created a tech-dependent educational environment, accelerating AI integration in both classroom instruction and school administration. As generative AI tools, such as large language models (LLMs) and chatbots, become increasingly accessible, school leaders face new opportunities and challenges in leveraging these tools to support instructional design, data-driven decision-making, and school governance. This chapter explores how AI is reshaping educators’ roles, enabling real-time feedback, streamlining administrative tasks, and personalizing learning experiences, while also requiring ethical oversight, digital literacy, and sustained professional development. Attention is given to the complexities of equity, access, and teacher readiness, emphasizing the need for thoughtful implementation and culturally responsive AI use.

title: Inverse design of terahertz metasurface polarization converters based on generative adversarial networks
container-title: Optics Continuum
739abe95c331ed3ee886745c2727c1c6332ce894.abstract: A reflection-type broadband terahertz metasurface polarization converter with a three-layer structure—comprising a patterned metal layer, a dielectric layer, and a metallic ground plane—is inversely designed based on a Wasserstein generative adversarial network with gradient penalty (WGAN-GP). By incorporating the Wasserstein distance and a gradient penalty term, the WGAN-GP effectively overcomes the training instability inherent in conventional generative adversarial networks, thereby enabling the construction of an end-to-end mapping model from target spectra to metasurface structural parameters. The results demonstrate that the WGAN-GP achieves efficient and high-accuracy inverse design, with a single inference time of only 30 ms and a mean absolute error of structural parameter prediction as low as 0.1263. The optimized metasurface polarization converter exhibits a consistently high polarization conversion ratio exceeding 0.8 over the 3–7.5 THz frequency range, corresponding to a relative bandwidth of up to 86%, and maintains excellent angular stability within an incidence angle range of 0° to 50°. This work not only verifies the efficiency and reliability of WGAN-GP in the inverse design of complex electromagnetic devices, but also provides an effective solution for the development of high-performance terahertz metasurfaces, with the potential to accelerate device innovation and applications of terahertz technologies in key fields such as communications, sensing, imaging, and spectrum security.

title: Generative structure-guided denoising diffusion probabilistic model for MR to CT image synthesis in radiotherapy planning
container-title: Physics in Medicine & Biology
cfa98f94b57aed8a928c9fb300f2a97663467510.abstract: Abstract Objective . Radiotherapy (RT) planning uses magnetic resonance (MR) imaging for soft tissue information, while computerized tomography (CT) imaging is necessary for dose calculation. Synthetic CTs generated from MR images (MRI) streamline the clinical workflow by reducing the need for an actual CT acquisition while minimizing radiation exposure, enabling adaptive RT workflows. The objective of this study is to propose a new RT planning model combining stable structure-guided denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) with MRI conditioning, for generating synthetic CT (sCT) images. Approach . The model combines a hybrid network architecture with a dynamic guidance mechanism, conditioned on MR images, to direct the reverse diffusion process and preserve structural details. The model integrates both a denoising and a refinement network: the denoising network predicts and progressively removes the noise added during the forward diffusion process, while the guidance strength adapts at each timestep based on the noise level. This adaptive guidance mechanism uses a non-linear formulation that satisfies noise constraints, optimizing the denoising process while preserving structural integrity. The training process includes a weighted structure-guided loss function that combines the DDPM noise loss with a dynamic guidance regularizer term for sCT image generation via noise prediction, along with a reconstruction loss for refinement. Main results . Evaluated on three paired MR/CT datasets (head and neck (HaN), as well as brain), our model outperforms recent MR to CT synthesis models, showing the best performance in image quality based on the mean absolute error in Hounsfield units, as well as improved peak signal-to-noise ratio, structural similarity index and gradient magnitude similarity deviation compared to other DDPM and generative adversarial network approaches. When comparing tumor segmentation quality, it achieves the best results in Dice score (0.76 ± 0.04), Hausdorff distance (7.9 ± 2.0), intersection over union (0.69 ± 0.04), geometric consistency index (0.84 ± 0.04) and precision-recall index (PRI) (0.88 ± 0.03) for segmented tumor regions in the generated sCT images. Finally, it achieves the best mean square error of 10.1 ± 2.6 Gray (Gy) in the head-and-neck cohort, when evaluating dose planning on sCT, with a conformity index of 0.61 ± 0.02 and a homogeneity index of 0.10 ± 0.02. Significance . Performance shows promise in integration for RT in HaN, as well as in brain cancers.

title: Credibility displacement in algorithmic financial reporting: a critical review of AI, disclosure credibility and capital-market consequences
container-title: Journal of Accounting Literature
18243e89dcb911f6253cee203ff5a4e80cabeb04.abstract: Purpose This review examines how financial-reporting credibility is shaped when algorithmic systems enter the reporting chain. It asks where credibility is produced, tested and understood when artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, large language models, eXtensible Business Reporting Language (XBRL) analytics and related tools affect reporting information. Design/methodology/approach The paper combines a search and screening procedure informed by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) with a concept-centric synthesis. The evidence base comprises a 226-paper curated core and a 144-paper close-synthesis subset. Sensitivity analyses re-examine the 39-record outlet boundary and the close-synthesis threshold. Findings The evidence remains dispersed across research on textual disclosure and natural language processing (NLP), audit analytics and assurance, structured reporting using XBRL, market interpretation, accounting information systems (AIS) implementation and AI governance. Across these streams, algorithms can improve reporting processes but may also alter the grounds on which reporting assertions are accepted. We describe the latter possibility as credibility displacement: model-related output, provenance or validation partly substitutes for scrutiny of the underlying assertion or for identifiable professional and institutional safeguards. Originality/value The review defines algorithmic financial reporting as a reporting-chain phenomenon rather than a general label for technology adoption. It distinguishes four sites: preparation, assurance, machine-readable presentation and algorithmic interpretation. Governance operates across these sites as a cross-cutting condition, making the proposed displacement mechanism more focused and empirically testable.

title: Beyond grades to learning enhancement: development, implementation and evaluation of a conversational AI agent in medical education
container-title: Education + Training
084b6523ad822ed6a663bd21d0cf5dfd788d527b.abstract: Purpose The integration of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) in medical education shows promise but lacks empirical evidence of effectiveness. This study evaluated a customized generative pre-trained transformer (GPT)-4-based conversational agent designed explicitly for a pharmacology block in undergraduate medical education. Design/methodology/approach A mixed-methods sequential explanatory design was employed in a four-week elective pharmacology block at the College of Medicine, Sulaiman Al-Rajhi University. Phase 1 involved a cross-sectional survey of enrolled students (n = 58) who used the AI tool, with a comparative analysis of their academic performance against historical cohorts without access to AI (2022–2023: n = 33; 2023–2024: n = 37). Academic performance was measured through mid-block quizzes, end-of-block examinations, and total block score. Phase 2 comprised semi-structured interviews (n = 9), transcribed and analyzed thematically. Findings The survey response rate was 89.6% (52/58), and 98.1% (51/52) reported using the tool. Among users, 74.5% engaged with the GPT tool daily. Students reported exceptionally high satisfaction: 92.2% found it more effective than traditional methods, 94.1% felt it made learning more engaging, and the likelihood of recommending it averaged 4.65 ± 0.73 (on a 5-point scale). Frequency of use was significantly associated with perceived improvement in learning (χ2 = 15.84, p &lt; 0.05). Academic performance showed marginal, non-significant improvements: total scores increased by 2.5% (75.52 vs. 77.40, p &gt; 0.05), with pass rates improving from 92.9% to 98.3% (p &gt; 0.05). Qualitative analysis revealed six themes: learning support and academic enhancement; efficiency and accessibility; GPT's supplementary role in learning; perceived strengths and unique features; limitations and challenges; and suggestions for improvement. Originality/value The disconnect between exceptional user engagement and minimal performance improvements challenges traditional evaluation paradigms. While conversational AI may not directly enhance examination scores, students' accounts suggest it may support metacognitive development, reduce cognitive load, and foster critical-thinking skills essential for modern medical practice, thereby necessitating multidimensional assessment frameworks.

title: AI Integration in Automotive Packaging Engineering for Multi-Constraint Component Optimization
container-title: International Journal of Sustainability and Innovation in Engineering
31c5e065257fd8076186c66a65576fe16420241c.abstract: This paper introduces a framework for the packaging of components in a vehicle's threedimensional structure that is grounded in evidence and reproducible when taking advantage of the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) tools. The public OSU–Honda CarHoods10k dataset provides over 10,000 3D hood-frame designs based on 109 parameterized designs, along with design parameters and finite element (FE) performance data. The data package is about 45.66 GB, including design parameters and finite-element (FE) performance data. This dataset is not a multi-component vehicle-layout dataset and can't be used for a complete validation of a vehicle packaging optimizer: thermal, service access, or assembly data of the vehicle are not available at the component level. The studies of published adjacent work have shown that an improved solution with 3 times less computational budget could be offered, a result specific to this study but not predicted for automotive packaging. The proposed framework formalizes the placement variables, geometric constraints, engineering constraints, a model of screening by an artificial neural network (ANN), and a genetic search by NSGA- II, where the two objectives change. It also defines a controlled validation protocol to manual and rule-based baselines. There are no new vehicle-program performance gains since no proprietary vehicle-program layout dataset, executable code, or experimental logs for auditing were provided. The applicable vehicle-program specifications and relevant standards should supply acceptance limits.

title: Nitrosyl coordination compounds: a comprehensive review of synthetic strategies, bonding elucidation, spectroscopic diagnostics, and computational intelligence from DFT to machine learning and generative AI
container-title: Reviews in Inorganic Chemistry
fb44627afb7e4316f5fdce03a3394158793f96a4.abstract: Abstract Nitrosyl coordination compounds have undergone a remarkable evolution from Priestley’s serendipitous discovery of nitric oxide to their current standing as versatile molecular platforms at the forefront of modern coordination chemistry, bioinorganic signaling, catalysis, and materials science. This comprehensive review presents an integrated and forward-looking examination of metal–nitrosyl chemistry that systematically bridges classical synthetic methodologies, fundamental bonding paradigms, advanced spectroscopic diagnostics, and cutting-edge computational intelligence. The synthetic landscape is critically surveyed as a decision-oriented framework encompassing direct NO gas reactions, nitrosonium salts, hydroxylamine-mediated protocols, nitrite-based routes, coordinated NO transfer strategies, and emerging green chemistry approaches, with particular emphasis on method selection criteria based on metal identity, ligand sensitivity, scalability, and sustainability imperatives. The bonding narrative is rigorously dissected through the classical lenses of valence-bond theory and molecular orbital analysis, culminating in the modern DFT-based understanding that has revolutionized our comprehension of the elusive M−NO interaction; the linear–bent dichotomy, elegantly captured by the Enemark–Feltham formalism, is established as a predictive tool for rationalizing electron counting, donor capacity, and reactivity patterns, while the non-innocent behaviour of NO-manifesting as valence tautomerism, electron-sink functionality, and dynamic geometric isomerism, is underscored as a fundamental property underpinning catalytic and signalling functions. Spectroscopic characterisation is presented as an integrated diagnostic toolkit wherein complementary techniques, including IR and Raman vibrational spectroscopy, UV–Vis–NIR electronic spectroscopy, electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), 15 N nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and Mössbauer spectroscopy, collectively resolve structural, electronic, and magnetic ambiguities through a logically tiered workflow. A distinctive and transformative feature of this review is the extensive coverage of computational intelligence paradigms that have reshaped nitrosyl chemistry: density functional theory (DFT) and time-dependent DFT (TD-DFT) for accurate geometry optimization, vibrational prediction, spectral simulation, and mechanistic elucidation; machine learning algorithms including random forests, support vector machines, XGBoost, and Gaussian processes for rapid high-throughput property prediction of ν (NO) frequencies, M−N bond lengths, M–N–O bond angles, and magnetic properties; generative artificial intelligence through variational autoencoders and generative adversarial networks for de novo molecular design with targeted property constraints; physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for inverse problem-solving and kinetic modelling; and Bayesian uncertainty quantification for robust decision-making through aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty assessment. This work establishes nitrosyl chemistry as a vibrant, interdisciplinary frontier where molecular innovation converges with computational intelligence, and it serves as an authoritative, decision-oriented reference for both newcomers and experienced practitioners across inorganic chemistry, catalysis, bioinorganic chemistry, and materials science.

title: AI Literacy and Science Self-Efficacy as Predictors of Senior High School Students’ Perceived Scientific Research Skills
container-title: Davao Research Journal
18124df4420feb678361cb8ce7575b017450836f.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in education underscores the need to understand how AI literacy and science self-efficacy relate to students' research capabilities. This study examined senior high school students' perceived levels of AI literacy, science self-efficacy, and scientific research skills in Lupon West District, Davao Oriental, Philippines. It aimed to assess whether AI literacy and science self-efficacy uniquely predict scientific research skills. The study employed a cross-sectional predictive-correlational design, involving 261 Grade 12 students selected through proportionate stratified random sampling, with simple random selection within each school. Data were collected using paper-and-pencil questionnaires comprising three adapted instruments. Students reported moderate AI literacy (M = 3.22, SD = 0.65) and science self-efficacy (M = 3.39, SD = 0.71), but high perceived scientific research skills (M = 3.53, SD = 0.70). AI literacy was positively correlated with perceived scientific research skills, r(259) = .623, p < .001, as was science self-efficacy, r(259) = .79, p < .001. The regression model was significant, F(2, 258) = 224.66, p < .001, explaining 63.5% of the variance in perceived scientific research skills. AI literacy (B = 0.19, β = .17, p < .001) and science self-efficacy (B = 0.67, β = .67, p < .001) each made significant unique statistical contributions, with science self-efficacy having the larger standardized coefficient. These findings may inform research instruction by integrating responsible AI use and creating opportunities to enhance students’ confidence in science.

title: How Generative AI Shapes Undergraduate Academic Writing Development in Higher Education: A Literature Review
container-title: Exploring Science Academic Conference Series
4e198f70618a461c5743e2b44293df587136caef.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has become part of undergraduate academic writing through tools such as ChatGPT, which can support brainstorming, drafting, revision, and feedback. Its educational value, however, remains contested. These tools may help students produce more polished texts, but this does not necessarily mean that students are developing stronger writing abilities. This review synthesises peer-reviewed empirical, review, and conceptual studies published between 2023 and 2026. It examines how generative AI shapes undergraduate academic writing in higher education, with a focus on the distinction between lower-order writing skills and higher-order writing abilities. The reviewed literature indicates that generative AI provides the most consistent support for lower-order writing skills, including grammar, vocabulary, formatting, sentence clarity, and proofreading. Findings on higher-order skills, such as argumentation, critical thinking, originality, academic voice, and content depth, are more mixed. AI effectiveness also depends on teaching guidance, student ability, feedback type, and feedback literacy. Generative AI is therefore best understood as a complementary writing support rather than a replacement for human instruction.

title: Animating microbiology and immunology: student tool preferences and pedagogical insights in an AI era
container-title: Microbiology Australia
63d557c1bf410d68eb411a71fe3cef9a8ca093dd.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools have changed how undergraduate students approach written coursework, often bypassing required levels of active reading and conceptual engagement. To encourage genuine interaction with course content without resorting to high-stress invigilated exams, a low-stakes digital animation task (2% weighting) was integrated into an undergraduate microbiology and immunology course, to pilot students’ preferences on using animation tools to construct visuals. Students created a 30-s animation, illustrating dynamic biological processes, such as viral replication or phagocytosis. Pre- and post-exercise surveys evaluated students’ prior tool experience, selection criteria and software adoption. Pre-survey results showed that only 57% of students had prior animation experience – predominantly using Microsoft PowerPoint (32%). Key tool selection criteria included user-friendliness (32%), available tutorial support (18%) and zero cost (15%). Following targeted tutorial support for in-house digital tools (e.g. Adobe Express, Adobe Animate, Adobe Character Animator) and autonomy to select Adobe or other preferred tools for the task, post-survey analysis demonstrated a substantial rise in preference for Adobe Express, growing from 2 to 41%, while maintaining high levels of student engagement. Tutors observed that translating biological concepts into moving representations required greater time-on-task, research and deconstruction of study content to construct an accurate visual, thus offering an effective, AI-resistant assessment strategy for science education.

title: Australia will impose mandatory safety rules on AI. Are we focused on the right risks?
Design, Implementation, and Empirical Evaluation of a Human–AI Collaborative Adaptive Assessment Model in Higher Education
container-title: Journal of General Education and Humanities
c4fc7c2df67e25e958c78f59c8dc7e87340a3c13.abstract: AI-supported assessment increasingly enables adaptive tasks, automated analysis, and personalized feedback, yet their integration into coherent, human-supervised formative assessment remains insufficiently established. This study developed and evaluated the Human–AI Collaborative Adaptive Assessment Model (HA-CAAM) using Design and Development Research structured through the ADDIE framework. Implemented in a higher-education Media Education course, the model employed performance-responsive task adaptation using predefined thresholds, rubric-guided AI-assisted scoring, formative feedback, and instructor verification. Five experts validated the model, 148 students provided quantitative and qualitative implementation feedback, and 50 student responses were independently assessed by two human raters and AI. Expert validation provided initial evidence of content validity (mean Aiken's V = 0.818). Students reported generally favorable experiences, particularly regarding clarity and feedback usefulness, although Learning Support and Overall User Experience received comparatively lower ratings. AI-generated scores demonstrated strong agreement with human-reference scores (ICC = 0.898), despite individual discrepancies. These findings provide initial evidence of content validity, positive implementation experiences, and scoring agreement, rather than demonstrated improvements in learning outcomes or equivalence between AI and human assessment decisions. HA-CAAM contributes an empirically refined, seven-stage assessment framework that coordinates performance-responsive adaptation, AI-assisted analysis, formative feedback, and instructor-led quality assurance within a human-supervised assessment process.

title: Exploring the Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Learning Effectiveness Through Motivations
container-title: Innovation Discovery
6a7f63b78e52176bfe56f10390208ae15c23afa7.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is an important learning tool in academia and practice for the development of contemporary science and technology. However, few studies have investigated the effect of GenAI on perceived learning effectiveness (LE) through intrinsic psychological states and extrinsic technological features concerning motivation. This study developed and validated an integrated framework based on flow theory (Flow), acting as an intrinsic motivation with its antecedents, interactivity (INT), and challenges (CHA), and the technology acceptance model (TAM), acting as an extrinsic motivation. Data collected from 112 respondents in Macau were tested against the research model using the partial least squares approach. The results indicate that INT and CHA positively influence flow (Flow), which, in turn, promotes LE and attitudes (ATT) toward GenAI. Furthermore, perceived ease of use (PEU) plays a critical role in determining perceived usefulness, which affects subsequent ATT and, ultimately, LE, although PEU does not have a significant effect on ATT. The findings reveal that joint intrinsic and extrinsic motivation could significantly improve learners’ LE in a GenAI-using environment.

title: AI-Assisted Negotiation Training: A Quasi-Experimental Examination of Buyers’ and Sellers’ Perceived Negotiation Performance in a Used-Car Sales Simulation
container-title: Suranaree Journal of Social Science
ddd15b60d7479b08cb39c441d3870714dc3d739f.abstract: Background: Evidence on artificial intelligence (AI) as a preparatory learning aid for novice human negotiators remains limited in consumer negotiation simulations. Existing work emphasizes automated agents rather than students preparing to negotiate. Against this backdrop, the present study examined changes in students’ perceived negotiation performance, differences in those changes between buyer and seller roles, and the purposes for which students used AI during a simulated used-car sale. The outcome was perceived performance, not economic results. Methodology: A single-group, repeated-measures quasi-experiment involved 74 undergraduate business students enrolled in a negotiation course at a university in Bangkok, Thailand. Thirty-seven students served as buyers and 37 as sellers. Participants completed two negotiations outside regular class hours within a 24–48-hour period, retaining their assigned roles and using the same scenario. The first round was conducted without AI assistance. Before the second round, students spent approximately five minutes preparing with generative AI tools of their choice for information analysis, strategy planning, role-play, or feedback. Each negotiation lasted approximately five to seven minutes. Perceived negotiation performance was assessed using five-item self-report scales in each condition. Paired-samples t-tests and a mixed-design analysis of variance (ANOVA) examined differences between conditions and across roles. Reported purposes of AI use were summarized descriptively. Results: Students reported higher perceived negotiation performance after AI-assisted preparation (M = 4.45, SD = 0.42) than after the preceding non-AI round (M = 3.78, SD = 0.58). The mean difference was 0.67 points, t(73) = −9.23, p < .001, with a large standardized difference (|d| = 1.07). The mixed-design ANOVA identified a significant condition effect, F(1, 72) = 83.97, p < .001, partial η² = .54, but no significant condition-by-role interaction. Buyers' mean scores increased by 0.68 points and sellers' by 0.66 points. Information analysis was the most frequently reported purpose of AI use (91.9%), followed by strategy planning (60.8%), role-play practice (51.4%), and feedback (40.5%). These descriptive patterns do not establish the effectiveness of individual AI functions. Discussions: The findings suggest that AI may provide useful analytical and strategic support during experiential negotiation preparation. Similar patterns of change across buyer and seller roles indicate that the observed increase in perceived performance was not statistically distinguishable between the two groups; the groups do not demonstrate equal bargaining power or equivalent economic outcomes. Students' greater use of information analysis and planning than of interactive practice also points to a possible area for instructional development. However, the fixed order of conditions and repetition of the same scenario mean that practice and familiarity may have contributed to the higher ratings in the second round. Conclusions: AI-assisted preparation was associated with substantially higher self-reported negotiation performance in this educational simulation. The findings reflect students' perceptions, not independently assessed negotiation quality, agreed prices, fairness, or information asymmetry. Accordingly, they should not be interpreted as a causal estimate of AI's contribution to objective negotiation performance. Future studies should counterbalance condition order, include behavioral measures, and recruit more diverse participants.

title: Trust Conditions and Conditional Willingness to Use AI Legal Information in Bangladesh
c1257491bd48d1fdc1ce8673813ba2431c023798.abstract: Abstract A person can express willingness to use an artificial intelligence (AI) legal service under transparent conditions while remaining cautious about acting on its information. This cross-sectional study distinguishes conditional willingness, trust expectations and verification caution using 385 adult questionnaire records from Bangladesh. We report full response distributions, paired comparisons and exploratory adjusted models of willingness attributed to transparent explanations. The willingness statement was endorsed by 337 respondents (87.5%); trust conditional on clear sources was endorsed by 260 (67.5%) and trust conditional on qualified professional oversight by 266 (69.1%). Within respondents, willingness endorsement exceeded these two trust conditions by 20.0 and 18.4 percentage points, respectively (both Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Of the 337 respondents who endorsed conditional willingness, 233 also endorsed the professional oversight condition. In the adjusted original-rating model, perceived access utility (b = 0.275, 95% CI 0.111 to 0.439) and verification caution (b = 0.154, 95% CI 0.060 to 0.248) were positively associated with conditional willingness (both adjusted p = 0.003). Neither association met the adjusted threshold when willingness was dichotomised. The findings distinguish openness to a transparent service from confidence in an answer or readiness to act on it. They motivate separate evaluation of source checking, professional escalation and service use. The study does not identify the causal effect of transparency or estimate actual adoption or national prevalence.

title: Explainable AI for Small-Sample Macroeconomic Forecasting: A Structural Analysis of the Bangladeshi Economy
049567816f4726bd43573fa87c70b94df1df59b7.abstract: Abstract Gross Domestic Product Growth (GDPG) is an essential indicator of the economic development of a state. The GDPG is understood as the annual percentage change in the value added of goods and services provided within an economy. This paper deal with the problem of GDPG forecasting for volatile emerging economies due to structural instability and small sample sizes leading to high variance in both econometrics and machine learning methods. The XAI technique is proposed to forecast GDPG of Bangladesh by using the dataset from the World Bank covering years from 1991 to 2024. After the necessary econometric pre-processing to ensure stationarity and eliminate multicollinearity, five machine learning models were tested. The model with the highest level of regularisation is L2-regularised XGBoost algorithm, providing the best out-of-sample forecast (R-squared = 0.6245). The introduction of SHAP allowed for the automatic global dimensionality reduction, hence the detection of spurious variables. The model revealed structural asymmetries like short-term dilution of capital-labor and lagged limitations caused by the volatility of the real interest rate. In general, it could be stated that the correct calibration of the model made possible by the use of the proposed technique could provide accurate macroeconomic information for making decisions.

title: Risk-Aware AI Procurement in the U.S. Public Sector: Stochastic Optimization and Technology Governance
879c5c856a1fd91683a8a2fd2c01e6b398dcc947.abstract: Abstract Public institutions acquire artificial intelligence (AI) services under established procurement, appropriation, and governance requirements, while commercial offers often state a rate and leave the quantity to later use. Executive leaders, procurement officers, financial authorities, and governance professionals need coordinated decision support so that a required review, a funding figure, and a management control are considered together. The objective is to give these decision-makers transparent, comparable financial estimates for AI service arrangements under uncertain demand. Operational controls and optimization are complementary parts of the proposed solution. The framework maps the reviewed rules onto subscription, consumption-based, prepaid-credit, and hybrid arrangements and labels each step as a legal requirement, a point the reviewed sources do not settle, or a recommended management practice. Ceilings, quotas, usage alerts, incremental funding, and named human approval are recommended practices, not Texas mandates. The proposed governance-constrained, riskaware decision optimization framework supports executive and institutional decision-making under uncertain AI consumption, financial exposure, and public-sector procurement requirements, while preserving human oversight and legally authorized decision authority. The model reports expected expenditure, conditional value-at-risk, demand ambiguity, budget exposure, and process timing. The experiments use synthetic data and characterize model behavior rather than institutional savings. Solver outputs are planning estimates; legal determinations and purchase authority remain with authorized officials.

title: Patient Rights Safeguards and Conditional Acceptance of AI Assisted Diagnosis in Bangladesh
bef36896c086d5b6b10e27a269d1e8be0ca284fb.abstract: Abstract Acceptance of artificial intelligence in diagnosis raises questions about what people consider useful and which patient safeguards they endorse. This study examines their relationship in 385 adult, AI-aware questionnaire records supplied as empirical data from Bangladesh. Five diagnosis-and-rights statements are analysed separately because their content and low block reliability do not support a validated common acceptance scale. Response distributions, paired endorsement contrasts, eight combinations of rights preferences, Spearman correlations and exploratory logistic models distinguish professional usefulness, information, questioning, human judgement and conditional acceptance. The statement that patient-rights safeguards increase acceptance received 81.6% endorsement, compared with 56.9% for usefulness when AI supports qualified professionals. Information about material AI involvement received 81.0%, opportunities to ask questions 57.7%, and continuing human clinical judgement 63.9%. All three specific safeguards were jointly endorsed by 32.7%. Information preference had a small positive rank association with conditional acceptance after Holm correction. Adjusted information and questioning coefficients were positive but uncertain after correction and sensitivity checks. The findings identify differentiated endorsement of safeguards rather than an observed effect of rights protection on service uptake. They suggest evaluating communication as an opportunity for participation, not merely notification, while keeping normative rights distinct from an adoption strategy. Mixed respondent status, absent verification of patient experience, undocumented recruitment and fieldwork dates, and unresolved Codebook provenance labels restrict generalisation. The study provides an item-specific basis for further research connecting patient communication, professional oversight and conditional acceptance without claiming clinical effectiveness or tested legal knowledge.

title: Governing Artificial General Intelligence in Future Healthcare Institutions: Risk-Adaptive Institutional Authorization for Clinical and Operational Authority
container-title: AI & Future Society
139dc85cfaba50cf1707ed977b21a84a4f9c8b31.abstract: Increasingly general and agentic artificial intelligence raises an institutional question of authority: which actions may a system perform, how may it combine them, and who may revise or withdraw permission? For prospective artificial general intelligence (AGI), cross-domain planning makes unfamiliar combinations of familiar tasks a central problem of authorization. This article develops a Risk-Adaptive AGI Governance Framework through conceptual synthesis, purposive document comparison, and three constructed scenarios. Four determinants—task risk, demonstrated capability, institutional preparedness, and accountability—inform five authorization gates. The governing rule grants the least authority sufficient for a justified service objective within mandatory constraints. Information, recommendation, and bounded execution permissions can be combined only through additional authorization of their dependencies. A versioned record binds component permissions, configuration, and cross-service ownership; changes to a shared condition reopen affected grants. Administrative scheduling illustrates professional and patient challenges to an otherwise technically eligible grant. Emergency coordination traces partial execution, shared infrastructure failure, unavailable fallback, and conditional restoration. Four testable propositions address risk-sensitive allocation, preparedness, calibrated reliance, and precommitted containment. RAGF connects established lifecycle safeguards to continuing institutional authorization, dispute resolution, and patient remedy. The proposed evaluation agenda examines safety, workflow benefit, equitable access, and the costs of maintaining and withdrawing permission. For future healthcare institutions, preparation for AGI entails an accountable allocation of discretion across services, professionals, and patients.

title: Chatgpt Acceptance among Students: An Information Systems Perspective in the Era of Generative
container-title: International Journal of Accounting and Business Finance
4d2ed33e753ae8bdeeee6ea7126abccc732273ad.abstract: This study investigates the factors influencing university students’ acceptance and use of ChatGPT from an information systems perspective in the context of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). As AI technologies become more common in society, their adoption within higher education has been rapidly increasing․ Students are utilizing tools such as ChatGPT for a variety of purposes, including information retrieval, writing support, and comprehension of complex academic topics․ Despite their educational potential, concerns about academic integrity, accuracy, and their effect on students' critical thinking have been raised. This study adopts a quantitative approach using a survey method to collect data from 650 undergraduate students of the Faculty of Management Studies and Commerce at the University of Jaffna (UOJ), Sri Lanka․ This study is based on information systems success theory and technology acceptance model․ This model depicts the impact of information quality, system quality, service quality, trust in service and self-confidence on system use, user satisfaction, and student achievability, as well as the effect of on student perceived benefits․ In order to test the relationships above, the data was analyzed using the Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) approach via the SmartPLS software․ Furthermore, system quality, service quality, trust, and self-confidence significantly influence user satisfaction and system use. Student achievability and user satisfaction were found to have a strong positive impact on perceived student benefits․ However, information quality did not significantly influence system use, satisfaction, or achievability. Overall, the findings underscore the importance of both technological and psychological factors in shaping students' experiences and attitudes towards generative AI tools, providing valuable insights for educators and institutions interested in utilizing these technologies responsibly and effectively in higher education contexts․

title: Teachers’ Assessment of the Effectiveness of AI and Digital Tools Among Middle School Students in an International School: A Tool for Deeper Learning
container-title: QualiSearch Journal of Educational Research and Practice
3d23d8d784c06aa981f8246e271db5c47577db1b.abstract: This study examined teachers’ assessments of middle school students’ dependency on artificial intelligence (AI) and digital tools and the effectiveness of these technologies in supporting deeper learning at an international school in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. The quantitative correlational study included 82 Grades 6–8 teachers through total enumeration. Data from a researcher-developed questionnaire were analyzed using frequencies, percentages, weighted means, standard deviations, independent-samples t tests, one-way analyses of variance, and Spearman’s rank correlation. Teachers rated student dependency as high across critical thinking, independent study habits, problem-solving, and reliance on technology for outputs. They rated the tools effective for content delivery, student engagement, and academic performance, but less effective for skill development and for deeper learning overall. Selected dependency ratings differed by sex, educational attainment, and frequency of tool use. Effectiveness ratings differed by frequency of use. Perceived dependency and effectiveness were moderately and positively associated (ρ = .537, p < .001). These findings informed the Deeper Learning Pathway, a proposed school-based program that pairs guided use of AI and digital tools with opportunities for independent reasoning and problem-solving.
